task_statements.title: What makes a system an agent (vs. a plain LLM call or chatbot)
The perceive-reason-act loop and agent control flow
Agent types: reactive, deliberative, and hybrid architectures
ReAct and interleaving reasoning with action
Task decomposition and planning (plan-and-execute, tree-of-thought)
Reflection and self-critique loops
Handling uncertainty, ambiguity, and reasoning errors
Why agents need tools: grounding, fresh information, and real-world actions
Tool selection and invocation strategies
Tool-use failure modes and recovery strategies
Short-term/working memory vs. long-term memory
Episodic, semantic, and procedural memory for agents
Memory retrieval, relevance, and forgetting
Why and when to decompose into multiple agents
Coordination patterns: orchestrator-worker, debate, hierarchical
Communication protocols and shared state between agents
Emergent behavior and failure modes in multi-agent systems
Evaluating agent performance: task success, efficiency, robustness
Safety risks specific to autonomous agents (tool misuse, goal misgeneralization)
Guardrails, human oversight, and alignment techniques

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A single fixed call with no loop or decision point about further action is not agentic, regardless of how sophisticated the model behind it is.
explanation.why_correct: Agency requires the system to decide what to do next across some number of steps; a single fixed prompt-to-completion call has no decision point about subsequent actions, so there is no autonomy being exercised.

why_incorrect.A: Response speed is unrelated to whether a system exhibits autonomous decision-making.
why_incorrect.B: Language models are the typical reasoning core of agentic systems; the issue is the absence of a decision loop around the model, not the model's presence.
why_incorrect.C: Token count has no bearing on whether a system is agentic; agency is about decision-making structure, not response length.

options.text: It responds too quickly to be an agent
It uses a language model, and language models can never be part of an agent
It does not use enough tokens to qualify as agentic
It has no autonomy over deciding its own next step -- there is only one fixed step

questions.stem: A system takes a user's question, sends it to an LLM in a single call, and returns the completion directly to the user with no further processing. Why is this NOT considered an agent?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A fixed sequence of LLM calls executed the same way regardless of input is a prompt chain (workflow), not an agent -- agentic classification depends on whether the control flow is decided at runtime, not on how many steps exist.
explanation.why_correct: Because the sequence, count, and order of steps are fixed in advance and never change based on input or intermediate results, this is a fixed prompt chain -- a workflow, not an agent, despite using multiple LLM calls.

why_incorrect.A: Three LLM calls happening does not mean three autonomous decisions were made; the sequence was predetermined by the developer, not chosen by the model at runtime.
why_incorrect.C: Step count alone does not determine position on the agentic spectrum; a router that dynamically selects among branches exhibits more runtime decision-making than this fixed three-step chain, even with fewer total steps.
why_incorrect.D: The choice of underlying LLM has no bearing on whether the system's control flow is fixed or dynamic -- the architecture, not the model, determines agentic classification.

options.text: Fully agentic, because it makes three decisions
Not agentic -- it is a fixed prompt chain with no runtime decision-making
More agentic than a router, because it has more steps
Impossible to classify without knowing which LLM is used

questions.stem: A system always executes exactly three LLM calls in a fixed order (summarize, translate, format) regardless of the input or intermediate results. Where does this system sit on the agentic spectrum?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The minimal agent loop needs a decision-maker, an action space, observation/feedback, and a stopping condition -- memory and planning are valuable additions layered on top, not strict requirements.
explanation.why_correct: Long-term persistent memory is a common and valuable enhancement to agentic systems, but it is not one of the strictly minimal required components -- a reactive agent can loop through reasoning, action, and observation within a single task without any memory that persists beyond that task.

why_incorrect.A: A defined action space is required because the agent must have some set of possible actions to choose from; without one, there is nothing for the reasoning core to select.
why_incorrect.B: A reasoning core that decides the next action is a minimum requirement -- without it, there is no decision-making loop at all.
why_incorrect.D: A termination condition is required to prevent the agent loop from running indefinitely; without one, the system has no way to know when the task is complete.

options.text: A defined action space of things the agent can do
A reasoning core that decides what action to take
A long-term memory store that persists across sessions
A termination condition that determines when to stop

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the minimum functional components typically required for a system to be considered a complete agent?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A single LLM call's knowledge is frozen at training time plus whatever is in the prompt -- anything requiring live or private data needs an external lookup, which is exactly the gap tool-using agents are designed to fill.
explanation.why_correct: A single LLM call can only draw on what it learned during training plus whatever is included in the prompt; it has no built-in mechanism to fetch live, current data such as today's stock price unless something external (like a tool call) supplies that information.

why_incorrect.A: There is no general legal filtering of stock-price questions across language models; the limitation described is about knowledge access, not content policy.
why_incorrect.B: Representing a number like a stock price is not a complexity problem for language models; the issue is lack of access to current data, not an inability to represent numeric values.
why_incorrect.C: Language models routinely output numeric text; there is no physical limitation preventing this.

options.text: Stock-related questions are filtered out by all language models for legal reasons
Stock prices are too mathematically complex for any language model to represent
Single LLM calls are physically incapable of outputting numbers
The model's knowledge is limited to its training data and prompt context, which does not include real-time external information

questions.stem: Why can a single LLM call struggle to answer a question about today's stock price, even for a very capable model?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The number of branches does not determine agentic classification -- what matters is whether the branch set and routing logic were fixed in advance (workflow) or decided dynamically by the model at runtime (agent).
explanation.why_correct: Even with ten branches, the full set of possible execution paths was defined in advance by a developer, and no model is deciding at runtime which action to take or improvising beyond the predefined branches -- this is the defining characteristic of a workflow, not an agent.

why_incorrect.A: Using an LLM to generate a response within a branch does not retroactively make the overall control flow agentic if the branch selection itself was not an autonomous, open-ended decision.
why_incorrect.B: Having many branches does not make a system agentic; what matters is whether the branch is selected by model-driven runtime decision-making versus a fixed classifier mapping to a fixed branch set, which is the case here.
why_incorrect.D: The system fits clearly into the workflow category precisely because of its fixed, developer-authored branching structure -- the presence of a classifier does not disqualify it from being a workflow.

options.text: An agent, because an LLM is involved in generating the responses
An agent, because it has ten possible paths, which shows flexibility
A workflow, because all branches and the routing logic were authored in advance by a developer
Neither a workflow nor an agent, since it uses a classifier

questions.stem: A product has many conditional branches: depending on the detected intent of a user message, it routes to one of ten different developer-authored response templates, each possibly calling an LLM. No branch is ever chosen by the model itself -- intent classification uses a separate fixed classifier. Is this system best described as an agent or a workflow?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: When deciding how much autonomy to grant, weigh the reversibility and stakes of the specific action in question -- hard-to-reverse, high-stakes actions are prime candidates for human-in-the-loop gating even within an otherwise agentic system.
explanation.why_correct: Actions that are difficult or impossible to reverse once taken, especially where a mistake (wrong recipient, wrong content, embarrassing error) carries real cost, are a textbook case for keeping a human-in-the-loop checkpoint rather than granting full unattended autonomy.

why_incorrect.A: The simplicity of drafting is not the relevant factor here -- the concern is specifically about the SENDING action's reversibility and stakes, not the complexity of the overall task.
why_incorrect.B: Language models are generally capable of drafting email text without supervision; the autonomy question here is about the irreversible SEND action, not the drafting capability.
why_incorrect.D: Human approval steps typically add latency rather than speed, since they introduce a wait for human review; this is a cost of the safety tradeoff, not a benefit being claimed.

options.text: Email drafting is too simple a task to need any agentic behavior at all
Language models cannot generate email text without supervision
Sending an email is a hard-to-reverse, potentially high-stakes action if the content or recipient is wrong
Human approval always makes a system faster

questions.stem: A team is building a system to help users draft emails. They are deciding whether to give it full autonomy to also SEND emails on the user's behalf without confirmation, or to require human approval before sending. Which consideration most directly supports requiring human approval?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Goal-directedness is about actions being organized around pursuing an objective across steps -- it says nothing about guaranteed success or a fixed single goal.
explanation.why_correct: Goal-directedness refers to actions being organized around pursuing an objective across potentially multiple steps, not a guarantee of success or a restriction on how goals are specified.

why_incorrect.A: Goal-directed systems commonly receive different goals for different tasks or user requests; the property does not require a fixed, unchanging goal.
why_incorrect.B: Goal-directedness describes the organizing principle behind the agent's behavior, not a guarantee that the objective will actually be achieved -- agents can fail to reach their goals.
why_incorrect.D: Many agent designs can pursue sub-goals or multiple objectives in service of a larger task; goal-directedness does not restrict the system to exactly one goal.

options.text: The system has a single hard-coded goal that never changes across any task
The system always achieves its goal successfully
The system's actions are organized toward achieving an objective, not just producing one isolated response
The system can only have exactly one goal at a time, ever

questions.stem: Which best describes 'goal-directedness' as a property of agentic systems?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Real systems often combine fixed workflow structure with embedded agentic sub-processes -- correctly describing such a system means identifying which parts are fixed and which parts involve genuine runtime decision-making, rather than forcing one label onto the whole.
explanation.why_correct: The system combines a fixed, developer-authored routing workflow with a genuinely agentic sub-process (dynamic question count and tool choice decided by the model at runtime) embedded within one branch -- this kind of hybrid composition is common and should be described in terms of its parts rather than forced into a single label.

why_incorrect.A: Mixed control-flow styles within one product are common and well-understood in practice; the correct response is to describe the hybrid composition, not declare it unclassifiable.
why_incorrect.B: Labeling the whole system a workflow ignores the embedded agentic decision-making happening inside the billing branch, where the model dynamically controls its own steps.
why_incorrect.C: Labeling the whole system an agent overstates the flexibility of the overall routing layer, which is a fixed, predetermined classification step with no runtime decision-making about which category to create or how to route.

options.text: Not classifiable, since it mixes two different control-flow styles
Entirely a workflow, since classification is fixed
Entirely an agent, since one part of it is agentic
A hybrid system: a fixed workflow for routing, with an embedded agent for the billing sub-process

questions.stem: A customer support product classifies incoming tickets into one of five fixed categories using a classifier, then for the 'billing' category only, hands off to a sub-process where the model dynamically decides how many clarifying questions to ask and which internal billing tools to query before responding. How should this overall product be classified?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Self-critique/reflection loops specifically address the lack of a verification-and-revision step inherent in single-shot generation -- they do not fix knowledge gaps (that's tool use) or permanently retrain the model.
explanation.why_correct: A single-shot generation is produced and returned without any built-in opportunity to check it against the task requirements or catch mistakes; a self-critique step explicitly reintroduces that missing verification/revision capability by having the model review its own prior output.

why_incorrect.A: Self-critique addresses the verification/revision gap, not the knowledge-grounding gap -- a model can still lack access to external facts even while critiquing its own reasoning.
why_incorrect.B: Single-shot calls are not always wrong -- many are correct; the issue addressed by self-critique is the LACK of a verification step, not a guarantee of error.
why_incorrect.D: Self-critique applied within one task does not persist as a permanent improvement to the underlying model's future performance on unrelated tasks; it is a per-task mechanism, not a training update.

options.text: Self-critique eliminates the need for any grounding or external tools
Single-shot calls are always factually wrong
A single pass has no mechanism to verify or revise its own output before it is finalized
Self-critique makes the model permanently more accurate on all future tasks

questions.stem: An agentic design adds a self-critique step: after generating a draft answer, the system asks the model to review its own draft for errors and revise if needed. What limitation of single-shot LLM calls does this address?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Observation is specifically about feeding action results back into context for the next decision -- it's the 'perceive' half of the perceive-act loop, distinct from memory storage or final answer generation.
explanation.why_correct: The observation step closes the loop between acting and reasoning: whatever happened as a result of the agent's last action (e.g. a tool's return value) is fed back into the context so the reasoning core has up-to-date information to decide the next action.

why_incorrect.A: Permanent long-term storage is a memory-system concern, which is an optional enhancement layered on top of the minimal loop, not the core function of the observation step itself.
why_incorrect.C: Generating the final answer is the job of the reasoning core once the termination condition is met, not the observation step, which happens after each individual action.
why_incorrect.D: Model selection is a design-time or configuration decision, not a runtime step within the agent's perceive-act loop.

options.text: Permanently storing all past actions in long-term memory
Feeding the results of a prior action back into the agent's context so it can decide its next step
Generating the final answer shown to the user
Selecting which LLM model to use for the task

questions.stem: In the minimal agent loop, what is the role of the 'observation' step?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The strictly minimal agent loop needs a decision-maker and a stopping condition; memory and explicit planning are valuable but optional enhancements.
explanation.why_correct: A reasoning core and a termination condition are both part of the strictly minimal agent loop -- without a decision-maker there is no agency, and without a stopping condition the loop would never end.

why_incorrect.C: Long-term memory is a common enhancement but not a strict requirement -- a reactive agent can operate within a single task with no persistent memory across sessions.
why_incorrect.D: Explicit upfront planning is one strategy among several for sequencing actions, but reactive agents can decide one action at a time without a separate planning module.

options.text: A reasoning core that decides what action to take
A termination condition that determines when to stop
A long-term memory database
A planning module that creates multi-step plans in advance

questions.stem: Which of the following are considered minimum functional components of a complete agentic loop? (Select 2)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The real motivations for agentic design are grounding (fresh/external knowledge) and self-correction (verification/revision) -- not basic language fluency, which single-shot calls already handle well.
explanation.why_correct: A single-shot call cannot fetch live or external data beyond its training and prompt, and it has no built-in step to check its own answer -- both are real gaps that tool use and self-critique/reflection loops respectively address.

why_incorrect.C: Modern LLMs are generally capable of producing grammatically correct text in a single pass; this is not the limitation agentic designs target.
why_incorrect.D: LLMs process input as sequences of tokens with full context, not strictly one word at a time in the sense implied; this is not a genuine limitation driving agentic design.

options.text: Inability to access information outside its training data and prompt context
Inability to verify or revise its own output before it is finalized
Inability to generate grammatically correct sentences
Inability to process more than one word at a time

questions.stem: Which of the following are genuine limitations of a single-shot LLM call that agentic designs are intended to address? (Select 2)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: If the whole execution path can be drawn as a fixed flowchart before any input arrives, it is a workflow; if the model chooses the next step and when to stop, it is an agent.
explanation.why_correct: The invoice pipeline's control flow is fully authored by a developer in advance: the same steps run in the same order for every document, and the model never chooses what happens next or when to stop. That fixed, developer-defined sequence is the defining trait of a workflow, even though individual steps may call an LLM.

why_incorrect.A: Choosing between another search and writing the report is a runtime decision made by the model about its own next step, which is characteristic of an agent.
why_incorrect.B: Looping until the model itself judges the tests to be passing means both the step count and the stopping point are model-determined, an agentic trait.
why_incorrect.C: Picking among many tools and sequencing them per request is open-ended, model-driven control flow, which is agentic rather than a fixed workflow.

options.text: A research assistant that decides at runtime whether to run another web search or to write up its final report
A coding helper that keeps editing files and re-running tests until it judges the test suite to be green
A travel bot that chooses, for each request, which of fifteen booking tools to call and in what order
An invoice pipeline that extracts fields, validates totals, and files the record in the same order for every document

questions.stem: A finance operations team inventories four internal AI features. Which one is best classified as a workflow rather than an agent?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Autonomy limits are a deliberate risk/predictability tradeoff, driven by the cost of errors and auditability needs -- not a technical limitation or an error-elimination guarantee.
explanation.why_correct: High-stakes, hard-to-reverse actions and the need for predictable, auditable behavior are both well-established, legitimate engineering reasons to constrain an agent's autonomy rather than maximizing it.

why_incorrect.C: Full autonomy is technically achievable in many systems; the reasons to limit it are about risk and predictability tradeoffs, not technical impossibility.
why_incorrect.D: Limiting autonomy reduces risk surface and improves predictability, but it does not guarantee error-free behavior -- a constrained agent can still make mistakes within its narrower scope.

options.text: The task involves actions that are costly or impossible to reverse if done incorrectly
The system needs to be predictable and auditable for compliance reasons
Full autonomy is always technically impossible to implement
Limiting autonomy guarantees the agent will never make mistakes

questions.stem: Which of the following are legitimate reasons to deliberately LIMIT an agent's autonomy rather than maximizing it? (Select 2)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Agency is characterized by autonomy and goal-directedness, not by any guarantee of accuracy or a fixed tool-usage quota.
explanation.why_correct: Autonomy over deciding next actions and goal-directedness are the two core properties most commonly used to characterize what makes a system agentic, as opposed to a fixed function or script.

why_incorrect.C: No accuracy guarantee is implied by or required for a system to be considered an agent; agents can and do make mistakes while still being agentic.
why_incorrect.D: There is no fixed minimum tool-count requirement for agency; a minimal agent could use zero or one tool depending on the task.

options.text: Some degree of autonomy in deciding its own next action
Goal-directed behavior organized toward an objective
Guaranteed perfect accuracy on every task
A requirement to always use at least three different tools per task

questions.stem: Which of the following properties are commonly used to characterize an AI agent? (Select 2)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Each turn of the agent loop follows decide, then act, then observe -- the observation of one turn becomes part of the context for the next turn's decision.
explanation.why_correct: Within one cycle of the agent loop, the reasoning core first decides an action based on current context, that action is then executed to produce a result, and finally that result is observed and folded back into context to inform the next decision -- the canonical decide-act-observe sequence.

options.text: The reasoning core decides which action to take given the current context
The chosen action is executed and produces a result
The result is observed and fed back into the context for the next decision

questions.stem: Place the following steps of a minimal agent loop in the order they typically occur, from first to last, for a single action cycle.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Rank agency by who decides the number of steps, the choice of action, and the stopping point: the more the model decides at runtime, the more agentic the design.
explanation.why_correct: Only the looping design lets the model decide, at runtime, how many steps to take, which tool to call at each step, and when to stop. The single call has no control flow at all, the chain is fixed in advance, and the router makes one bounded choice among predefined branches, so each of those sits further toward the workflow end of the spectrum.

why_incorrect.A: A single call involves no multi-step decisions; it sits at the least agentic end of the spectrum.
why_incorrect.B: A fixed chain runs multiple steps, but the order and count are hard-coded, so the model decides nothing about control flow.
why_incorrect.D: A router lets the model make one bounded selection among predefined scripts, which is limited agency but far short of open-ended step, tool, and stopping decisions.

options.text: A single prompt that classifies the email and drafts a reply in one model call
A fixed chain that extracts details, looks up the account, and drafts a reply, always in that order
A loop in which the model picks among lookup, ledger-query, and escalate tools, repeating until it decides the dispute is resolved
A router that sends each email to one of four pre-written handling scripts based on a classifier label

questions.stem: A bank's operations group is comparing four designs for handling customer dispute emails. Which design gives the model the most runtime control over its own control flow, making it the most agentic?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Chatbot = turn-taking dialogue focus; workflow = developer-fixed control flow; agent = model-decided control flow at runtime.
explanation.why_correct: A chatbot's core unit is the conversational turn, a workflow's control flow is fixed in advance by a developer regardless of which LLM calls it includes, and an agent is defined by the model making its own runtime decisions about which actions to take and in what sequence.

left.text: Chatbot
Workflow
Agent

right.text: Centers on turn-by-turn conversational dialogue
Executes a developer-authored, fixed sequence of steps
The model decides its own sequence of actions at runtime

questions.stem: Match each system type on the left to the description that best characterizes its control flow on the right.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Reasoning core decides, action space permits, observation feeds back, and the termination condition stops; an agent that works but never ends is missing the last one.
explanation.why_correct: The agent can act (it searches), observe (it reads the results), and reason (it writes thoughts), so the gap is the component that ends the loop. Without a final-answer criterion or a step cap, nothing forces the cycle to stop, and the agent keeps cycling through repetitive thought-action pairs even when it already has enough evidence.

why_incorrect.A: The agent is demonstrably calling a search tool and receiving results, so its action space already includes evidence retrieval.
why_incorrect.C: The scenario states that the agent reads every result, so observations are being fed back; the problem is not a broken observation channel.
why_incorrect.D: The agent is producing written thoughts at every iteration, so the reasoning core is functioning; its output just never leads to a stop decision.

options.text: The action space, because the agent has no tool capable of retrieving evidence
The termination condition, because nothing tells the loop to stop and return a final answer once the evidence suffices
The observation step, because search results are never fed back into the context
The reasoning core, because the model is unable to produce a written thought at all

questions.stem: A research agent reads each search result it receives, yet it keeps writing 'Thought: the evidence still looks thin, search again' and issuing another search, dozens of iterations in a row, long after it has gathered ample evidence. Which minimal agent-loop component is missing or ineffective?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Agency, in the general AI sense, is about perceiving and acting toward a goal -- it applies to simple reactive systems like thermostats just as much as to LLM-based systems, which are a more recent and more flexible implementation.
explanation.why_correct: The general AI-theory definition of an agent -- perceiving an environment and acting on it toward a goal -- does not require a language model; a thermostat exhibits a simple, reactive form of exactly this perceive-act loop.

why_incorrect.A: There is no requirement for multiple tools; a thermostat has a minimal action space (heat on/off) and still qualifies as a simple reactive agent.
why_incorrect.B: Agency as a concept predates and is broader than LLM-based systems; LLMs are simply one modern way to implement the reasoning core of an agent.
why_incorrect.D: Logging is unrelated to whether the system qualifies as an agent; the defining factors are perception and goal-directed action, not data logging.

options.text: No -- agents must use multiple tools to qualify
No -- only systems built on large language models can be considered agents
Yes -- it perceives its environment (temperature) and acts on it (heating) toward a goal (maintaining temperature range), even without an LLM
Yes, but only if it logs its temperature readings to a database

questions.stem: A simple thermostat turns on heating when the temperature drops below a set point and turns it off when it rises above another set point, with no learning or language model involved. Can this be considered a (non-LLM) agent in the general sense used in AI theory?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Agentic tool use is justified by a GENUINE gap (missing data, needed verification, needed real-world action) -- when the prompt already supplies everything needed, a single call may well suffice.
explanation.why_correct: If the current price is already supplied directly in the prompt, the knowledge-access gap that motivates tool use is already closed, and a single-shot call can frequently perform the subsequent calculation correctly within that one pass -- the scenario is a reminder that whether agentic machinery is needed depends on what's actually missing, not an automatic requirement.

why_incorrect.A: There is nothing to browse for if the needed data was already provided directly in the prompt; browsing is only relevant when data is missing.
why_incorrect.B: Language models can and often do perform basic arithmetic correctly within a single pass, especially for simple calculations with the needed numbers already present.
why_incorrect.C: Whether a dedicated calculator tool is needed depends on the complexity of the calculation and the model's reliability at that specific type of math -- it is not an absolute requirement for all arithmetic.

options.text: The model would need to browse the internet even if the data was already provided
Single-shot calls can never perform arithmetic under any circumstances
Calculations always require a dedicated calculator tool regardless of context
It may not be insufficient at all -- if all needed data is supplied in the prompt, a single call can often perform the calculation correctly

questions.stem: A question requires looking up a company's current stock price AND performing a calculation on it (e.g. percent change from last week). Why might a single-shot LLM call be insufficient even if the model is told the current price directly in the prompt?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Maximum step/iteration limits exist to bound worst-case cost and runtime, protecting against unproductive loops -- they are a safety net, not a correctness guarantee.
explanation.why_correct: A maximum step count is a common safety and cost-control mechanism: without it, an agent that gets stuck in a non-productive loop (e.g. repeatedly trying a failing action) could run indefinitely, consuming unbounded time and API cost.

why_incorrect.A: Step limits are an application-level design choice made by developers, not a universal requirement imposed by LLM providers.
why_incorrect.B: A step limit has no direct relationship to the creativity of the agent's outputs; it is a control-flow safeguard, not a quality or style lever.
why_incorrect.C: A step cap bounds the worst case but provides no guarantee of correctness -- the agent might still be wrong even within the limit, or might need more steps than allowed for a genuinely hard task.

options.text: Required by all LLM providers' terms of service
Making the agent's answers more creative
Guaranteeing the agent always reaches the correct answer within 10 steps
Bounding worst-case cost and run time in case the agent gets stuck in an unproductive loop

questions.stem: A team imposes a maximum of 10 reasoning/action steps on their agent before it is forced to return its best current answer. What is the primary purpose of this kind of limit?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Match the autonomy level to the task's actual open-endedness -- narrow, well-understood tasks are well served by constrained agents; only genuinely open-ended problems justify the risk and cost of full autonomy.
explanation.why_correct: For a narrow, well-scoped task like querying one of three known databases, a constrained agent (small tool set, bounded steps) covers the real need while minimizing unpredictable behavior and runaway cost -- exactly the kind of situation where full autonomy's extra flexibility isn't worth its extra risk.

why_incorrect.A: Full autonomy is not universally better engineering; it trades predictability and cost control for flexibility that may not be needed for a narrow, well-understood task.
why_incorrect.B: An open-ended agent with no step limit typically risks HIGHER cost in the worst case (unbounded steps), not lower cost, compared to a constrained design.
why_incorrect.C: A single LLM call cannot query a live internal database on its own; some tool-calling capability is still needed to retrieve current data, even if the overall autonomy is kept low.

options.text: The fully open-ended agent, because more autonomy is always strictly better engineering
The fully open-ended agent, because it will always be cheaper to run
Neither -- a single LLM call with no tools is always sufficient for database lookups
The constrained agent, because the task is narrow and well-scoped, so bounding tool choice and steps reduces risk without sacrificing much capability

questions.stem: A team is choosing between a fully open-ended agent (unbounded tool choice, no step limit) and a constrained agent (fixed small tool set, 5-step limit) for an internal data-lookup assistant used by employees. The task is well-scoped: answer questions by querying one of three internal databases. Which design is more appropriate, and why?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Think of agency as a spectrum of runtime decision-making autonomy, not a binary label -- many real systems sit in a middle ground worth describing explicitly rather than forcing into 'agent' or 'not agent.'
explanation.why_correct: Real systems fall along a spectrum of how much runtime decision-making they exhibit -- from none (single call) to bounded choice (router) to fully open-ended (unconstrained agent loop) -- which is why classifying borderline systems often requires describing their degree of autonomy rather than applying a strict binary label.

why_incorrect.A: Memory is an optional enhancement, not a binary gate for agency, and plenty of memoryless systems still exhibit meaningful autonomous decision-making.
why_incorrect.B: The term has reasonably well-established characterizing properties (autonomy, goal-directedness) even though edge cases exist; it is not simply undefined.
why_incorrect.D: Model size has no direct bearing on whether a system's control flow is agentic; a small model inside an open-ended loop can still be more agentic than a huge model used in one fixed call.

options.text: Because only systems with memory can be agents, and memory itself is binary
Because the word 'agent' is undefined in AI research
Systems can exhibit partial autonomy -- e.g. a router with several fixed branches is more flexible than a single call but less autonomous than an open-ended loop
Because agency depends entirely on the size of the underlying model

questions.stem: Which statement best captures why 'is this an agent?' is sometimes a matter of degree rather than a strict yes/no question?

why_incorrect.D: An explicit account cancellation is a clear, deliberate action, not an ambiguous one-off exception.

options.text: A user who has consistently stated a preference for email over many interactions mentions, just once, in an unusual context, that they'd prefer a phone call for this one specific urgent matter
A user explicitly states, clearly and directly, that they have permanently moved to a new address
A user explicitly and clearly states a permanent change to their name
A user explicitly cancels their account permanently

questions.stem: Which scenario best illustrates a contradiction that likely reflects noise or a one-off exception, rather than a genuine update?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Ranking by a relevance/similarity score and returning only the top few results is how relevance-based retrieval surfaces the most pertinent content.
explanation.why_correct: Scoring candidates by similarity/relevance and returning only the top few directly implements the goal of surfacing the most pertinent memories, rather than everything or an arbitrarily ordered subset.

why_incorrect.B: Returning everything regardless of score is exactly the undifferentiated approach that relevance-based retrieval aims to avoid.
why_incorrect.C: Random ordering with no ranking provides no assurance that the most pertinent memories are actually surfaced.
why_incorrect.D: Alphabetical ordering by first letter has no relationship to actual pertinence or usefulness for the current need.

options.text: Ranking candidates by a similarity/relevance score and returning only the top few results
Returning every single stored memory regardless of score
Returning results in a completely random order with no ranking at all
Returning results sorted purely alphabetically by their first letter

questions.stem: Which design choice best supports surfacing the 'most pertinent few' memories rather than everything that loosely matches a query?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Recency fixes staleness at ranking time; forgetting and decay fix it in the store -- use both.
explanation.why_correct: Recency weighting acts at retrieval time by favoring newer information when ranking, while forgetting or decay acts on the store itself by removing or deprioritizing stale entries. They are complementary answers to the same staleness problem.

why_incorrect.A: Similarity-only ranking has no notion of age, so an old entry that matches well can outrank the current one.
why_incorrect.C: Retrieving more items adds more stale and marginal material rather than fixing staleness.
why_incorrect.E: Without a link to the superseded version, nothing signals which entry is current, which makes staleness worse.

options.text: Ranking candidates purely by textual similarity to the query
Weighting recency alongside relevance when ranking candidates at retrieval time
Raising the number of retrieved items so current entries are more likely to be included
Removing, deprioritizing, or letting unused low-importance entries decay out of the retrieval pool
Saving each new fact with no link to the older version it replaces

questions.stem: A long-running assistant keeps surfacing outdated entries from its memory store. Which TWO mechanisms address this staleness from different angles? (Select TWO)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A memory system with no contradiction-resolution policy risks inconsistent behavior, since there's no principled basis for choosing which stored version reflects reality.
explanation.why_correct: With no policy to reconcile contradictory stored versions, the agent lacks a clear basis for deciding which version actually reflects reality, risking inconsistent behavior (e.g. sometimes using the old fact, sometimes the new one, with no principled reason).

why_incorrect.B: With no reconciliation policy, there's no mechanism ensuring the correct version is reliably chosen; the choice becomes essentially arbitrary or inconsistent.
why_incorrect.C: This approach has a real, meaningful downside: inconsistent or confusing agent behavior from unresolved contradictions.
why_incorrect.D: A retrieval mechanism is still needed to surface whichever (possibly contradictory) versions are stored; this issue doesn't eliminate that need.

options.text: The agent may have no clear basis for deciding which version of the fact to actually use, risking inconsistent or confusing behavior
This guarantees the agent will always use the correct version automatically
This approach has no downside of any kind
This eliminates the need for any retrieval mechanism

questions.stem: What is the main risk of a memory system that has NO policy at all for handling contradictions, simply storing every version of a fact with no reconciliation?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Consolidate episodes into lessons only with multi-episode support, keep provenance to the evidence, and keep every lesson revisable.
explanation.why_correct: Reflections are model-written inferences from limited evidence, so a wrong one is retrieved as confidently as a right one. Linking each to its source episodes allows auditing, requiring support from several episodes avoids generalizing from a single outage, and allowing new evidence to revise or retire a lesson keeps the semantic layer correctable.

why_incorrect.A: Reflection writes text into memory that is retrieved into context; hard-coding lessons into weights would make a mistaken lesson permanent and far harder to correct.
why_incorrect.C: Deleting the evidence removes the ability to check or repair a bad lesson, and it discards details that later reflections may need.

options.text: Fine-tune the model weights on every reflection so each lesson becomes permanent
Store each reflection with links to the source episodes it was derived from, so a questionable lesson can be traced and corrected
Delete the raw episodic notes once a reflection is written so only one version of the truth remains
Trigger reflection from accumulated importance and require support from several episodes before stating a general rule
Let later contradicting episodes revise or retire a reflection instead of treating it as fixed

questions.stem: A research-assistant agent stores raw notes from each literature-search session. A weekly job has the model reread recent notes and write higher-level 'lessons', which are stored back and retrieved in later sessions. After a month, the agent keeps steering users away from one database because of a lesson derived from a single outage. Which THREE changes best improve this consolidation design? (Select THREE)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Treat every memory write as a trust decision: track provenance, isolate scopes, allow deletion, and never treat retrieved memory as instructions.
explanation.why_correct: Memory is a persistent attack surface: anything written from an untrusted source can steer later answers across sessions. Provenance and screening reduce what gets in, separation plus audit and deletion limits blast radius and lets bad entries be removed, and treating retrieved memory as data limits damage when a poisoned entry is retrieved anyway.

why_incorrect.B: Dilution is not a defense: a crafted entry only needs to be retrieved and followed, and larger result sets add distractors and position effects.
why_incorrect.D: Being stored does not make content verified; it may have come from an untrusted source, and ranking it above the system prompt would hand an attacker more control.

options.text: Record source and trust level for every memory entry and screen untrusted content before it is written to shared memory
Raise top-k so legitimate entries outnumber the planted one
Keep per-user memory separate from shared memory and support auditing and deletion of entries
Give retrieved memories higher priority than the system prompt because they have been stored and are therefore verified
Treat retrieved memory as data to reason about, not as instructions the agent must follow

questions.stem: A customer-support agent with long-term memory shared across all users summarizes web pages it browses and emails it reads into that memory. Later it starts recommending a competitor's refund link whenever refunds come up, traced to a stored note that originated from an inbound email. Which THREE measures best reduce this risk? (Select THREE)

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Parallelize breadth, serialize dependencies: split along independent branches and add one join step.
explanation.why_correct: The 40 company investigations do not depend on each other's outputs, so they can run concurrently, and the only coupling is the final join. This is the breadth-style, parallelizable work where decomposition pays off: wall-clock time is bounded by the slowest branch plus the synthesis step rather than by the sum of all branches.

why_incorrect.A: Chaining makes independent work artificially sequential, so it keeps the one-hour latency and adds handoff overhead with no specialization benefit.
why_incorrect.B: Giving two agents identical full context duplicates tokens and effort; decomposition helps when responsibilities differ, not when everything is repeated.
why_incorrect.D: Drafting paragraphs in isolation splits tightly coupled writing work, so the pieces would be inconsistent and need costly reconciliation.

options.text: Chain the agents so each one waits for the previous agent's notes before researching its own company
Add a second agent that rereads all 40 companies' notes so both agents hold identical full context
Dispatch the per-company research subtasks to workers in parallel, then join the results in one synthesis step
Assign one agent to each paragraph of the final brief so each drafts its text without seeing the others

questions.stem: A market-intelligence team must produce a competitor brief covering 40 independent companies. Each company needs its own web research and filings review, and the results are only combined in a final summary. One agent working sequentially takes over an hour. Which design best justifies decomposing the work across multiple agents?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Treat each extra agent as a purchase: it must buy measurable quality or speed that exceeds its added tokens and latency.
explanation.why_correct: The task is short, deterministic, and tightly coupled, and the single agent already meets the requirement. Adding agents means each one carries its own prompt, re-reads shared artifacts, and adds sequential delegation turns, so total tokens and latency go up while specialization adds nothing the current agent lacks. The single agent is the baseline any multi-agent design must beat.

why_incorrect.A: Multi-agent systems can use deterministic tools just as single agents do; tool access is not what limits this design.
why_incorrect.B: Total spend usually rises because every agent repeats instructions and re-reads shared findings, so shorter individual prompts do not offset the overhead.
why_incorrect.C: The roles could be arranged sequentially, so parallelism is not required; the real problem is that the split buys nothing here.

options.text: Multi-agent systems cannot call deterministic tools such as OCR engines or schema validators
Splitting the work lowers total token spend because each agent receives a shorter prompt than the original
The four agents would have to run fully in parallel, which no invoice workflow can support
The extra handoffs and repeated context would raise cost and latency without adding capability the single agent lacks

questions.stem: A finance-operations team has one agent that reliably converts incoming invoice PDFs into a fixed JSON schema using an OCR tool, in a short, tightly sequential flow. A colleague proposes replacing it with four agents: reader, validator, formatter, and reviewer. What is the strongest argument against the change?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Create a role only when it has a different tool set, success criterion, or perspective that one generalist would handle poorly.
explanation.why_correct: A persona label changes framing, not capability. A genuine role has a distinct tool set, a narrower context, and its own success criterion, for example the security reviewer gets a static analysis scanner and reports findings in a defined structure. That makes its outputs inspectable, attributable, and scoped by least privilege, which is what separates agents from repeated prompts to one model.

why_incorrect.A: More labels on an identical prompt, tools, and context still produce the same underlying capability and only add noise.
why_incorrect.C: Temperature changes sampling variability, not roles or responsibilities, so it yields diverse wording rather than specialized review.
why_incorrect.D: Sharing everything with everyone removes the role boundaries and pushes the agents toward the same conclusions instead of independent perspectives.

options.text: Add more persona labels such as 'Principal Engineer' and 'Architect' to the shared prompt
Give each reviewer its own tool set, scoped context, and output contract tied to its success criterion
Run the three calls at a higher sampling temperature so their outputs diverge from one another
Pass each reviewer's full transcript to the others so all three converge on a single shared view

questions.stem: A team says its code reviewer is a three-agent system, but all three are the same model call with the same tools and full repository context, differing only in a persona line reading 'Security', 'Style', or 'Performance'. Which change would most make this a genuine role-specialized design?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Explicit roles with defined outputs turn a single opaque answer into stages you can inspect, test, and attribute.
explanation.why_correct: Separating retrieval, verification, and synthesis gives each stage a bounded responsibility and an inspectable artifact: the retrieved passages, the verifier's per-claim verdicts, and the final text. An unsupported claim can then be traced to the stage that introduced or failed to catch it. The verifier also checks against evidence the synthesizer did not control, which is stronger than self-review.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating the same retrieval in every agent wastes tokens and does not make errors easier to attribute.
why_incorrect.B: A writer reviewing its own output shares its blind spots; the separate verifier is exactly what adds an independent check and it still needs to be evaluated.
why_incorrect.D: A shared scratchpad with no output format blurs responsibilities and makes it harder, not easier, to see which stage produced a given claim.

options.text: Each agent re-runs every retrieval call, so the same evidence is fetched three times for redundancy
The verifier's judgments are unnecessary in evaluation because the synthesizer already checks itself
Retrieval, claim checking, and writing are separate roles with defined outputs, so errors can be attributed to one stage
All three agents write to one shared scratchpad, so no stage needs a defined output format

questions.stem: A pharma literature assistant uses a retrieval agent that gathers papers, a verifier that checks each claim against the retrieved passages, and a synthesizer that writes the final answer. After launch, reviewers find unsupported statements much easier to locate and fix. Which architectural property best explains this?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Measure quality, cost, and latency against a single-agent baseline before adding agents.
explanation.why_correct: The multi-agent benefit is real only when specialization or parallelism gains exceed communication, token, and failure costs, and that depends on the task. A side-by-side run on representative tasks measures quality, cost, and latency against the single-agent baseline, which is exactly the comparison needed before committing to the extra architecture.

why_incorrect.B: Demo results for other task types do not transfer automatically; more agents are not a free quality multiplier.
why_incorrect.C: Persona wording does not measure capability or outcomes, so it cannot show whether the design pays for itself.
why_incorrect.D: Overhead is not a simple multiple of agent count, and skipping quality measurement ignores whether the extra spend buys anything.

options.text: Run both designs on the same representative tasks and compare quality gains against added tokens, latency, and failure modes
Adopt the five-agent team because published demos show that more agents tend to produce better results
Compare the agents' persona descriptions to decide which design sounds more specialized and therefore stronger
Estimate the cost as five times the single agent's token usage and skip quality measurement to save time

questions.stem: A logistics startup is weighing a five-agent route-planning team against its current single agent, which already meets accuracy targets on most requests. Leadership wants a decision grounded in evidence. Which approach is best?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: The orchestrator assigns work from global state; workers execute bounded subtasks and report back.
explanation.why_correct: The orchestrator owns decomposition, assignment, and completion decisions using global task state. It can dispatch independent subtasks such as flights and car rental concurrently while sequencing the hotel search after the venue lookup, because that subtask depends on an upstream result. Workers stay bounded and return results to it.

why_incorrect.A: A worker sees only its own slice of the task, so letting it route work gives up the global view that justifies central coordination.
why_incorrect.B: First-responder bidding ignores dependencies and the plan, which can assign work that cannot yet be done or duplicate effort.
why_incorrect.C: Requiring user approval of every internal message removes automation and is not how coordination responsibility is normally allocated.

options.text: The flight worker decides which other workers to consult, based on its own partial view of the request
Each worker bids for subtasks and the first to respond is awarded them without reference to any plan
The user must approve every message passed between workers before the next subtask can start
The orchestrator splits the request, assigns subtasks from shared task state, and holds the hotel search until the venue is known

questions.stem: In a travel-booking system with an orchestrator and flight, hotel, and car-rental workers, a user asks for a three-day conference trip with a hotel within walking distance of the venue and a flight landing before 2 p.m. Which behavior best reflects orchestrator-worker coordination?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Specify what each worker takes in and returns, and validate it at the boundary.
explanation.why_correct: The failure comes from undefined expectations at the boundary between workers. An explicit input and output contract states what each worker must return, makes responsibilities and integration expectations inspectable, and lets the orchestrator validate the result before passing it on or rejecting it for retry.

why_incorrect.A: Making a downstream worker guess from a transcript is brittle and enlarges its context, while the missing contract remains unresolved.
why_incorrect.B: A larger context window does not specify the required format, so replies can remain inconsistent.
why_incorrect.D: Sharing all private state couples workers, bloats context, and still does not define what a valid result looks like.

options.text: Let the chart worker read the SQL worker's full reasoning transcript and infer the result itself
Enlarge the SQL worker's context window so that its replies become more consistent in form
Define a typed output contract with the query, a status, and row-count evidence, and validate it before handoff
Require the SQL worker to share all of its private state with every other worker in the team

questions.stem: In a data-analytics team, an orchestrator passes a request to a SQL worker and then hands its output to a chart worker. Integration keeps failing because the SQL worker sometimes returns prose, sometimes a query with commentary, and sometimes a file path. Which fix best addresses the root cause?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Every retry loop needs an externally enforced bound and a defined behavior when the bound is hit.
explanation.why_correct: Retries need an explicit coordination policy. An externally enforced attempt budget stops the loop regardless of what the model decides, and a defined escalation or stop condition (re-planning, a different approach, or human review with the failure trace) gives the system a way to make progress or fail gracefully instead of burning spend.

why_incorrect.A: More workers repeating the same failing subtask multiply cost and attempts without changing the cause of the failure.
why_incorrect.B: A longer view of past failures does not itself force a stop; the orchestrator can still choose to retry indefinitely.
why_incorrect.C: Hiding results removes the signal needed to detect failure and hands the orchestrator no basis for completion decisions.

options.text: Add three more patcher workers with different personas and send the same subtask to all of them every cycle
Raise the context limit so the orchestrator can keep the full history of failed attempts in view
Stop collecting worker results so the orchestrator no longer sees the repeated error message
Cap attempts per subtask outside the model, and on exhaustion re-plan or escalate to a human with the failure trace

questions.stem: An orchestrator in a DevOps remediation system keeps reassigning the same failing 'apply patch' subtask to the patcher worker, which returns the identical error each time. Overnight logs show 40 attempts and rising cloud spend. Which control is most important to add?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A single coordinator is easy to inspect but limits scale; add levels or partitions when it saturates.
explanation.why_correct: Centralized coordination gives inspectability but concentrates routing and collection in one component. Idle workers with a growing queue indicate the orchestrator is the throughput limit, and stalled claims on restart show it is a single point of failure. Delegating to sub-orchestrators limits each one's span of control, and persisting task state lets work resume after a failure.

why_incorrect.B: Fast worker responses are not the problem; the queue builds at the orchestrator, and adding waits would lower throughput further.
why_incorrect.C: Worker identity is not the cause, and personas do not change the orchestrator's capacity or recovery behavior.
why_incorrect.D: Dropping shared state and self-assignment trades away visibility and coordination, and decentralization does not guarantee resilience.

options.text: The central orchestrator is a bottleneck and single point of failure; partition claims across sub-orchestrators and persist task state
Workers are returning results too quickly, so inserting a wait before each collection would balance the load
Workers have become identical to one another, so giving each a new persona would restore throughput
Global task state is the root problem, so removing it and letting workers self-assign guarantees resilience

questions.stem: A claims-processing platform routes thousands of claims per hour through one orchestrator that decomposes, assigns, and collects every result. Workers sit idle half the time while the orchestrator's queue grows, and when it restarts, in-flight claims stall. Which diagnosis and fix fit best?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Accept 'done' only with an artifact, a status, and evidence the orchestrator can independently check.
explanation.why_correct: Completion is the orchestrator's decision, and it needs something it can validate. The diff or artifact shows what changed, the status states the outcome, and evidence such as a passing build and tests lets the orchestrator check the claim independently of the worker's self-assessment. A confident adjective does not meet that standard.

why_incorrect.A: A more elaborate confidence statement is still self-report with nothing to verify, which is how the failed build got through.
why_incorrect.B: Reading a full reasoning transcript is costly and not reliable proof; checkable outputs are a better basis for validation.
why_incorrect.D: Proposing new work does not show the assigned subtask was completed.

options.text: A longer confidence statement with the worker's rationale for why the change is probably correct
The worker's complete hidden reasoning transcript, reviewed line by line by the orchestrator
The changed artifact, a status, and checkable evidence such as build and test results it can verify
A reply proposing the next follow-up task the worker thinks the team should take on

questions.stem: A code-migration orchestrator delegates 'upgrade the payments module to the new API' to a worker, which replies 'Done, high confidence.' The orchestrator marks the subtask complete, and the build later fails. What should the orchestrator have required before marking it complete?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A handoff moves bounded ownership plus the context needed to continue, not a copy of everything and not a restart.
explanation.why_correct: A handoff transfers responsibility for a bounded piece of work together with the context needed to continue it. Here the specialist becomes the owner of the estimate and receives the policy number, loss date, and photos, so the claimant is not asked the same questions twice. The result is a clear change of ownership with just enough information to proceed.

why_incorrect.A: If the intake agent keeps responsibility and the specialist only advises, no ownership has changed, so this is a consultation rather than a handoff. Accountability for the estimate would stay ambiguous.
why_incorrect.B: Copying the full tool set and permissions ignores the authority boundary. A handoff should grant only the authority the delegated task needs, not everything the sender can do.
why_incorrect.D: Restarting from scratch discards the context already collected and wastes effort. Independence of view is a goal of debate or critique patterns, not of a handoff meant to continue work.

options.text: The intake agent forwards the claimant's raw messages but stays fully responsible for the final estimate, while the specialist only offers advice.
The intake agent copies its complete tool set and permissions to the specialist so the specialist can continue without any restrictions.
The intake agent transfers responsibility for the estimate to the specialist along with the compact set of claim facts needed to continue without re-asking the claimant.
The intake agent restarts the claim from scratch so the specialist forms an independent view without inheriting any of the collected facts.

questions.stem: An insurance claims intake agent has gathered the policy number, loss date, and photos for a water-damage claim, and must pass the claim to a specialist estimation agent. Which description captures what this handoff is meant to accomplish?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A handoff package states the task, the relevant context, the authority, and the expected return.
explanation.why_correct: A good handoff package names the task and its success check, includes only the context relevant to it (the service and the evidence gathered), states the authority boundary (which actions are allowed), and defines the expected return. This lets the remediation agent work without guessing and lets the triage agent verify the outcome.

why_incorrect.A: Dumping the full history and unrelated material buries the relevant evidence and leaves the receiver to guess what matters. The package should be compact and task-relevant.
why_incorrect.B: A confidence score and a label carry too little information to continue the work, forcing the receiver to redo the diagnosis. It also gives no task definition or return condition.
why_incorrect.C: Leaving permissions at the default means the authority boundary is implicit and possibly too broad. There is also no success criterion or defined return path.

options.text: The complete alert history, every earlier triage conversation, and the on-call roster, so the remediation agent can decide for itself what matters.
The triage agent's confidence score and a one-word alert category, since the remediation agent will rediscover the supporting details on its own.
The affected service name and the remediation goal, with permissions left at the platform default so the agent can use whatever tools it finds.
The affected service and the symptom evidence so far, the remediation task with a success check, the actions it may take, and what it must report back.

questions.stem: In a DevOps platform, a triage agent has identified a p99 latency spike on a checkout database and delegates the fix to a remediation agent. Which handoff package gives the remediation agent what it needs to act safely and report back?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Enforce delegated authority through the tools and permissions granted, not through prompt wording alone.
explanation.why_correct: The failure is an authority boundary that was not enforced in the handoff contract: the sub-agent held a tool that its task never required. Restricting the delegated tool set to read-only complaint access makes the unwanted action impossible rather than merely discouraged, which is what least privilege means for delegation.

why_incorrect.A: A larger context window may improve comprehension, but it does not remove the capability to issue vouchers. The problem is excess authority, not insufficient understanding.
why_incorrect.B: Comparing two summaries addresses summary quality or diversity, and both sub-agents would still hold the compensation tool. It does nothing to bound authority.
why_incorrect.C: A prompt instruction is a soft request that can be ignored or misread. Boundaries on side-effecting actions should be enforced by the tool set granted, not only by wording.

options.text: Give the sub-agent a larger context window so that it understands the complaint well enough to judge that a voucher is premature.
Run a second summarization sub-agent in parallel and compare the two summaries before either one is allowed to return a result.
Add an instruction to the sub-agent's prompt asking it to be careful about compensation decisions and to avoid issuing vouchers.
Scope the handoff to read-only complaint tools with no compensation tool, so the action is outside the delegated authority regardless of the prompt.

questions.stem: A travel-support orchestrator delegates "summarize this baggage-loss complaint" to a sub-agent. The sub-agent also called the compensation tool and issued a voucher, because it inherited the orchestrator's full tool set. Which change best addresses the root cause?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Hand off the smallest context that lets the receiver do the task, not the whole history.
explanation.why_correct: A handoff should carry a focused, task-relevant context package. Extra material competes for attention, can mislead the receiver, and raises cost; here the sub-agent was distracted by pricing threads. Passing the clauses, criteria, and constraining decisions gives it what it needs with less noise, at the price of the sender having to select carefully.

why_incorrect.A: Cutting to the last few messages is arbitrary and may drop exactly the clauses that matter. Receivers can read long inputs; the problem is relevance, not capacity.
why_incorrect.B: Structure can help clarity, but models do read free-form text. Reformatting the same irrelevant content does not remove the distraction.
why_incorrect.D: Asking the receiver to ignore noise still leaves the noise in its context, so it can still influence the output. Selecting what to hand off is the sender's job.

options.text: Truncate the transcript to its last few messages, because a receiving agent cannot process more than a small amount of context.
Convert the transcript to structured JSON, because models ignore free-form text in a handoff and only attend to structured fields.
Pass the clause texts, the comparison criteria, and any decisions that constrain the review, because irrelevant material dilutes attention and adds ambiguity.
Keep passing the full transcript and instruct the sub-agent to ignore anything unrelated, since filtering is cheap for the receiver.

questions.stem: A sales-operations orchestrator delegates a contract-clause comparison to a legal-review sub-agent and passes the entire 90,000-token account-manager chat, which includes pricing negotiations and unrelated side threads. The sub-agent's report starts citing discount discussions that have nothing to do with the clauses. Which handoff change fixes this, and why?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Every delegated loop needs a measurable completion criterion and an externally enforced bound with a defined fallback.
explanation.why_correct: A delegated loop needs explicit stop conditions: a measurable definition of done, and a bound enforced outside the agent (retries, tokens, time) with a defined behavior when the bound is hit, such as returning a partial result or escalating. That prevents runaway loops while still letting the sub-agent finish when the validation succeeds.

why_incorrect.A: A self-declared 'good enough' is an unverifiable stopping rule. The agent that is stuck in a loop is the least reliable judge of when to stop.
why_incorrect.C: Repeated refinement requests keep the loop alive and wording stability says nothing about correctness. This option drives a ping-pong rather than ending one.
why_incorrect.D: A successful call only means the tool ran, not that the mapping passed validation. Stopping on it would accept failing mappings as done.

options.text: The sub-agent's own statement that the mapping seems good enough after its latest revision, with no external check.
A defined completion criterion, such as validation passing on a sample, plus an externally enforced retry and token budget that escalates to the orchestrator when exceeded.
The orchestrator sending another refinement request each time until the wording of the sub-agent's output stops changing.
The first successful call to the validator tool, regardless of whether the checks it returned actually passed.

questions.stem: A data-pipeline orchestrator delegates schema mapping to a sub-agent, which keeps tweaking its mapping and calling the validator tool, burning tokens for hours without returning. What should end the sub-agent's loop?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Verify returned artifacts against the contract; on a gap, request a bounded fix with the deficiency recorded, then escalate.
explanation.why_correct: The returned artifact violates the agreed communication contract, so the orchestrator should not trust the 'completed' status alone. Recording the specific deficiency and requesting a bounded correction keeps the audit trail and gives the specialist a fair chance, while an escalation path prevents endless retries or unverified claims reaching the final output.

why_incorrect.A: A status flag is not proof that the contract was met. Accepting unsourced figures pushes unverified claims downstream and makes the later fix harder to attribute.
why_incorrect.B: Deleting the task history removes the evidence of what went wrong, and an identical rerun is likely to repeat the same deficiency without new guidance.
why_incorrect.D: Unlimited retries can loop indefinitely and consume budget. Corrections should be bounded and followed by escalation when they fail.

options.text: Accept the brief because the task status is completed, and add the missing citations during final editing.
Discard the brief and the task record, then rerun the same delegation with an identical instruction.
Return the task as incomplete with the missing-evidence deficiency recorded, allow a bounded number of corrections, and escalate if still deficient.
Let the specialist retry as many times as it needs to produce citations, since meeting its own contract is its responsibility.

questions.stem: A research orchestrator delegates a competitor-pricing brief to a market-analysis specialist, whose contract requires every figure to cite a source. The task returns with status "completed", but none of the figures include sources. What is the best next step?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Give every shared artifact one owner and a version, and detect stale writes instead of overwriting.
explanation.why_correct: When two agents both believe they own a shared artifact, concurrent writes can overwrite one another and the same work can be done twice. The fix is protocol-level: assign a single owner (or defined writers), version the artifact, and detect stale or conflicting updates rather than overwriting silently.

why_incorrect.B: Redundant edits do not self-correct; without versioning, the last writer wins and may erase the other agent's valid change.
why_incorrect.C: Turn order does not guarantee consistency. An agent may write based on a stale read, and shared state does not by itself provide serialization or conflict detection.
why_incorrect.D: The problem is conflicting content, not merely cost. A smaller context window does not resolve who is allowed to change the record.

options.text: Silent overwrites and duplicated effort, prevented by naming one owner per artifact and versioning writes so stale edits are detected.
Faster convergence through redundancy, since either agent's edit corrects the other's, so no ownership rule is needed.
A guaranteed consistent listing, because shared-state writes are automatically serialized by the order of the agents' turns.
Higher token cost only, with no effect on the listing content, prevented by giving each agent a smaller context window.

questions.stem: In an e-commerce catalog system, a pricing sub-agent and a promotions sub-agent each believe they own the draft product-listing record, and both write to it during the same run. Which outcome is most likely, and what prevents it?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Prevent handoff loops with explicit ownership, return conditions, and an externally enforced hop budget.
explanation.why_correct: Ping-pong delegation arises when ownership and return conditions are vague and nothing limits the number of transfers. A single accountable owner, explicit rules for when a return is allowed, and an externally enforced hop budget with escalation make the loop impossible to run forever and make the outcome predictable.

why_incorrect.A: Forwarding on any uncertainty is exactly what causes the loop. With no ownership, the ticket can bounce indefinitely.
why_incorrect.B: Hiding the original description removes the context agents need to decide, making routing worse. The objective must stay visible through each hop.
why_incorrect.C: Randomizing routing via temperature does not create ownership or a stopping condition, and may produce erratic routes. Loop prevention needs structural limits.

options.text: Let each agent forward the ticket whenever it is uncertain, so the most suitable agent eventually receives it.
Remove the original customer description from each handoff so neither agent is anchored by the other's framing.
Increase both agents' sampling temperature so they diversify their routing decisions between attempts.
Assign one accountable owner per ticket, define when a ticket may be returned, and enforce a hop budget that escalates to a human.

questions.stem: In a customer-support system, a billing agent and a technical agent keep returning the same ticket to each other with "this belongs to the other team", reaching 40 hops before a customer complains. How can the coordinator best reduce this handoff looping?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Escalate with a clear description of the gap when evidence or authority is missing and the risk is material.
explanation.why_correct: Escalation is appropriate when required evidence or authority is missing and the risk is material. Submitting a false attestation or hiding the gap would create a harmful, possibly irreversible action. Reporting what is missing and what is needed lets a higher level or a human decide, which is the purpose of a defined escalation path.

why_incorrect.A: Improvising an attestation exceeds the sub-agent's authority, and a log entry afterwards does not undo a submitted false statement.
why_incorrect.B: Marking an incomplete packet as complete misrepresents its status and hides the risk from the orchestrator that must decide what to do.
why_incorrect.D: Retrying the extraction is reasonable for transient errors, but the note is simply absent. Silent retries only delay the decision and cannot supply the missing authority.

options.text: Fill in the attestation based on the closest earlier case, record it in a log afterwards, and continue so that the deadline is met.
Return a finished-looking packet marked complete without mentioning the gap, because the orchestrator asked for a completed appeal.
Stop before submitting and escalate to the orchestrator or a human reviewer, stating what is missing and what authority is needed.
Retry the same document extraction quietly until the note appears, since escalation is only meant for tool errors.

questions.stem: A prior-authorization sub-agent is assembling an insurance appeal. It finds that a required clinical note is missing, and the only way to submit on time is to include a form attesting that the physician approved the treatment, which the sub-agent is not authorized to sign. What should it do?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A safe handoff makes ownership, context, authority, and the return path explicit and observable.
explanation.why_correct: A safe handoff has an observable change of ownership, a relevant context package, a bounded authority (here read-only access), and a defined way to return results or escalate. This makes the delegation auditable and limits what can go wrong if the verifier errs or is manipulated by content it reads.

why_incorrect.A: Inheriting all permissions and memory removes the authority boundary and exposes unrelated data. The verifier should receive only what the task needs.
why_incorrect.B: Treating silence as success hides failures and gives no completion or failure signal. Handoffs need explicit status, return, and escalation semantics.
why_incorrect.C: A state transition that exists only in private reasoning is not observable or auditable, so no one else can tell who owns the task or what happened.

options.text: The verifier inherits the planner's complete permissions and memory so that it never needs to ask for anything.
The planner stays silent after delegating and treats the verifier's silence as success, so that it never blocks on replies.
The verifier's work is tracked only inside the planner's private reasoning, which keeps the interface between them simple.
The verifier is recorded as owner of the check, receives the relevant documents, has read-only access to sources, and can return results or escalate.
