questions.stem: A legal-research platform's planner agent will hand a citation-verification task to a verifier sub-agent. Which design best reflects a safe handoff?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: If no one assigns the work and the global pattern comes from many agents applying local rules to nearby signals, it is a swarm.
explanation.why_correct: Swarm coordination is defined by agents acting on local observations and local interaction rules, with global organization emerging rather than being planned. In this store, no component owns the aisle plan; coverage appears from many agents applying the same neighbor-based rule. That is the signature that separates a swarm from patterns where some structure decides who does what.

why_incorrect.A: This describes orchestrator-worker coordination, where one coordinator decomposes the task and assigns subtasks. The scenario explicitly has no such planner.
why_incorrect.B: This is a sequential pipeline: a fixed order and artifact hand-off between stages. The scanners react to nearby agents, not to a predecessor's output.
why_incorrect.D: This is a blackboard architecture, where a controller selects the next agent from shared-workspace content. The scenario relies on direct local signals, not a shared board or scheduler.

options.text: A lead agent decomposes the audit into aisle assignments and dispatches each one to a specialist worker
The agents run in a fixed order, and each consumes the structured artifact produced by the previous agent
Each agent applies the same local rule to nearby agents' signals, and store-wide coverage emerges with no global plan
Agents post findings to a shared workspace, and a scheduler picks the next agent to act based on its contents

questions.stem: A retailer runs 200 shelf-scanning agents across a large store. Nobody wrote an aisle-assignment plan; each agent only reads the signals of agents within a few meters and follows the same simple rule about which direction to scan next. Coverage of the store nonetheless emerges over time. Which characteristic makes this coordination swarm-like rather than another multi-agent pattern?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Choose decentralization for resilience when a single coordinator would be a point of failure; do not expect optimality or predictability in return.
explanation.why_correct: Because swarm agents act on local observations and local rules, no single controller owns every decision. Losing one agent, or the link to the base station, degrades coverage gracefully instead of halting the whole system. That resilience is the main reason to choose decentralization when a coordinator would be a single point of failure.

why_incorrect.A: Emergent coordination offers no optimality guarantee; local rules can produce inefficient global outcomes. Resilience is the benefit, not a provably best plan.
why_incorrect.B: Decentralizing control does not remove the need for global safety constraints. Local rules can still produce harmful collective behavior.
why_incorrect.C: This is the opposite trade-off. Swarms usually give up centralized predictability in exchange for autonomy and resilience.

options.text: The agents' combined plan becomes globally optimal even when links drop, since local decisions average out errors
Safety limits become unnecessary because no single agent has authority over the behavior of the others
The base station gains tighter step-by-step predictability over every agent's movement and individual choices
Remaining agents can keep working from local observations when a single agent or the coordinator link fails

questions.stem: A flood-response team deploys mapping agents over a wide area where the link to the base station drops often. A design review notes that if one coordinating agent crashes, every other agent stalls waiting for assignments. The team considers moving to decentralized swarm-style coordination. What is the principal benefit they should expect?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: If the decision uses only nearby information and a common rule, the property at work is local interaction.
explanation.why_correct: Each robot reacts only to what it senses nearby, using the same simple rule. The jam-dissolving pattern on the whole floor is a global effect produced by local interaction, with no agent having a view of the full system. That is the defining mechanism of swarm coordination.

why_incorrect.A: Nothing in the scenario involves a parent agent delegating to children. The rule is shared, but each agent applies it independently.
why_incorrect.B: No central workspace or arbiter exists; agents sense neighbors directly. A blackboard would require a shared state store and a controller choosing who acts.
why_incorrect.C: Global replanning requires full-system knowledge and a planner. The agents explicitly lack the full map and others' destinations.

options.text: Hierarchical delegation, because the slow-down rule is pushed down from a parent agent to its children
Shared-blackboard arbitration, because neighbors post positions to a central workspace that resolves conflicts
Global replanning, because the agents jointly recompute an optimal route for the entire fleet each cycle
Local interaction, because behavior is driven by nearby observations and a shared rule rather than system-wide knowledge

questions.stem: In a delivery-robot simulation, each agent slows down when it senses more than three neighbors within five meters and steers away from the most crowded direction. No agent knows the full map or the other agents' destinations, yet traffic jams dissolve across the whole floor. Which property of swarm-style coordination does this primarily illustrate?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Decentralized control still needs centralized safety bounds; safe local rules do not guarantee a safe collective.
explanation.why_correct: Local rules that are acceptable in isolation can interact through feedback and amplify, producing unsafe behavior at population scale; here, mutual undercutting can spiral prices downward. Decentralized control does not remove the need for global constraints, and those bounds should be enforced outside the agents' own rules so they hold even when emergent dynamics go wrong.

why_incorrect.B: Global bounds are not meant to make agents identical. Their purpose is to cap harmful collective outcomes that no individual rule would reveal.
why_incorrect.C: Testing each agent's rule in isolation does not predict population behavior. Emergence must be evaluated at the system level.
why_incorrect.D: This reverses the lesson of emergence: collective behavior can differ qualitatively from individual behavior, which is exactly why system-level checks are needed.

options.text: Keep independently enforced system-level bounds, because feedback among safe-looking local rules can compound into a harmful collective outcome such as a price collapse
Keep the bounds only so that every agent behaves identically, which makes the run reproducible rather than safer
Drop the bounds, because per-agent unit tests of the local rule are sufficient evidence that the aggregate cannot breach market limits
Drop the bounds, because swarms have no collective effects beyond what each individual agent's behavior already shows

questions.stem: A marketplace team runs a swarm of pricing agents. Each follows a rule that looks safe locally: lower my price by one percent whenever a nearby seller undercuts me. Because every rule passes review, an engineer proposes dropping system-wide price floors and spend limits. How should the team respond?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Judge a swarm rule by population-level outcomes; locally valid moves do not prove a good global result.
explanation.why_correct: Swarm rules are judged by the collective outcome, not by whether each move is locally valid. A repeated, population-level pattern, such as everyone converging on one corridor, shows that the rule produces an undesirable emergent behavior despite every individual action being legal. This is why population-level metrics must be monitored.

why_incorrect.A: Differing local states are expected in a decentralized system, since each agent sees different neighbors. They do not indicate a bad global outcome.
why_incorrect.B: Short, low-volume local signals are a normal property of swarm communication and say nothing about the quality of the emergent behavior.
why_incorrect.D: A small latency increase with more neighbors is a performance detail. It does not show that the collective behavior is wrong.

options.text: Individual agents occasionally hold slightly different local states than the neighbors they are observing
Per-agent message volume is low because agents exchange only short signals with nearby peers
Across many runs, the crowd repeatedly piles into the same exit corridor even though each single move satisfies the rule
Average per-agent decision time rises slightly when more neighbors fall inside the sensing radius

questions.stem: A team monitors a 500-agent evacuation simulation in which every agent follows a local rule to avoid neighbors and move toward the nearest open exit. Logs show every individual move is valid and collision-free. Which observation is the strongest sign that the rule is not producing the intended global behavior?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Orchestrator buys predictability and inspectability; swarm buys autonomy and resilience at the cost of global predictability.
explanation.why_correct: An orchestrator gives explicit assignments and an inspectable global state, but it can become a bottleneck or single point of failure. A swarm trades that centralized predictability for local autonomy and potential resilience, while accepting that global behavior is emergent and harder to predict and audit.

why_incorrect.A: This inverts both sides. Swarms tend to improve resilience, and they provide no guarantee of optimal allocation.
why_incorrect.B: A swarm relies on continual local interaction, and its decisions are harder, not easier, to audit than an orchestrator's explicit assignments.
why_incorrect.C: Swarms do not require human sequencing; they remove the need for any central sequencer, human or automated.

options.text: Lower resilience to failures, in exchange for a guarantee that work is allocated optimally across the fleet
Fewer interactions between trucks, in exchange for an easier audit of why each individual decision was made
A requirement for human sequencing of each truck's tasks, in exchange for faster average runtime across the fleet
Less predictable and harder-to-audit global behavior, in exchange for local autonomy and tolerance of a lost coordinator

questions.stem: A yard-logistics team is choosing between two designs for 300 autonomous trucks. In the first, an orchestrator assigns every truck's route. In the second, trucks adjust their routes using signals from nearby trucks and no one holds the full plan. What does the team accept by choosing the second design?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Test collective behavior at realistic scale, with bounds and stop conditions, before and during a staged rollout.
explanation.why_correct: Changing a local rule changes the interaction dynamics, so its effect has to be observed on the collective. A bounded simulation at realistic population size, with stop conditions and population-level metrics, reveals emergent problems before they affect production, and a staged rollout limits the blast radius if something still goes wrong.

why_incorrect.A: Single-agent results do not transfer to population behavior, and deploying everywhere without observation removes any chance to contain a harmful emergent effect.
why_incorrect.C: Evaluating one agent in isolation cannot show feedback or crowding effects, which only appear when many agents interact.
why_incorrect.D: Removing stop conditions eliminates the externally enforced bounds that contain runaway behavior during exactly the period of greatest uncertainty.

options.text: Deploy to the full fleet at once, since a rule validated on one agent behaves the same way at any population size
Run the revised rule in a bounded simulation at realistic fleet size, track collective metrics with stop conditions in place, then stage the rollout
Approve the change from the single-agent test, extending it to the fleet once that agent's individual behavior stays correct
Disable the stop conditions during the pilot so the swarm can settle into its natural steady state before evaluation

questions.stem: A drone-inspection swarm will have its repulsion threshold changed so agents keep a larger distance from each other. The rule behaves correctly in a single-drone test. What is the safest way to roll the change out to production?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Group-level patterns can arise from feedback among local interactions; do not infer a hidden planner from an unplanned outcome.
explanation.why_correct: In interacting agents, memory and repeated exchanges create feedback loops: what one agent says or does changes what its neighbors remember and do next. Over time this can produce coherent group behavior that no single agent explicitly planned. Emergent patterns are a property of the interaction dynamics, not evidence of a hidden planner.

why_incorrect.A: Nothing in the scenario indicates a controlling agent. Attributing the pattern to a hidden planner overlooks that interaction alone can generate it.
why_incorrect.B: Emergent behavior is a known, legitimate outcome of repeated interaction. Its absence from the prompts does not make it a bug.
why_incorrect.D: Identical prompts do not give an agent a global schedule; it would still need information about the others. The coordination arises from interaction and shared memory.

options.text: One agent is silently acting as a central planner and instructing the others to gather at noon
The behavior must come from a software bug, because anything absent from every agent's prompt cannot appear in the simulation
Repeated interactions and shared memories feed back into each agent's local decisions, producing a system-level pattern none of them planned
The agents share identical prompts, so each one independently computed the same global schedule for the whole town

questions.stem: In a town simulation with 25 language-model agents, developers notice that most agents gather at the same café around noon, although no agent's prompt mentions that place or time. A reviewer suspects a hidden global plan. Which explanation best accounts for the behavior?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Audit decentralized behavior with rules, origin-tagged interaction logs, and collective metrics, not just the final answer or one agent.
explanation.why_correct: In a decentralized system, the outcome comes from rules plus the history of interactions, so an audit needs all three: which local rules were in force, who signaled what to whom and when, and how collective quantities such as total order volume evolved. Origin-tagged logs also support provenance, showing where a questionable value first entered and how it spread.

why_incorrect.A: The final output and one prompt cannot explain a collective, feedback-driven outcome. Neither shows how other agents influenced the decision.
why_incorrect.B: A roster identifies participants but records no events or interactions, so it cannot reconstruct how the excess developed.
why_incorrect.C: The largest spender may only be the last link in a chain. Looking at one agent hides the amplification among the others.

options.text: The final purchase order and the system prompt of the agent that submitted it
A roster listing every agent's name, version, and configured model
The full conversation transcript of the single agent that spent the most money
Versioned local rule definitions, timestamped interaction logs with agent origin, and population-level metrics over time

questions.stem: A decentralized fleet of procurement agents over-ordered a component by a factor of ten. No orchestrator exists, and each agent adjusts orders based on neighbors' signals. An auditor must reconstruct how the excess arose. Which set of artifacts is most useful?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: When agents feed on one another's outputs, errors can amplify and agreement is not verification.
explanation.why_correct: Repeated local averaging and rebroadcast forms a feedback loop that reinforces and propagates the original error, so a small fault becomes a population-wide one. Agreement is also weak evidence here: the agents are not independent, because they are consuming each other's estimates. Correlated errors can produce confident consensus on a wrong value.

why_incorrect.A: The values are well-formed but wrong. A schema would validate the format of messages, not stop an error from being amplified by the exchange process.
why_incorrect.B: Nothing here is limited by a context window. The failure comes from interaction dynamics among agents, not from one agent's capacity.
why_incorrect.D: The agents are not independent, since each updates from the others' outputs. Close agreement among correlated agents does not verify correctness and here reflects the error spreading.

options.text: A message-formatting problem that a stricter output schema would fully resolve on its own
A single-agent context-window limit that would disappear if each agent were given a larger window
A feedback-driven collective failure, where each exchange round reinforces and spreads the initial error among correlated agents
A sign of high consensus quality, since close agreement among independent agents indicates the estimate is correct

questions.stem: A group of sensor-fusion agents each average their own reading with neighbors' latest estimates and rebroadcast the result. One thermometer is miscalibrated by 2 degrees. After several rounds, nearly all agents report values 8 degrees too high and agree closely with each other. One engineer says the tight agreement shows the estimate is reliable. What kind of risk is this?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Use debate to expose candidate reasoning to critique before aggregation; it is verification, not a free accuracy guarantee.
explanation.why_correct: The point of debate is to put candidate answers and their reasoning in front of independent critics before an aggregation step picks a result. A rationale that sounds plausible to its author can still contain an error that a second agent, checking the claim directly, will notice. This makes debate a verification strategy: it can catch mistakes a single pass lets through, at additional cost.

why_incorrect.A: Debate does the opposite of saving tokens: every agent produces its own reasoning and critiques, so total token use rises compared with one pass.
why_incorrect.B: Debate gives no statistical guarantee of correctness; agents can agree on the same wrong answer, so it reduces risk without eliminating it.
why_incorrect.D: Partitioning work by chapter is task decomposition for throughput, not debate; in debate the agents evaluate the same question rather than separate portions.

options.text: It lowers token spend because the agents reuse one cached rationale instead of each producing their own reasoning
It turns uncertain model output into a statistically guaranteed correct code once three agents are involved
It exposes each candidate's reasoning to critique from other agents, so flaws that one pass misses can be caught before a code is chosen
It splits the code list by chapter so each agent only handles a portion of the claim and the work finishes sooner

questions.stem: A medical-coding team finds that a single LLM pass sometimes assigns the wrong billing code and backs it with a plausible-sounding rationale. They replace it with three agents that each propose a code and then critique one another's rationales before a final code is selected. What is the primary benefit this design is meant to deliver?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: For debate to find errors, generate answers independently first, then compare them against evidence.
explanation.why_correct: Independence plus evidence-sensitive comparison is what makes debate effective. When agents produce answers separately, a wrong figure shows up as a disagreement; the judge can then resolve it by checking quoted source text rather than by counting heads. Reading each other's drafts early, rubber-stamp approval, or deference to a label all collapse independence and hide errors.

why_incorrect.A: Agents with identical prompts and context who edit one shared draft anchor on its first content and share the same blind spots, so errors are carried forward rather than surfaced.
why_incorrect.B: A request to approve invites rubber-stamping; the reviewers never produce their own figures, so there is nothing to disagree with and little pressure to check the source.
why_incorrect.C: Deferring to a seniority label is the conformity pattern that debate is meant to avoid; it suppresses independent evaluation instead of encouraging it.

options.text: Three copies of the same prompt and context read one another's drafts live and keep refining a single shared draft
One agent drafts the summary, and the other two are asked only to reply 'approve' if the draft looks reasonable to them
Each agent is told to align with the answer from the agent labeled most experienced, to keep the final summary consistent
Each agent drafts its figures independently from the covenant text, then a judge compares the drafts against quoted source passages and investigates discrepancies

questions.stem: A fintech team wants a verification step for LLM-generated loan-covenant summaries and plans to use three agents plus a judge. Which design gives the debate the best chance of surfacing a wrong figure in a summary?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Agreement among correlated agents is not verification; require independence or evidence, not just a majority.
explanation.why_correct: Majority voting assumes that voters err independently. Agents built on the same model with the same retrieved context tend to make the same mistakes, so a 5-0 outcome adds little evidence beyond a single agent's answer. A stronger aggregator weighs evidence and reasoning quality, and the system needs real diversity of model, prompt, or evidence source.

why_incorrect.A: Model outputs can be tallied just fine; the weakness is correlated error, not the identity of the voter, and adding humans would not by itself fix a shared misreading.
why_incorrect.B: More copies of the same correlated agents would repeat the same mistake; the number of voters does not substitute for independence.
why_incorrect.D: Votes can follow retrieval and tool use, and many designs do exactly that; the failure here is the shared misreading, not the ordering of the vote.

options.text: Votes are only meaningful when cast by human reviewers, because model outputs cannot be compared on the same scale
Five participants are too few; reliable voting would have caught the error with roughly ten or more agents in the group
Agents that share a model and context have correlated errors, so unanimous agreement can reflect a shared misreading instead of independent confirmation
Votes are cast before any evidence is retrieved, so the tally can never be improved by adding tools or source documents later

questions.stem: A compliance team runs five debate agents, all backed by the same model and the same retrieval context, to fact-check regulatory claims. Last week all five voted 'compliant' on a filing that an auditor later showed was non-compliant because of a rule that all five misread. Why does majority voting alone fail to protect against this?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A judge should weigh evidence, consistency, and task correctness, not length, order, or labels.
explanation.why_correct: A judge adds value only if it compares the substance of the arguments: whether claims are supported by evidence it can check, whether the reasoning holds together, and whether it addresses the actual task question. Here the affected-version range in the advisory can settle the dispute. Length, arrival order, and role labels are surface features that LLM judges are known to over-weight.

why_incorrect.A: Verbosity is a known judge bias; a longer argument can be wrong, and rewarding length encourages padding instead of evidence.
why_incorrect.B: Arrival order is irrelevant to correctness, and position effects are another known bias that a well-designed judge must not let decide the result.
why_incorrect.C: A role label describes the prompt, not verified knowledge; deferring to it replaces evaluation with authority and invites conformity.

options.text: Which agent produced the longer, more detailed argument, since thoroughness usually signals a stronger analysis
Which agent replied first, since an early answer has been less influenced by the opposing agent's framing
Which agent has the more specialized role label, since stated expertise should outweigh the other side's claims
Whether each claim is backed by checkable evidence, such as the advisory's affected-version range, and whether the reasoning is internally consistent

questions.stem: In a vulnerability-triage workflow, one agent argues that a dependency CVE affects the deployed version and another argues that it does not. A judge agent must choose between them. What should the judge primarily base its decision on?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Bound debate with a hard budget plus a quality-based early exit, never an open-ended or unanimity-only loop.
explanation.why_correct: A good stopping rule pairs an externally enforced budget with a quality-based exit. The hard cap guarantees the loop cannot run away, while the early exit avoids paying for rounds that add no new information. Together they bound cost and latency without cutting off useful critique prematurely.

why_incorrect.A: Requiring unanimity can loop forever when agents keep disagreeing, and it can also reward conformity, so it is neither bounded nor a reliable sign of correctness.
why_incorrect.B: Removing the cap eliminates the external bound that prevents runaway loops and uncontrolled spend; agents cannot be relied upon to stop themselves.
why_incorrect.D: Stopping before any critique has been exchanged removes the verification benefit that justified the debate in the first place.

options.text: Stop only when every agent states full agreement, since unanimity shows that the question is truly settled
Remove the round cap so agents can keep going until some agent finally raises a new objection
Combine a hard budget on rounds and tokens with an early exit when another round no longer changes the evidence-based verdict
Stop after the first round so that later critique cannot raise cost or introduce additional disagreement

questions.stem: A legal-research assistant debates contract-clause interpretations. In the last three rounds no agent has raised a new objection or changed its evidence-based confidence, yet the loop keeps consuming tokens until it reaches a 12-round hard cap. Which stopping design would fit this system best?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: When agents agree without citing evidence, suspect conformity rather than verification.
explanation.why_correct: The other agents adopted the senior reviewer's answer without consulting the policy text, so their agreement carried no independent information. This is conformity or sycophancy: reading a prior or authoritative answer before committing anchors later agents on it. Counter-measures include collecting independent first answers and requiring each agent to cite evidence.

why_incorrect.A: Deadlock is a circular wait with no progress; here the agents replied immediately, they simply did not evaluate the claim.
why_incorrect.B: Nothing indicates contention over the document; the agents never opened it, so the problem is lack of independent checking, not competition for a resource.
why_incorrect.C: The issue is not that the task was split too finely; it is that the agents deferred to one answer instead of verifying it.

options.text: Deadlock, because the agents wait on one another's output and none can proceed until another finishes
Resource contention, because several agents compete for the same policy document at the same moment
Over-decomposition, because the task was split among more agents than the structure of the work justified
Sycophantic conformity, where agents adopt a first or senior answer instead of independently evaluating the evidence

questions.stem: In a product-support debate, a lead agent labeled 'senior reviewer' posts first and states that the refund window is 60 days. Three other agents each reply 'I agree with the senior reviewer' without opening the policy document, which says 30 days. Which failure does this illustrate?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Debate rounds cost tokens and latency on every run; apply them only where verification value justifies it.
explanation.why_correct: Every debate round requires each agent to read the accumulated discussion and produce a new response, so token use and latency both grow with rounds and agents. Because rounds run in sequence, they delay the final answer even if agents within a round run in parallel. Debate is therefore best saved for high-stakes or error-prone tasks, not applied to trivial tickets where it buys nothing.

why_incorrect.B: Storage is a minor cost; the observed token and latency growth comes directly from additional model calls in each round.
why_incorrect.C: Cost scales with both agents and rounds, since every round repeats the calls and re-reads a longer transcript; cutting rounds would reduce spend.
why_incorrect.D: Debate overhead recurs on every ticket as new model calls; transcripts from other tickets are not reusable answers for a new one.

options.text: Each extra round multiplies inference tokens and adds sequential delay, so debate should be reserved for tasks where verification is worth that cost
Extra rounds mainly increase transcript storage costs, while the changes in tokens and response time come from unrelated model upgrades
Cost grows only with the number of agents and not with the number of rounds, so trimming rounds would not reduce spend
The overhead is a one-time setup fee that disappears once the debate transcripts from earlier tickets are cached for reuse

questions.stem: A support team's debate pipeline runs four agents for three rounds on every ticket, including simple password resets. Finance reports that per-ticket token usage and response time have risen sharply, while accuracy on simple tickets did not change. What does this most directly show about adding debate rounds?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Count debate as useful when a specific critique leads to an evidence-based correction, not when text merely agrees or grows.
explanation.why_correct: Useful disagreement is specific and resolvable: a critic points to a concrete contradiction, and the judge settles it by checking evidence, so an error was actually found and fixed. Identical outputs may reflect shared mistakes, length growth is not correctness, and always deferring to the historical best agent skips the verification that debate is for.

why_incorrect.A: Identical wording across agents is more likely a sign of copying or correlated errors than independent confirmation, especially if they share a model.
why_incorrect.C: A longer summary shows more text, not more correctness; added caveats may be unverified and can even dilute accurate content.
why_incorrect.D: Adopting the historically strongest agent's answer each time means the debate never changed an outcome, so it demonstrates no verification benefit.

options.text: All four agents produced word-for-word identical dosage statements, which shows that the claim was robustly confirmed
A critic flagged a cited dosage that contradicted the source label, and the judge corrected the summary after checking the label text
The summary grew from 200 to 900 words over three rounds as agents added caveats and elaboration to the first draft
The agent with the most previous correct answers won every round, so its verdict was adopted each time without changes

questions.stem: A research team reviews logs from a debate system that screens drug-interaction summaries. Which logged outcome is the strongest sign that the debate added real verification value?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Fight shared blind spots with diversity of model, prompt, and evidence plus adversarial checks, not with more identical voters.
explanation.why_correct: A shared blind spot persists when agents share the same model, prompt, and evidence. Real independence comes from diversity in those inputs, and an adversarial reviewer is explicitly rewarded for finding what the rulebook misses. This raises the probability that at least one agent notices the new pattern.

why_incorrect.A: Duplicating the same configuration adds correlated voters; the larger majority would reproduce the same miss with more confidence.
why_incorrect.B: Reading the first analysis encourages anchoring and conformity, so later agents are less likely to notice what the first one missed.
why_incorrect.D: A repetition threshold is just a majority vote in disguise; correlated agents will repeat the same wrong answer and nobody checks it against evidence.

options.text: Add two more agents with the same model and prompt so that the final vote has a larger majority
Have every agent read the first agent's analysis before it forms an opinion, so later agents can build on it
Give agents different models or prompts and different evidence sources, and add an adversarial reviewer tasked with finding cases the rulebook misses
Replace the judge with a rule that accepts any answer repeated by at least three agents, to avoid judge bias

questions.stem: An e-commerce team's fraud-review debate keeps missing a new gift-card abuse pattern because all agents use the same model, the same prompt, and the same internal rulebook retrieval. Which change most reduces the chance that this shared blind spot survives?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Debate adds verification with cost and failure modes; it never replaces checking claims against sources.
explanation.why_correct: Debate can catch errors, but agents may share the same mistake, defer to each other, or converge on an unsupported claim, and every round adds cost. Agreement is therefore not proof of factuality, and removing the source-citation check would eliminate the one control grounded in external evidence. The right design keeps source checks alongside debate.

why_incorrect.A: Unanimity does not guarantee factuality; correlated agents can all repeat the same unsupported claim, as in the common failure of shared blind spots.
why_incorrect.B: An odd number of agents only avoids ties; it does nothing to make agents independent or to ground their claims in sources.
why_incorrect.C: Debate is not a fixed chain, since agents critique competing candidates before aggregation; and this objection also overlooks the real reason to keep citation checks.

options.text: Agree, because unanimous agreement among three agents is enough to guarantee that the summary is factual
Agree in part: debate can replace source checking as long as an odd number of agents is used to avoid ties
Disagree, because debate is simply a fixed prompt chain and adds nothing beyond what a sequential pipeline already provides
Disagree, because debate is a verification mechanism with its own cost and failure modes, so agent agreement does not replace checking against sources

questions.stem: A CTO proposes adding a three-agent debate to a clinical-summary pipeline and removing the existing source-citation check to save cost, arguing that three agreeing agents make the summary reliably factual. Which response is most accurate?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Splitting an agent adds tokens before it saves any; count the repeated prompts and handoffs.
explanation.why_correct: Each added agent carries its own instructions, tool descriptions, and intermediate reasoning, and agents re-communicate findings through handoff messages. Those repeated and relayed tokens mean total usage typically goes up, not down, even when each individual prompt is shorter. Here the three roles are also sequentially dependent (route, look up, draft), so there is little parallelism to offset the cost.

why_incorrect.A: Shorter per-agent prompts do not offset the repeated instructions and handoff summaries; total tokens across all agents normally exceed the single-agent total.
why_incorrect.B: The roles depend on each other's output, so they run in sequence and each handoff adds delay; latency can even increase.
why_incorrect.D: Dividing work does not keep cost constant, because coordination messages and duplicated context are extra tokens that the single agent never spent.

options.text: Total token usage usually falls because each agent works from a shorter prompt
End-to-end latency always falls because the three roles run at the same time
Total token usage usually rises because each agent repeats instructions and handoffs add summaries
Cost stays about the same because the same ticket work is simply divided up

questions.stem: A logistics startup's single agent resolves delivery-exception tickets acceptably. An engineer proposes splitting it into a router agent, a shipment-lookup agent, and a reply-drafting agent. Compared with the single agent, what is the most reliable expected change in resource use?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Let the sub-agent read the pile; the caller should receive only the conclusion.
explanation.why_correct: The sub-agent explores the long document in its own fresh context window and passes back only a condensed result. The coordinator therefore never has to hold the 200 pages, which keeps its context compact and focused on the overall task. This is context isolation and compression, one of the genuine reasons to decompose.

why_incorrect.A: A separate context window is not a permission boundary; access rights must be enforced separately through tool and credential limits.
why_incorrect.B: Compression is lossy, so the summary can omit or distort details; nothing guarantees completeness or accuracy.
why_incorrect.C: The coordinator must still give a clear task description, because the sub-agent starts with none of the coordinator's context.

options.text: The sub-agent's permissions are automatically restricted to read-only access
The guideline summary is guaranteed to be complete and accurate
The coordinator no longer needs to define what the sub-agent should look for
The coordinator's context stays small and focused while the heavy reading happens in a separate context

questions.stem: A coordinator agent delegates reading a 200-page clinical guideline to a sub-agent, which returns a half-page list of the dosing rules relevant to the patient. What is the main benefit of this design?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Decide per workload: pay for extra agents only where value and breadth justify the tokens.
explanation.why_correct: The multi-agent gain was measured on broad, valuable research questions and came with a large token increase. Quick lookups are low value and tightly capped on spend, so the extra quality and parallelism buy little while the multiplied cost is a real problem. Routing by task value and breadth, with a single agent for simple queries, matches the cost-benefit logic of decomposition.

why_incorrect.B: Parallel agents often finish sooner while spending more tokens in total, so lower wall-clock time says nothing about lower cost.
why_incorrect.C: Benefits measured on one task type do not automatically transfer; simple lookups are exactly where a single agent is already adequate.
why_incorrect.D: Higher token usage is acceptable when task value is high and the measured gain justifies it; the research workload may still deserve the design.

options.text: Keep a single agent for the quick lookups and reserve the multi-agent design for high-value, breadth-heavy queries where the extra tokens are justified
Adopt it everywhere, because finishing faster in wall-clock time shows it is also cheaper per query
Adopt it everywhere, because a quality gain on research questions will transfer to any question type
Reject it entirely, because any increase in token usage makes a multi-agent design unacceptable

questions.stem: A team's multi-agent research prototype, with four parallel sub-agents, beat its single-agent baseline on deep market-analysis questions at roughly ten times the tokens, finishing faster in wall-clock time. The product owner now wants it for a free-tier assistant that answers quick factual lookups under a tight per-query spend cap. Which conclusion is best supported?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Parallelism buys time, not tokens; the join step is still serial.
explanation.why_correct: Independent branches can run at the same time, which shortens elapsed time, but every branch carries its own prompt, tool results, and reasoning, so the total compute spent goes up. The merge or synthesis step must wait for all branches and adds its own latency, so it can become the new bottleneck.

why_incorrect.A: More parallel agents mean more repeated prompts and results, so total cost generally rises rather than falls.
why_incorrect.C: A baseline comparison is still needed to show that the quality or speed gain justifies the extra cost.
why_incorrect.E: Each agent carries its own instructions and tool descriptions, so parallel agents add token overhead rather than avoiding it.

options.text: Total cost falls roughly in proportion to the number of parallel agents
Wall-clock time can drop while the total number of tokens spent rises
Running in parallel removes the need to compare against a single-agent baseline
The final join step still adds sequential latency that parallelism does not remove
Parallel agents avoid repeating instructions, so their prompts add no extra tokens

questions.stem: A news-monitoring team fans a broad survey task out to several parallel sub-agents, then merges their findings. Select TWO statements that are accurate about this design.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Isolate context, but brief precisely, return verifiable summaries, and measure against a baseline.
explanation.why_correct: A sub-agent starts with a clean context, so it needs a self-contained task description to know what to look for and what to return. Because compression is lossy, briefs should keep sources and key figures that allow verification. Finally, the extra agents spend more tokens, so the design should be justified by comparing quality, cost, and latency with a single-agent baseline.

why_incorrect.A: Copying the full transcript to every sub-agent defeats isolation, inflates token cost, and reintroduces the long-context dilution the design aims to avoid.
why_incorrect.C: A one-sentence brief is over-aggressive compression that will drop details the coordinator later needs.

options.text: Copy the coordinator's full transcript into every sub-agent so none lacks context
Give each sub-agent a self-contained task description stating objective, scope, and output format
Require every brief to be a single sentence so the coordinator's context is as small as possible
Require briefs to include source references and key figures so the coordinator can spot-check claims
Measure quality, tokens, and latency against a single-agent baseline on the same questions

questions.stem: A coordinator for competitive-intelligence reports was overflowing its context with raw web pages, so the team delegates each competitor to a sub-agent that returns a condensed brief. Select THREE practices that let this design keep its benefit without losing information the coordinator needs.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Split on real differences in tools, permissions, or context load, not on labels or org charts.
explanation.why_correct: A separate agent is justified when it has a different tool set or permission scope, which supports least privilege, or when its work generates a lot of intermediate material that the caller does not need, so isolating and compressing context helps. Both reasons give the new agent something real that a single generalist handles poorly.

why_incorrect.B: A persona prompt changes framing, not capability, so a role distinguished only by persona adds handoff cost without real benefit.
why_incorrect.C: Mirroring an organizational chart is not a performance reason; human structures are not automatically optimal agent topologies.
why_incorrect.E: Tightly coupled steps sharing one evolving artifact are costly to split because the shared context must be rebuilt at each handoff.

options.text: One step needs a distinct tool set with narrower permissions than the rest of the workflow
The proposed new agent would differ from the generalist only by a persona such as "senior partner"
The team wants the agent layout to mirror the law firm's organizational chart
One step reads very long filings, producing large intermediate material when the caller needs only a short conclusion
Every step edits the same evolving draft and needs the full details of the previous step's reasoning

questions.stem: An in-house legal-intake assistant is currently one generalist agent. Select TWO observations that would justify splitting a separate sub-agent out of it rather than keeping everything in one agent.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Baseline, diagnose, targeted prototype, same-set comparison, then selective adoption.
explanation.why_correct: The single-agent baseline comes first because every decomposition must beat it, and it provides the quality, token, and latency numbers for comparison. Inspecting its failures then shows what actually needs fixing, for example an overloaded context that sub-agents could isolate. The prototype should target that bottleneck rather than copy a generic team layout. Re-running the same evaluation set makes the comparison fair, and adoption comes last and only where the measured gain justifies the extra tokens and coordination latency.

options.text: Re-run the same evaluation set on the prototype and compare quality, tokens, and latency with the baseline
Run the strong single-agent system on a fixed evaluation set and record quality, tokens, and latency
Adopt the multi-agent design only for the workloads where the measured gain justifies the added cost
Prototype a decomposition aimed at the specific bottleneck that was identified
Inspect the baseline's failures to find the bottleneck, such as context overflow, breadth, or conflicting tool needs

questions.stem: A data-pipeline team suspects that its single debugging agent is struggling with log-heavy incidents and wants to know whether splitting into sub-agents is worthwhile. Arrange the evaluation steps in the sequence that best supports a sound decision.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Overhead costs tokens, compression loses detail, the baseline sets the bar, and the critical path caps speedup.
explanation.why_correct: Token overhead is the extra usage from repeated instructions, tool results, and agent-to-agent messages. Lossy compression describes the risk that a summary returned by a sub-agent drops something the coordinator needs. The single-agent baseline is the comparison point a multi-agent design must beat. The critical path is the longest dependency chain, which bounds speedup regardless of agent count. R5 describes least privilege, a separate concern that context isolation does not provide by itself.

left.text: Token overhead
Lossy compression
Single-agent baseline
Critical path

right.text: The reference system that any decomposition must outperform on quality, cost, and latency
The longest chain of dependent steps, which limits the speedup no matter how many agents are added
Repeated prompts, tool results, and handoff messages that raise total usage as agents are added
A condensed sub-agent result may omit a detail the coordinator later needs
A guarantee that each sub-agent receives only the permissions its subtask needs

questions.stem: Match each term used when deciding whether to decompose a task across agents to the statement that describes it.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Match the split to the real constraint: context load, tools or permissions, coupling, or independence.
explanation.why_correct: Long contracts that yield a short conclusion are the classic case for context isolation and compression, since sub-agents absorb the bulk and return condensed results. A bloated toolkit with differing credential needs points to role specialization with narrow tool sets and least-privilege permissions. A chain of dependent edits to a shared interface is tightly coupled, so a single agent avoids the cost of re-sharing context and conflicting changes. Independent sources are a breadth task that parallelizes well, and the results are joined at the end. Debate verifies answers but addresses none of these workloads.

left.text: An assistant must read dozens of long vendor contracts, yet the caller needs only a list of termination clauses
One agent with a 60-tool toolkit often picks the wrong tool, and the payment tools need tighter credentials than the rest
A refactor touches three modules that share one changing interface, and each edit depends on the previous one
A literature survey covers 25 sources whose findings do not depend on each other

right.text: Fan out to parallel agents over the independent branches, then join the results
Role-specialized agents with narrow tool sets and permissions
Keep a single agent, because tight coupling would make the cost of rebuilding shared context exceed the benefit
Delegate the reading to sub-agents with fresh contexts and take back condensed results
Add a debate round so that agents can verify one another's answers

questions.stem: Match each workload on the left to the design decision that best fits it on the right.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A role label is not a role: separate agents need a different tool set, success criterion, or perspective.
explanation.why_correct: A role is only worth its handoff cost when it differs in tool set, success criterion, or perspective. Here every substantive element is identical, so the title is just a persona label that changes framing, not underlying knowledge or permissions. The team is paying for extra prompts, transfers, and tokens while a single agent would behave essentially the same way.

why_incorrect.A: A persona prompt changes tone and framing, not the model's knowledge or tools, so a seniority label does not create new capability.
why_incorrect.B: Independence needs different evidence, tools, or criteria. Agents with identical model, prompt body, and checks share the same blind spots whatever they are called.
why_incorrect.D: Least privilege requires different enforced permissions per role. A title in the prompt grants or restricts nothing, because the tool access is identical.

options.text: Each title unlocks deeper expertise, so the three agents bring genuinely different capabilities
The title differences guarantee independent verification because each agent holds a different rank
The roles differ in name only, so the handoffs add cost without a new tool set, criterion, or perspective
The titles enforce least-privilege boundaries because each agent now has a separate level of authority

questions.stem: A startup runs three agents titled 'Senior Engineer', 'Staff Engineer', and 'Principal Engineer'. All three use the same model, the same tools, the same instructions, and the same success check; only the job title in the system prompt differs. Which assessment is most accurate?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Independent subtasks fan out in parallel and then join; dependent subtasks wait for their inputs.
explanation.why_correct: Subtasks that do not depend on each other's outputs can run concurrently, which cuts wall-clock latency compared with a strictly sequential loop. The independent results are then combined in a single join or synthesis step. Parallelism comes from the independent branches in the task, not from adding more agents for their own sake.

why_incorrect.A: Sequential execution is needed only when a step consumes an upstream result. Here nothing is consumed, so serializing wastes time.
why_incorrect.B: Letting one agent do everything while others idle gives up the available concurrency and adds agents with no benefit.
why_incorrect.C: A pre-approval gate adds latency and a coordination step, yet it does nothing about the independence of the lookups.

options.text: Run the lookups one after another so each call can read the previous results
Have one agent perform all lookups while the others wait for it to finish
Add a review agent that must approve the plan before any lookup is allowed to begin
Dispatch the three lookups concurrently and join their results in one synthesis step

questions.stem: A travel assistant must retrieve the weather forecast, current flight prices, and hotel availability for the same city. None of the three lookups needs the output of another. Which execution strategy best fits this structure?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: If roles share one tightly coupled artifact and gain nothing in tools or criteria, merge them and keep a single-agent baseline.
explanation.why_correct: The work is tightly coupled around one shared artifact, so each role boundary forces the shared context to be reconstructed, which is the cost seen in the traces. The roles add no distinct permissions or criteria except executing tests, and that capability is a tool, not a separate agent. A single agent with a test runner is the baseline any specialization must beat, so extra roles should return only with measured gains.

why_incorrect.B: A Manager adds another agent and another summarization step, which increases coordination cost and lossy compression on a task that is already over-split.
why_incorrect.C: Longer persona text changes framing, not tools, permissions, or knowledge, so it cannot repair handoff overhead that comes from the task being tightly coupled.
why_incorrect.D: Parallel editing and review of the same module creates conflicting changes and stale reviews, because the reviewer needs the finished edit as its input.

options.text: Collapse to one agent that has a test-runner tool, and reintroduce a role only if measurements show it beats this baseline
Add a fifth Manager agent that summarizes every handoff so the four roles stay informed
Lengthen each role's persona description so the agents specialize more deeply
Let the Coder and Reviewer work in parallel so the shared module is edited and judged simultaneously

questions.stem: A team fixes bugs in a single 400-line module using four agents: Planner, Coder, Reviewer, and Tester. Traces show the Coder re-pasting the whole module for the Reviewer, the Tester re-deriving the intent from scratch, and fix quality matching a single-agent baseline at roughly three times the token cost. What is the best change?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Justify a role by different permissions, criteria, or evidence, never by a name or a tone.
explanation.why_correct: A role earns its handoff cost when it differs in a way a single agent would handle poorly. Distinct permissions support least privilege, since the drafter never touches the ledger. A separate success criterion makes the output checkable on its own terms. Independent evidence gives a genuinely different perspective instead of repeating the drafter's view. Each of these changes what the agent can do or verify, not just how it is described.

why_incorrect.A: Mirroring a human org chart is not evidence of a better agent topology; the roles must justify themselves by tools, criteria, or perspective.
why_incorrect.C: Tone and persona names alter framing only, so they add handoff cost without new capability or independence.

options.text: The role's title matches a job that already exists on the human organization chart
The role needs read access to a payments ledger that the drafting role must not hold, so permissions differ
The role is given a friendlier tone and a distinct persona name in its system prompt
The role is judged against a separate success criterion, such as a policy checklist, rather than writing fluency
The role brings an independent perspective by using evidence from a source the drafting role never sees

questions.stem: A claims-processing team is deciding which responsibilities deserve their own agent instead of staying inside one generalist agent. Select THREE reasons that justify a separate role.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Parallelism buys wall-clock time, not savings: speedup is capped by the critical path, and cost usually goes up.
explanation.why_correct: Speedup is limited by the longest chain of dependent work: the slowest lookup must finish, and then the join and synthesis still run sequentially after it. Parallelism also does not make the work cheaper. Each agent repeats its own instructions and tool results, so a faster run usually spends more tokens in total. Treating speed and cost as the same quantity is a common mistake.

why_incorrect.A: Speedup is bounded by the critical path and the join step, so more agents give diminishing returns and not a proportional halving.
why_incorrect.C: Each agent carries its own prompt and intermediate results, so parallel agents repeat context and usually raise total token use.
why_incorrect.D: Concurrent branches still produce separate findings that must be merged and reconciled, so the synthesis step remains necessary.

options.text: Doubling the lookup agents to ten will halve end-to-end latency because the work splits evenly
End-to-end latency is bounded below by the slowest branch plus the join and synthesis step
Parallel lookups reduce total tokens consumed because shared instructions are read only once
After the branches finish concurrently, no synthesis step is needed to reconcile their findings
Wall-clock time can fall while total token spend rises, because each agent carries its own prompt and results

questions.stem: A report builder fans out five independent source-lookup agents and then uses one synthesis agent to combine their findings. Select TWO statements that correctly describe the performance of this design.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Serialize dependencies, parallelize independent branches, and give every shared artifact one owner and a conflict rule.
explanation.why_correct: The failure comes from fanning out work that is not actually independent: table B needs table A's output, so running them concurrently forces guesses that later conflict. Respecting the dependency edge removes the conflict at its source while still parallelizing the independent tables. Because parallel branches may still write to shared artifacts, single ownership and conflict flagging at the join stop silent corruption and wasteful retries.

why_incorrect.B: A vote among agents that all guessed the missing dependency produces consensus on a guess, and extra agents also add tokens and conflicts.
why_incorrect.D: A longer prompt cannot supply information that does not exist yet; the branch still has to guess table A's decisions.
why_incorrect.E: Last-write-wins hides the conflict and can silently discard correct work, trading visible retries for undetected corruption.

options.text: Serialize along the dependency edge so table B starts only after table A's decisions exist, and parallelize only the truly independent tables
Add more parallel agents so conflicting schema choices are settled by majority vote
Give each shared artifact a single owner and have the join step flag conflicting writes instead of silently overwriting
Lengthen each worker prompt so it can anticipate what the other branches will decide
Let the last branch to finish overwrite earlier results so the join completes without retries

questions.stem: In a database migration, three agents run in parallel to rewrite three tables. The column types of table B depend on key decisions made while rewriting table A. At the join step the outputs conflict, and repeated merge retries consume most of the token budget. Select TWO changes that address the root cause.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Map dependencies, fan out the independent work, join, synthesize, then verify.
explanation.why_correct: Concurrent dispatch is only safe once the planner has made the dependency structure explicit, so the dependency graph comes first. The independent vendor lookups can then fan out together. A join point holds the flow until all branches return, because synthesis depends on every result. The synthesis step then compares vendors and drafts the recommendation, and the reviewer checks it against the gathered sources last, since it needs the finished draft as its input.

options.text: The independent per-vendor lookups are dispatched concurrently
The system waits at a join point until every upstream branch has returned
The planner expresses the task as subtasks and marks which ones depend on others
A synthesis step compares the collected findings and drafts the recommendation
A reviewer checks the claims in the recommendation against the collected sources

questions.stem: A planner is asked to compare three vendors on pricing and security posture and then recommend one. Arrange the steps of an efficient parallel execution in the correct sequence, from first to last.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Fan out independent breadth, keep coupled work in one agent, and split roles only for different permissions or criteria.
explanation.why_correct: Forty independent filings are breadth work with no dependencies between them, so parallel workers and a final join give real speedup. A chain of dependent edits on one shared function gains nothing from fan-out and risks conflicting changes, so a single capable agent with tools is the right baseline. The contract task has a genuine need for different permissions and a different success criterion, which justifies separate roles. Persona-labelled agents with identical tools add handoff cost without new capability, so that option fits none of the three.

left.text: Summarizing forty independent regulatory filings into one digest
Editing a single shared function through a series of changes that each depend on the previous one
Drafting a contract while a reviewer checks it against a clause database the drafter must not access

right.text: Role-separated agents with distinct tool permissions and criteria
Parallel fan-out workers followed by a join and synthesis step
A single agent with the right tools and no decomposition
Several persona-labelled agents with identical tools and prompts

questions.stem: Match each task on the left to the design that best fits its structure on the right.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Add a management level when span of control or sub-goal size demands it, and pass goals, budgets, and limits down explicitly while condensing results upward.
explanation.why_correct: The flat design fails on span of control and context load. Regional sub-orchestrators each own a coherent sub-goal and a manageable group of workers, and they return a condensed result so the lead's context stays small. Constraints do not propagate automatically, so the goal, budget, authority limits, and output contract must be passed down explicitly. The lead keeps a progress record so it can re-plan if a region fails.

why_incorrect.A: Telling sub-orchestrators only a region name omits the goal, budget, and authority limits they cannot infer, and forwarding raw transcripts defeats the purpose of condensing context upward.
why_incorrect.B: Each extra level adds delegation latency and another lossy summarization step. Managers with one or two reports give up the span-of-control benefit and make the hierarchy deeper than the problem needs.
why_incorrect.D: A larger window does not fix inconsistent assignment, since long contexts are used unevenly. Free worker-to-worker messaging removes central assignment and adds coordination traffic.

options.text: Create six regional sub-orchestrators that are told only their region name, let them run on their own, and have them forward every worker transcript to the top-level orchestrator for synthesis
Add three more management layers so each manager supervises only one or two agents, which maximizes parallelism and minimizes each manager's context

Create six regional sub-orchestrators, each given an explicit sub-goal, budget, authority limits, and output contract, supervising about five workers and returning a condensed structured result to the lead, which tracks progress and re-plans
Keep the flat orchestrator but switch to a larger context window and allow the workers to message one another freely to settle overlaps themselves

questions.stem: A compliance-audit system uses one flat orchestrator that directly supervises 30 worker agents reviewing filings for six regulatory regions. The orchestrator's context is filling with raw worker reports, and it has started assigning overlapping work and forgetting region-specific rules. The team wants to move to a hierarchy. Which design best addresses the problem without creating new ones?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Let the checker verify against criteria, evidence, or tests the generator did not control, and calibrate it against human labels.
explanation.why_correct: A reviewer that shares the generator's model, prompt, and context inherits its blind spots, so its approvals add little independent signal. A judge is stronger when it checks against something the generator did not control, such as a glossary, clause-coverage checks, or a rubric. It should return a structured verdict with actionable feedback, and calibration against human labels shows whether its approvals can be trusted. This also gives the pipeline a meaningful quality gate.

why_incorrect.A: A second reviewer with identical model, prompt, and context has correlated errors, so repeated approval is not independent verification.
why_incorrect.B: Changing the output scale does not add evidence or independence. A numeric score from the same blind-spotted judge is still unverified and harder to act on.
why_incorrect.C: Self-grading by the generator invites self-enhancement bias and removes the separation of production from evaluation that the pattern depends on.

options.text: Add a second review stage that uses the identical model, prompt, and context so approvals are confirmed twice
Have the reviewer output a score from 1 to 100 instead of an approve or reject verdict
Let the translation agent grade its own draft before passing it on, since it has the most context

Give the reviewer a distinct rubric and independent evidence such as glossary and clause-coverage checks against the source, return a structured verdict with feedback, and calibrate it on human-labeled samples

questions.stem: A contract-translation pipeline runs extract, translate, and review stages in a fixed order. The review agent uses the same model, the same prompt style, and the same context as the translation agent, and it approves 98% of drafts. A human audit finds many untranslated clauses and mistranslated defined terms in approved drafts. What is the most effective change to the review stage?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Fixed order and artifact handoffs mean pipeline; managers that assign and re-plan at run time mean hierarchy.
explanation.why_correct: In a hierarchical team, a top-level coordinator and sub-orchestrators decide at run time which agents handle which sub-goals and can re-plan. In a sequential pipeline the stage order is fixed in advance, and each stage consumes a defined input artifact and produces a defined output artifact. No central agent chooses the next step. This makes pipelines predictable and testable stage by stage, while hierarchies handle work whose steps are not known ahead of time.

why_incorrect.A: This reverses the two patterns: run-time routing and re-planning belong to hierarchies, and a fixed order belongs to pipelines.
why_incorrect.C: The patterns differ in how control works, not in agent count. A pipeline can have many agents and a hierarchy can be small.
why_incorrect.D: A pipeline has no central agent deciding the next step, and a hierarchy depends on coordinating managers, so both halves are wrong.

options.text: A pipeline relies on managers that re-plan at run time, while a hierarchy always executes its agents in one fixed order
A hierarchy delegates through managers that choose assignments and re-plan at run time, while a pipeline runs fixed stages that hand structured artifacts forward in a preset order
The two are the same pattern, and the only difference is how many agents each one contains
A pipeline needs a manager agent at every stage, while a hierarchy has no coordinating agent at all

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a hierarchical agent team from a sequential pipeline of agents?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Put an objective quality gate where errors enter a pipeline, and pair it with a bounded feedback edge.
explanation.why_correct: Pipelines propagate an upstream error into every later stage unless a gate stops it. A validation gate with objective checks, such as schema, range, and cross-field consistency against the source, catches the misread where it occurs and is stronger than opinion-only review. A feedback edge back to extraction lets the pipeline repair the problem. Bounding retries and escalating to a human prevents an endless loop when extraction keeps failing.

why_incorrect.A: Later stages treat upstream values as premises and are not designed to audit them, so a final stage cannot be relied on to repair upstream corruption.
why_incorrect.C: An unrestricted group chat gives up the defined artifacts, ownership, and stage-wise testability, and it introduces conflicting rewrites without adding any verification.
why_incorrect.E: An extra rewriting stage after the letter does not check the income value, so the wrong figure still reaches the customer, and it adds cost and latency.

options.text: Rely on the letter-writing stage to detect and silently correct inconsistent upstream values
Insert a validation gate after extraction that checks schema, value ranges, and cross-field consistency against the source document and halts the flow on failure
Replace the pipeline with an unrestricted group chat in which any agent may rewrite any artifact
Add a feedback edge from the gate back to extraction with a bounded retry count and escalation to a human reviewer when the limit is reached
Append a second letter-writing stage that rephrases the first draft for clarity

questions.stem: A loan-processing system uses a fixed pipeline: document extraction, eligibility check, risk summary, and customer letter. An audit shows that an OCR misread of annual income in the extraction stage flowed unchanged into the risk summary and the customer letter, and no later stage noticed. Select TWO changes that best contain this kind of upstream error.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Pass limits down explicitly, and verify claims on the way up against evidence the claimant did not control.
explanation.why_correct: The first failure is that constraints did not propagate down: a sub-orchestrator does not inherit the top-level goal, budget, or authority limits unless they are passed explicitly, and enforcing them outside the lead keeps them from being ignored. The second failure is an unverified summary moving upward. A verifier that is independent of the lead and checks the claim against objective evidence catches wrong resolutions before the commander acts on them.

why_incorrect.B: Constraints are not inherited implicitly. A shared title carries no budget or scope, so leads would guess.
why_incorrect.C: Another layer adds delegation latency and another lossy summarization step, and it does not give the commander any basis to verify claims.
why_incorrect.D: A hierarchy of authority is not a hierarchy of correctness. Accepting a summary unchecked lets a wrong claim propagate to the top.

options.text: Pass an explicit budget, scope, and authority limit with every delegation, and enforce them outside the leads' own judgment
Rely on each lead to infer the commander's constraints from the shared incident title
Insert a fourth management layer so that every manager supervises exactly one worker
Have the commander accept lead summaries without checking them, because leads have more specialist expertise than the commander
Have an independent verifier check each lead's resolution claim against evidence such as logs and health checks before the commander accepts it

questions.stem: An incident-response system has an incident commander agent, three team-lead sub-orchestrators (database, network, application), and worker agents under each lead. A postmortem found that the network lead exceeded its spending allowance and restarted a service outside the scope the commander intended, and that the commander accepted the database lead's summary 'root cause resolved' although the summary was wrong. Select TWO changes that best address these two failures.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Delegate with limits, produce, verify, condense upward, then let the top level record and decide.
explanation.why_correct: Delegation comes first, because limits and goals must be passed down explicitly before any work starts. The sub-orchestrator then runs its fixed pipeline, with each stage consuming and producing a defined artifact. Verification comes next, since an independent verifier should test the artifact with executable checks before anything is reported upward. Only then does the sub-orchestrator condense the verified result for the lead, avoiding an unverified claim moving up the hierarchy. Last, the lead records the outcome in its progress ledger and decides whether to finish or re-plan.

options.text: The sub-orchestrator condenses the verified result into a structured summary and reports it upward
The lead decomposes the request and gives the sub-orchestrator its sub-goal, budget, and authority limits
The lead records the result in its progress ledger and decides whether to finish or re-plan
An independent verifier runs executable tests on the artifact and returns a structured verdict
The sub-orchestrator runs its fixed design-then-implement pipeline, handing a structured artifact from each stage to the next

questions.stem: A lead orchestrator delegates a feature request to a sub-orchestrator whose team runs a fixed design-then-implement pipeline and is checked by an independent verifier. Put the steps in the correct sequence, from first to last.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: If agents coordinate through a shared workspace and a controller picks who acts next from its contents, it is a blackboard.
explanation.why_correct: In a blackboard architecture, agents communicate indirectly by reading from and writing to a shared workspace that holds the evolving problem state, and a controller or selection rule picks the next agent based on the current contents of that workspace. That matches the scenario: no direct agent-to-agent messages, a shared case workspace, and a controller that chooses who acts next from the workspace state rather than from a fixed order.

why_incorrect.A: A pipeline fixes the order of agents in advance; here the next agent is chosen from the current workspace contents.
why_incorrect.B: A swarm relies on decentralized local rules without a controller reading a global shared state, which is not what is described.
why_incorrect.D: Debate involves agents defending opposing positions to a judge; these agents contribute complementary partial findings instead.

options.text: A fixed sequential pipeline in which each agent passes its output to a predetermined successor
A swarm in which agents follow only local rules based on their nearest neighbours' messages
A blackboard architecture in which agents coordinate indirectly through a shared problem workspace
A debate setup in which agents argue opposing positions until a judge picks a winner

questions.stem: A clinical-triage research prototype has a radiology-findings agent, a lab-results agent, and a pharmacology agent. None of them message each other directly. Each reads an evolving case workspace and adds its partial findings, and a controller inspects the workspace to decide which agent should contribute next. Which architecture does this describe?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Tool-access protocols connect an agent to tools and data; agent-to-agent protocols connect it to peer agents.
explanation.why_correct: Tool-access protocols such as the Model Context Protocol connect an agent to tools and data through a client-server interface, which fits querying an inventory service. Agent-to-agent protocols support discovery of peer capabilities and delegation of tasks across independently built agents, which fits handing a customs-clearance task to a partner's agent. They address different layers rather than competing for the same job.

why_incorrect.A: Treating a data service as a peer agent adds negotiation and task-lifecycle overhead where a simple typed tool call is enough.
why_incorrect.B: Delegating a multi-step task to an autonomous peer needs capability discovery and task status semantics that a plain tool call lacks.
why_incorrect.C: This reverses the mapping: the inventory service is a tool or data source, and the broker's agent is the peer.

options.text: Use an agent-to-agent protocol for both, since every external capability is effectively another agent
Use a tool-access protocol for both, since delegating to a partner agent is just another function call
Use an agent-to-agent protocol for the inventory service and a tool-access protocol for the broker's agent
Use a tool-access protocol for the inventory service and an agent-to-agent protocol for the broker's agent

questions.stem: A logistics company wants its routing agent to query a warehouse inventory service for stock levels and, separately, to delegate a customs-clearance task to an independently built agent run by a partner broker. Which statement correctly matches the protocol type to each need?

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Default memory to private and promote to shared only with provenance and a policy check.
explanation.why_correct: Defaulting memory to private and promoting entries to shared memory only when provenance is recorded and a policy check passes keeps sensitive, role-specific information protected while still allowing deliberate reuse. Shared memory brings privacy, poisoning, and consistency risks, so promotion should be a controlled decision instead of the starting state.

why_incorrect.A: Sharing everything from the start exposes sensitive account data to agents that do not need it and lets one bad entry spread widely.
why_incorrect.B: A shared prompt is not memory: it is not retrieved selectively or persisted across tasks, and it still gives every agent the same content.
why_incorrect.D: Relevance ranks entries but does not authorize them; a highly relevant entry may still be off-limits to the requesting agent.

options.text: Make all memory shared from the start so each agent can reuse everything the others have learned
Place all memory in one shared prompt so every agent sees the same text on each turn
Keep memory private by default and promote entries to shared memory only with provenance and a policy check
Share memory freely but return only the entries that are semantically most relevant to each query
