Agentic designs emerged to address exactly these limitations: tool use lets the model fetch current or external information instead of relying solely on parametric knowledge; multi-step reasoning lets the model break a hard problem into smaller pieces solved incrementally rather than in one pass; self-correction (e.g. critiquing its own draft answer and revising) catches errors a single pass would miss; and persistent action lets the system actually DO something in the world (send an email, modify a file, query a database) rather than only describe what should be done.
TH-D1-004.title: Why agents emerged: limitations of single-shot LLM calls

common_confusions: Calling any LLM-powered conversational product an 'agent' purely as marketing language, when its actual control flow is a fixed chatbot turn-taking loop with no autonomous multi-step decision-making.

Assuming a workflow with many branches is 'basically an agent' -- no matter how many branches a workflow has, if they were all authored in advance by a developer rather than decided dynamically by the model, it remains a workflow, not an agent.
key_points: Chatbots center on conversational turn-taking; their primary unit of interaction is a dialogue turn, not a multi-step task.
Workflows have developer-authored control flow -- the sequence of steps is fixed in code, even if individual steps call an LLM.
Agents have model-authored control flow -- the model decides the sequence of actions at runtime within a space of possibilities the developer defines.
A system can combine these: e.g. a chatbot interface that, upon detecting a complex request, hands off to an agentic sub-process to complete a multi-step task before replying.
The distinction matters practically: workflows are more predictable and easier to test exhaustively; agents are more flexible but harder to fully predict or exhaustively test.
TH-D1-005.rule_of_thumb: If you can draw the system's entire possible execution path as a fixed flowchart ahead of time, it's a workflow. If the model's own output determines which branch of an open-ended decision tree gets taken at runtime, it's an agent.
TH-D1-005.summary: These three terms are often used loosely, but they describe meaningfully different systems. A chatbot is primarily a conversational interface: its core job is turn-by-turn dialogue, and even if an LLM powers it, its control flow is typically just 'take the latest message plus history, produce a reply.' A workflow (or pipeline) executes a predetermined sequence of steps -- possibly including LLM calls -- where the sequence and branching logic are authored in advance by a developer, not decided by the model at runtime. An agent, by contrast, is characterized by the model itself deciding, step by step, what action to take next, including whether and which tools to call, based on the evolving state of the task -- the developer defines the available actions and the stopping criteria, but not the exact sequence.
TH-D1-005.title: Agents vs. chatbots vs. workflows: a comparison

common_confusions: Treating maximum autonomy as the gold-standard design goal -- in production, bounded and partially-agentic systems are often the correct and more responsible choice.
Assuming a smaller action space necessarily means less useful agency -- a tightly scoped agent that reliably handles its narrow task well is often more valuable than a broad, unreliable one.
key_points: Full autonomy trades predictability and cost-boundedness for flexibility -- appropriate for genuinely open-ended tasks where the solution path cannot be known in advance.
Constraining the action space (limiting which tools/actions are available) reduces risk surface without necessarily removing autonomy over WHEN to use them.
A hard maximum step/iteration count is a common safety and cost-control measure that bounds worst-case autonomous behavior without eliminating agency.

High-stakes or hard-to-reverse actions (e.g. sending money, deleting data) are commonly kept OUT of a fully autonomous agent's action space, or gated behind human confirmation, even when the rest of the task is agentic.
The appropriate autonomy level is a design decision driven by error cost, auditability needs, and task open-endedness -- not a universal best practice to maximize.
TH-D1-006.rule_of_thumb: Before granting an agent more autonomy, ask: what's the worst thing it could do with that autonomy, and is that an acceptable risk for the value gained? If the worst case is unacceptable, constrain the action space or add human-in-the-loop checkpoints rather than removing structure elsewhere.
TH-D1-006.summary: More agentic autonomy is not automatically better engineering. Full autonomy -- where the model decides every step, every tool call, and when to stop, with no fixed structure -- maximizes flexibility but also maximizes unpredictability, cost (since the number of steps/calls is unbounded), and safety risk (since the system might take unintended actions). Many well-designed production systems deliberately choose a point partway along the autonomy spectrum: a workflow with a few agentic decision points, or an agent constrained to a small, carefully scoped action space and a hard step limit. The right level of autonomy depends on the cost of errors (how bad is a wrong action?), the predictability requirements (does this need to be testable/auditable?), and the complexity of the task (does it genuinely require open-ended problem solving, or is the space of valid solutions small and enumerable?).
TH-D1-006.title: Degrees of autonomy and when less agency is the better design choice

common_confusions: Assuming 'reason' always means an explicit, verbose chain-of-thought -- a reactive agent's reasoning step can be a near-instantaneous lookup or pattern match with no explicit deliberation shown.

Treating perceive-reason-act as three cleanly separated phases in all implementations -- some architectures blend them (e.g. a single LLM call that implicitly perceives context and reasons to produce an action in one pass).
key_points: Perceive = gather current information (user input, tool outputs, environment state).
Reason = process that information into a decision about the next action.
Act = execute the chosen action, producing effects and/or output.
The cycle is iterative: each action's consequences become the next cycle's perceptions, forming a closed loop.
Different agent architectures vary enormously in how much work happens in the 'reason' step -- from near-instant pattern matching to extended multi-step deliberation.
TH-D1-007.rule_of_thumb: When analyzing any agent's behavior, map what it's doing onto perceive/reason/act -- confusion about agent behavior often resolves once you identify which of the three phases is actually causing an observed problem.
TH-D1-007.summary: The perceive-reason-act cycle (sometimes called sense-think-act) is the canonical description of how an agent operates over time. Perceive: the agent gathers information about its current state -- the user's request, prior tool results, environmental signals. Reason: the agent processes that information to decide what to do next, which may involve weighing options, decomposing the problem, or simply pattern-matching to a known response. Act: the agent carries out the chosen action, whether that is calling a tool, producing output, or modifying its environment. The cycle then repeats, with the consequences of the action becoming new perceptions for the next iteration, continuing until a termination condition is met.
TH-D1-007.title: The perceive-reason-act cycle: the canonical agent control loop

common_confusions: Assuming perception failures always look like missing information -- malformed, truncated, or stale information fed into context is also a perception problem, even though something was technically perceived.

Overlooking implicit perception needs like current date/time -- many apparent reasoning errors (e.g. wrong relative date calculations) actually stem from the agent never having been given that contextual information to perceive in the first place.
key_points: Perception for a software agent is informational: text, structured data, API responses, retrieved documents -- not necessarily physical sensor data.
Every tool call's return value is a perception event for the next reasoning step, since it changes what the agent knows.
Perception can include implicit context like the current date/time or system configuration, which agents often need for correct reasoning (e.g. relative date calculations).
In a multi-agent system, messages or outputs from other agents are also perception inputs to a given agent's next reasoning step.
Poor perception (e.g. a tool returning truncated or malformed data) directly degrades reasoning quality downstream, even if the reasoning step itself is sound.
TH-D1-008.rule_of_thumb: If a software agent is behaving as though it 'doesn't know' something it should, check what's actually being fed into its context at the perceive step before assuming a reasoning failure.
TH-D1-008.summary: For a software-based AI agent (as opposed to a robot with cameras and sensors), perception means ingesting any information relevant to the current decision: the original user request, the results of previously executed tool calls, retrieved memory or documents, system state (e.g. the current date, or application state), and sometimes signals from other agents in a multi-agent system. Unlike a robot, a software agent's 'environment' is often entirely informational -- APIs, databases, files, and other software -- but the perceive step still serves the identical function of updating the agent's situational awareness before it reasons about what to do next.
TH-D1-008.title: What counts as 'perception' for a software agent

common_confusions: Assuming more reasoning steps always produce a better decision -- excessive deliberation on a simple task wastes latency and cost without improving the outcome.
Treating 'reasoning' as something that only happens via explicit chain-of-thought text -- a model can also reason implicitly within a single forward pass, without producing visible intermediate text.
key_points: Reasoning can range from near-instant reactive pattern matching to extended, explicit multi-step deliberation.
More thorough reasoning generally improves decision quality on complex tasks but increases latency and cost.

Techniques that make reasoning explicit (chain-of-thought, written-out reasoning traces) can also make the agent's decision process inspectable/debuggable, which implicit pattern-matching reasoning does not offer.
The appropriate amount of reasoning depth is task-dependent -- a simple lookup needs little deliberation, while a multi-constraint planning problem benefits from explicit decomposition.
Reasoning quality is bounded by the quality of perception feeding into it -- excellent reasoning over incomplete or wrong information still produces a bad decision.
TH-D1-009.rule_of_thumb: Match reasoning depth to task complexity: trivial, well-pattern-matched decisions don't need expensive deliberation, while genuinely difficult multi-step problems benefit from explicit, inspectable reasoning even at higher cost.
TH-D1-009.summary: The reasoning step is where the agent converts its current perceptions into a decision about the next action, and the amount of deliberation involved varies widely by design. At the fast end, a reactive agent reasons via near-instant pattern matching -- condition X observed, response Y triggered, with little to no explicit intermediate reasoning. At the deliberate end, an agent may generate an explicit chain of thought, weigh multiple candidate actions, simulate likely outcomes, or decompose the problem into sub-goals before committing to an action. Techniques like chain-of-thought prompting, ReAct-style reasoning traces, and explicit self-questioning are all ways of making the reasoning step more thorough, generally at the cost of additional latency and token usage.
TH-D1-009.title: The 'reason' step: from fast pattern-matching to deliberate multi-step thought

common_confusions: Treating all tool calls as equally risky -- a read-only lookup tool (e.g. search) carries far less risk than a write/mutate tool (e.g. send email), even though both are 'tool calls' in the action space.

Assuming output-only actions are entirely risk-free -- generated text can still cause harm (e.g. misinformation, offensive content) even without a direct external side effect, so 'low direct risk' does not mean 'no risk at all.'
key_points: Output-only actions (generating a reply, a summary, a draft) carry low direct risk, since they do not change external state by themselves.
Side-effecting actions (sending, deleting, purchasing, controlling) change state outside the conversation and may be difficult or impossible to reverse.
The irreversibility and real-world impact of an action -- not just its technical complexity -- determines how much scrutiny or confirmation it warrants.
An agent architecture can grant broad autonomy for output-only actions while still gating side-effecting actions behind additional checks (e.g. human confirmation), without contradiction.
Logging every side-effecting action (what was done, when, with what parameters) is a common mitigation that does not prevent mistakes but makes them auditable and recoverable after the fact.
TH-D1-010.rule_of_thumb: When evaluating the risk of an agent's action space, separate 'produces information' from 'changes something in the world' -- the second category deserves materially more caution regardless of how routine it might seem.
TH-D1-010.summary: The act step is where a decision becomes a concrete action, and these actions fall into two broad categories with very different risk profiles. Output-only actions produce text, images, or other content returned to a user or another system component, with no direct external side effect beyond the information conveyed. Side-effecting actions change state in the world outside the conversation -- calling an API that sends an email, writes to a database, moves money, or controls a physical device. Side-effecting actions are inherently higher-risk because, once executed, they may not be undoable, which is why many agent designs apply extra scrutiny (confirmation steps, narrower permissions, logging) specifically to this category of action rather than to output-only responses.
TH-D1-010.title: The 'act' step: output generation vs. real-world side effects

common_confusions: Assuming any system that takes multiple sequential actions is 'closing the loop' -- a fixed sequence that never inspects intermediate outcomes before proceeding is not adaptive, regardless of how many steps it has.

Overlooking silent failure as a loop-breaking problem -- if an action's error or failure is swallowed and not surfaced as a perception, the agent cannot adapt to it even though the architecture nominally supports feedback.
key_points: The defining feature of a loop (vs. a one-way sequence) is that outcomes feed back into future decisions.
Feedback enables error recovery: a failed tool call becomes a perception that can trigger a different action on the next cycle.
Feedback enables refinement: an unsatisfactory intermediate result (e.g. irrelevant search results) can prompt the agent to adjust its approach rather than blindly continuing.
A system that executes several steps in sequence WITHOUT examining each step's actual outcome before proceeding is not really closing the loop, even if it looks superficially similar to an agent.

The quality of an agent's adaptive behavior is bounded by how well action outcomes are surfaced back into its context -- a poorly surfaced outcome (e.g. an error swallowed silently) breaks the feedback loop even if the underlying architecture supports it.
TH-D1-011.rule_of_thumb: To tell a true agent loop apart from a blind fixed sequence, check whether each action's actual outcome is examined and allowed to influence the next decision -- if outcomes are ignored, it's not really closing the loop.
TH-D1-011.summary: What makes perceive-reason-act a LOOP rather than a one-way pipeline is that the outcome of an action is fed back in as a new perception, enabling the agent to adapt based on what actually happened rather than only what it predicted would happen. This feedback is what allows an agent to notice a tool call failed and try something different, discover that a search returned irrelevant results and refine its query, or recognize that a sub-task is complete and move to the next one. Without this feedback connection, a system could still take sequential actions, but it would be executing a fixed plan blindly rather than genuinely adapting -- closer to a workflow than an agent, even if it appeared to be 'looping.'
TH-D1-011.title: Closing the loop: how action outcomes become the next perception

common_confusions: Defaulting to 'the model needs a better prompt' for every failure, when the actual root cause may be missing/bad information reaching the model (a perception failure) or a tool execution error (an action failure) rather than a reasoning deficiency.

Assuming a tool error is always a reasoning failure (the agent 'chose the wrong tool') when it may simply be that the right tool was chosen but its execution failed for an unrelated reason (e.g. a transient network error).
key_points: Perception failures: missing, malformed, truncated, or stale information reaching the agent.
Reasoning failures: adequate information available, but an incorrect decision is drawn from it.
Action failures: a correct decision was made, but its execution did not succeed (tool error, timeout, rejected request).
Diagnosing agent misbehavior requires identifying WHICH phase failed before attempting a fix, since the three failure types have different remedies.

A single observed bad outcome can sometimes stem from a chain of failures across phases (e.g. a perception gap leading to a flawed-but-locally-reasonable decision), requiring root-cause analysis rather than fixing only the most visible symptom.
TH-D1-012.rule_of_thumb: When an agent misbehaves, trace the failure to perceive, reason, or act before fixing anything -- a reasoning fix (e.g. prompt tweaking) will not resolve a perception problem (e.g. missing context), and vice versa.
TH-D1-012.summary: Each phase of the loop has characteristic failure modes. Perception failures occur when the agent is missing needed information, receives malformed/truncated data, or is given stale information it treats as current. Reasoning failures occur when the agent has adequate information but draws an incorrect conclusion -- misapplies logic, hallucinates a fact, or misjudges which action is appropriate. Action failures occur when the correct decision was made but its execution fails -- a tool call errors out, times out, or an API rejects the request. Crucially, these failure types require different fixes: a perception failure is fixed by improving what information reaches the agent, a reasoning failure is fixed by improving the model/prompt/reasoning strategy, and an action failure is fixed by improving the execution layer (retries, error handling, better tool interfaces) -- misdiagnosing which phase failed leads to applying the wrong fix.
TH-D1-012.title: Common failure patterns within the perceive-reason-act loop

common_confusions: Assuming reactive agents cannot use an LLM -- an LLM-based agent that always responds based only on the immediate message with no broader context tracking is still architecturally reactive, regardless of the sophistication of the underlying model.

Confusing 'reactive' with 'fast and simple-minded in general' -- a reactive agent can still implement fairly sophisticated condition-action mappings, as long as the decision is a direct function of current perception without planning ahead.
key_points: A reactive agent maps current perception directly to an action via condition-action rules, with no internal world model.
Reactive agents do not plan ahead -- they do not simulate or consider the future consequences of an action before taking it.
Reactive agents are typically fast and computationally cheap, since there is no deliberation step beyond matching the current situation to a rule.
A classic limitation is handling novel situations that don't cleanly match any predefined rule, since there is no deeper reasoning to fall back on.
Reactive design is well suited to environments requiring fast responses to well-understood, recurring situations (e.g. a simple customer-service FAQ bot matching keywords to canned answers).
TH-D1-013.rule_of_thumb: If a system's action is a direct, fast function of only its current input with no internal model of the broader task state and no lookahead, it is behaving reactively.
TH-D1-013.summary: A reactive agent selects its next action based directly on its current perception, using a fixed mapping from situations to responses (often called condition-action rules), with no internal model of the world beyond what it currently perceives and no explicit planning ahead. Reactive agents are fast and simple to reason about, since behavior is a direct function of current input, but they struggle with tasks that require considering future consequences, remembering context from several steps ago that isn't currently visible, or handling situations that don't match any of their predefined condition-action rules well.
TH-D1-013.title: Reactive agents: stimulus-response with no internal world model

common_confusions: Assuming deliberative agents are always 'better' than reactive ones -- the added planning cost is only worthwhile when the task genuinely benefits from lookahead; for simple, well-understood tasks, the extra computation is often wasted.

Equating deliberation with simply generating a longer response -- deliberation specifically means reasoning over an internal model and considering consequences of future actions, not merely producing more verbose output.
key_points: A deliberative agent maintains and reasons over an internal model of the task/goal state, not just the immediately current perception.
Planning ahead means considering a sequence of future actions and their likely consequences before committing to the first one.
Deliberative agents generally handle novel or complex multi-step situations better than reactive agents, since they're not limited to matching predefined condition-action rules.
The cost of deliberation is higher latency and computation per decision, since the agent must explore and evaluate possibilities rather than directly react.
Explicit planning techniques (e.g. generating a multi-step plan before executing any of it) are a hallmark of deliberative agent design.
TH-D1-014.rule_of_thumb: If a system builds and reasons over an internal model of the task before acting, and considers consequences of candidate action sequences, it is behaving deliberatively -- at the cost of more computation than a direct reactive response.
TH-D1-014.summary: A deliberative agent maintains an internal representation (a 'world model') of its task, environment, or goal state, and uses that model to plan a sequence of actions before executing them, often considering multiple candidate plans and their likely consequences before committing. This planning-ahead capability lets deliberative agents handle novel situations and multi-step problems more robustly than purely reactive agents, since they can reason about consequences rather than only matching current input to a fixed rule -- but this comes at the cost of significantly more computation and latency per decision, since planning requires exploring possibilities rather than directly reacting.
TH-D1-014.title: Deliberative agents: internal world models and planning ahead

common_confusions: Assuming hybrid means 'deliberative all the time, just with some extra rules' -- the point of hybrid design is to AVOID invoking the expensive deliberative layer for the common/easy cases, not to always run both.

Believing the reactive and deliberative layers must be two different models -- the same underlying LLM could serve both roles (a quick low-effort pass vs. an extended reasoning pass), as long as the architecture distinguishes when to invoke which mode.
key_points: Hybrid architectures layer a fast reactive component with a slower deliberative component, routing decisions to the appropriate layer based on situation familiarity or stakes.
The reactive layer handles the common case efficiently; the deliberative layer is invoked selectively, which controls average latency/cost while preserving robustness for hard cases.
A common real-world pattern: fast classification/pattern-matching attempts first, escalating to expensive deliberate reasoning only when the fast path is insufficient or uncertain.
Hybrid design is a practical response to the tradeoff between reactive agents (fast but brittle on novel cases) and deliberative agents (robust but slow/expensive on every decision).
The decision of WHEN to escalate from reactive to deliberative processing is itself a design choice, often based on confidence thresholds, novelty detection, or explicit stakes classification.
TH-D1-015.rule_of_thumb: When a system seems to answer most things quickly but occasionally takes much longer on harder or unusual inputs, that's a signature of a hybrid architecture escalating from a reactive to a deliberative layer.
TH-D1-015.summary: Hybrid architectures combine a fast reactive layer for handling common, well-understood situations with a slower deliberative layer invoked for novel, complex, or high-stakes decisions, aiming to get the speed benefits of reactive behavior where it suffices and the robustness of deliberation where it's actually needed. A typical hybrid design might first attempt a fast reactive match; if no rule confidently applies, or if the situation is flagged as high-stakes or unfamiliar, control is escalated to a deliberative planning process. This layered approach mirrors how many practical systems are built: cheap pattern-matching or classification handles the bulk of routine cases, while a more expensive LLM-based reasoning process is reserved for cases that genuinely need it.
TH-D1-015.title: Hybrid agent architectures: combining reactive and deliberative layers

common_confusions: Assuming deliberative is always the 'more advanced' and therefore correct choice -- for genuinely fast, familiar, repetitive tasks, a reactive design is often the more appropriate engineering choice, not an inferior fallback.
Ignoring latency/cost budgets when selecting an architecture -- a theoretically ideal deliberative approach may be impractical if the task has a hard real-time response requirement.
key_points: Highly dynamic, time-sensitive environments with mostly familiar situations favor reactive architectures for speed.
Tasks requiring multi-step planning or handling novel situations favor deliberative architectures for robustness, despite higher cost.
Mixed environments (mostly routine, occasionally hard) favor hybrid architectures, which selectively invoke deliberation only when needed.
Latency and cost budgets are practical constraints that can force a faster (more reactive) approach even for tasks that would theoretically benefit from more deliberation.
There is no universally 'best' architecture -- the right choice depends on the specific task's novelty, time-sensitivity, and the acceptable cost of being wrong.
TH-D1-016.rule_of_thumb: Match architecture to task shape: fast and familiar favors reactive, complex and novel favors deliberative, and a mix of both favors a hybrid design that escalates selectively.
TH-D1-016.summary: The choice between reactive, deliberative, and hybrid architectures should be driven by properties of the task and environment, not by a general preference for sophistication. Environments that are highly dynamic, time-sensitive, and dominated by familiar, recurring situations favor reactive designs, since there is little time or benefit to deliberate before responding. Environments requiring multi-step problem solving, planning around constraints, or handling genuinely novel situations favor deliberative designs, since the extra computation buys real robustness. Environments with a mix -- mostly routine with occasional hard cases -- favor hybrid designs, which avoid paying the deliberation cost on every single decision. Latency and cost budgets are also a practical constraint: even a task that would theoretically benefit from deliberation may need a faster reactive approximation if real-time response is required.
TH-D1-016.title: Choosing an agent architecture based on task and environment properties

common_confusions: Treating ReAct as just chain-of-thought plus a tool -- the defining feature is the interleaving, so observations from actions can change the reasoning mid-trajectory instead of reasoning being completed before any action is taken.
Assuming the thought text is what does the work in the environment -- thoughts are internal and have no side effects; only the action portion interacts with tools or the world.
key_points: Each iteration follows a thought -> action -> observation pattern, and the observation is appended to the context before the next thought.
Thoughts do not change the environment; they help the agent decompose the goal, track progress, and adjust the plan after surprises or errors.
Actions fetch external evidence (search, lookup, calculation), which grounds later reasoning and reduces the hallucination and error propagation seen in reasoning-only chains.
The explicit trace makes trajectories interpretable and debuggable, but the extra reasoning tokens add latency and cost per step.
The loop ends when the model emits a final answer or a step limit is hit; without a limit, the agent can cycle through repetitive thought-action pairs.
TH-D1-017.rule_of_thumb: If the next step depends on what the last action returned, interleave a thought before each action and feed the observation back; if the whole sequence is known up front and observations cannot change it, a fixed plan or workflow is simpler and cheaper.
TH-D1-017.summary: ReAct is a widely used agent loop pattern in which the model alternates between producing a short natural-language reasoning step (a 'thought'), choosing an action such as a tool call, and then reading the resulting observation before thinking again. Reasoning-only prompting (e.g. chain-of-thought) can hallucinate facts and propagate early mistakes because nothing external checks it, while action-only prompting acts without an explicit running plan. Interleaving the two lets reasoning track and revise the plan and handle exceptions, while actions ground that reasoning in fresh external evidence, and the visible trace makes the agent's trajectory easier for humans to inspect.
TH-D1-017.title: ReAct: interleaving reasoning traces with actions in a single control loop

common_confusions: Confusing interleaved reasoning-action with simply printing a reasoning string before every tool call -- the key property is that the thought actually influences the next action AND the following observation feeds back into the next thought, not merely cosmetic logging.

Assuming more interleaving steps always means better outcomes -- excessive back-and-forth without converging on an answer can indicate the agent is stuck in a loop rather than making genuine progress.
key_points: The interleaved pattern alternates: thought -> action -> observation -> thought -> action -> observation, continuing until the task is resolved.
Explicit 'thought' steps make the agent's reasoning legible and inspectable, which helps with debugging and trust compared to action-only agents.
Observations from each action update the agent's understanding before the next reasoning step, enabling course correction based on real information rather than a static upfront plan.
This pattern directly addresses a weakness of pure chain-of-thought reasoning: it has no mechanism to pull in new external information partway through reasoning.

This pattern also addresses a weakness of pure action-only agents: without an explicit reasoning trace, it's hard to tell why a particular action was chosen or to catch flawed reasoning before it leads to a bad action.
TH-D2-001.rule_of_thumb: If an agent explicitly narrates why it's about to act, acts, observes the result, and then explicitly re-reasons from that observation, it is using an interleaved reasoning-action pattern.
TH-D2-001.summary: Interleaving reasoning and action means an agent alternates between generating an explicit reasoning trace (a 'thought') and taking a concrete action (e.g. calling a tool), rather than either reasoning fully upfront with no action, or acting immediately with no reasoning. After each action, the resulting observation is fed back into the next reasoning step, allowing the agent to adjust its approach based on what it actually learns rather than committing to a single fixed plan before seeing any results. This pattern improves on pure chain-of-thought reasoning (which has no way to incorporate new, external information mid-reasoning) and on pure action-only agents (which have no explicit record of why a given action was chosen).
TH-D2-001.title: Interleaving reasoning and action: the core idea behind ReAct-style agents

common_confusions: Assuming grounding only matters for factual lookup tasks -- grounding is equally important for intermediate computational or logical assumptions that could otherwise silently propagate downstream.

Believing that one grounding action at the very end of reasoning is equivalent to grounding throughout -- a single late check cannot catch an error that already caused many wasted or misdirected reasoning steps earlier in the chain.
key_points: Grounding means checking an assumption or claim against an external, verifiable source (e.g. a tool call result) rather than relying solely on the model's internal, possibly outdated or incorrect, knowledge.
Errors that go unchecked early in a reasoning chain tend to compound, since later reasoning steps build on top of the earlier flawed assumption.
Taking grounding actions throughout the reasoning process (not just at the end) allows earlier correction, which limits how far a wrong assumption can propagate.
A model's internal knowledge can be outdated, incomplete, or simply wrong for a specific case; grounding actions substitute verified, current information for that uncertain internal knowledge.
The earlier an incorrect assumption is checked and corrected, the less reasoning work has to be redone or discarded.
TH-D2-002.rule_of_thumb: The earlier a reasoning chain checks its assumptions against real, external observations, the less an initial error can compound into a confidently wrong final answer.
TH-D2-002.summary: When an agent's reasoning is grounded by real observations from actions (such as tool calls), errors in its internal assumptions get corrected by actual data before they can compound into a wrong final answer. Pure reasoning with no grounding action can confidently proceed from a flawed assumption all the way to a plausible-sounding but incorrect conclusion, since nothing in the process ever checks the assumption against reality. Interleaving actions throughout reasoning (rather than only at the very end) means incorrect assumptions can be caught and corrected early, before the agent has built an elaborate chain of reasoning on top of them.
TH-D2-002.title: Why grounding reasoning in actions reduces hallucination and compounding errors

common_confusions: Assuming longer reasoning traces are always better -- excessive reasoning with no corresponding action can be just as unproductive as acting with no reasoning at all, since the task may require actual external information that only an action can provide.
Treating the thought-to-action transition as governed by a fixed step count -- the appropriate point to act depends on task complexity and current confidence, not an arbitrary fixed schedule.
key_points: At each loop iteration, the agent must decide between continuing to reason or committing to a concrete action, based on whether a well-justified next step has been identified.
Acting too early, before sufficient reasoning, risks wasted, redundant, or incorrect actions (e.g. calling the wrong tool or calling a tool with wrong parameters).
Reasoning too long without ever acting risks never obtaining the real-world information or outcome the task actually requires, since reasoning alone cannot access external systems.
There is no universal fixed number of reasoning steps before acting -- the right balance depends on the task's complexity and how much the agent already knows with confidence.
A sign of a well-tuned interleaved agent is that actions are purposeful and justified by the preceding thought, not reflexive or arbitrary.
TH-D2-003.rule_of_thumb: An agent should act once its reasoning has identified a concrete, justified next step -- not before (risking wasted actions) and not indefinitely after (risking never making real progress).
TH-D2-003.summary: A well-designed interleaved reasoning agent must decide, at each step, whether it has enough information to act (and if so, which action), or whether it needs more reasoning (or more information) before taking any action. Acting prematurely, before sufficiently reasoning about the situation, risks wasted or incorrect tool calls; over-reasoning without ever acting risks never making progress on gathering the real-world information the task actually requires. The decision of when to transition from thought to action is typically driven by whether the current reasoning has identified a concrete, well-justified next step, not by a fixed number of reasoning tokens or a fixed schedule.
TH-D2-003.title: Deciding when to think vs. when to act within an interleaved loop

common_confusions: Assuming all interleaved-loop failures are the same 'the agent got confused' problem -- looping, ignoring observations, and premature conclusion are distinct failure patterns with different root causes and different fixes.
Assuming a step limit alone fixes every failure mode -- a step limit helps contain looping, but does nothing for an agent that ignores observations or concludes prematurely well within that limit.
key_points: Looping: the agent repeats a similar sequence of thought-action-observation without making genuine progress toward resolving the task.
Ignoring observations: the next reasoning step proceeds as if the most recent action's result was never received, effectively wasting that action.
Premature conclusion: the agent commits to a final answer before the gathered observations actually support that conclusion.

Each failure mode often requires a distinct mitigation: step/iteration limits and novelty checks for looping; prompt structuring that foregrounds the latest observation for ignoring-observations; and explicit completeness/confidence checks before finalizing an answer for premature conclusion.
Diagnosing which specific failure pattern occurred (by inspecting the thought-action-observation trace) is usually more productive than making a generic 'try harder' adjustment.
TH-D2-004.rule_of_thumb: When an interleaved agent fails, inspect its thought-action-observation trace to identify whether it looped, ignored an observation, or concluded prematurely -- each has a distinct, targeted fix.
TH-D2-004.summary: Interleaved reasoning-action agents can fail in characteristic ways: looping (repeating a similar thought-action-observation cycle without converging on an answer), ignoring observations (the next thought disregards what the latest action actually returned, as if the action had never happened), and premature conclusion (stopping and answering before the gathered observations actually justify the conclusion). Recognizing these failure patterns is important because they often require different fixes -- looping may call for a step-limit or novelty check, ignoring observations may call for making the observation more prominent in the next prompt, and premature conclusion may call for an explicit completeness check before finalizing an answer.
TH-D2-004.title: Common failure patterns in interleaved reasoning-action loops

common_confusions: Assuming interleaved reasoning-action is always strictly better than chain-of-thought or action-only agents -- for tasks that genuinely don't need external grounding, the extra action-taking overhead of the interleaved pattern may be unnecessary.

Treating chain-of-thought as inherently 'wrong' for needing no external actions -- for self-contained reasoning tasks (e.g. a logic puzzle with all needed information already given), chain-of-thought alone can be entirely appropriate.
key_points: Plain chain-of-thought: explicit reasoning trace, but no way to pull in new external information partway through -- entirely dependent on the model's internal (possibly incomplete or wrong) knowledge.
Plain action-only: takes actions based on current state, but with no explicit, inspectable reasoning trace explaining why a given action was chosen.

Interleaved reasoning-action keeps the inspectability benefit of chain-of-thought while adding the real-world grounding benefit of taking actions throughout the process, not just reasoning in isolation.
The combination specifically helps on tasks that require both multi-step reasoning AND access to external, dynamic, or current information that the model doesn't already have memorized.

None of the three approaches is strictly superior for every task -- simple tasks needing no external information may do fine with plain chain-of-thought, and simple reactive tasks may do fine with plain action-only behavior.
TH-D2-005.rule_of_thumb: Interleaved reasoning-action is most valuable when a task needs BOTH multi-step reasoning AND access to external, dynamic information -- for tasks needing only one of those, a simpler pattern may suffice.
TH-D2-005.summary: Plain chain-of-thought reasoning produces a step-by-step reasoning trace but has no mechanism to incorporate new external information mid-reasoning -- everything must come from the model's internal knowledge, generated upfront. Plain action-only agents take actions based on the current state with no explicit reasoning trace recorded, making their decisions harder to inspect, debug, or trust. The interleaved reasoning-action pattern combines benefits of both: it keeps an explicit, legible reasoning trace (like chain-of-thought) while also grounding that reasoning in real external observations gathered via actions (unlike chain-of-thought, which cannot do this), and unlike plain action-only agents, every action is preceded by an inspectable justification.
TH-D2-005.title: ReAct compared to plain chain-of-thought and plain action-only agents

common_confusions: Assuming decomposition is always worth the overhead -- for genuinely simple tasks, the cost of planning and coordinating sub-tasks can exceed the benefit of decomposing at all.
Treating decomposition as splitting a task into arbitrary equal-sized pieces -- effective decomposition splits along natural sub-problem boundaries, not an arbitrary count or length.
key_points: Decomposition breaks a complex goal into smaller, more tractable sub-tasks, each individually easier to solve and verify.
A monolithic, non-decomposed approach makes it harder to localize exactly where an error occurred within a large, complex response.
Decomposed sub-tasks can often be verified independently, catching errors earlier and more precisely than checking only a final combined output.
If one sub-task fails, a decomposed approach often allows retrying or fixing just that sub-task, rather than discarding and redoing the entire original task.
Decomposition is not free -- it adds overhead in planning how to split the task and in coordinating/combining sub-task results back into a final answer.
TH-D2-006.rule_of_thumb: A good decomposition produces sub-tasks that are individually easier to verify and fix than the original complex task would be as a single unit.
TH-D2-006.summary: Task decomposition is the process of breaking a large, complex goal into a set of smaller, more manageable sub-tasks that are individually easier to solve, verify, and recover from if they fail. Decomposition is valuable because large, monolithic tasks are harder to reason about directly, harder to verify piece by piece, and a single error anywhere in the process can be harder to localize and fix. By contrast, a well-decomposed task allows each sub-task's result to be checked independently, and if one sub-task fails, the agent can often retry or fix just that piece rather than redoing the entire task from scratch.
TH-D2-006.title: Task decomposition: breaking a complex goal into manageable sub-tasks

common_confusions: Assuming a plan generated upfront is fixed and must be followed exactly even if execution reveals it's wrong -- a well-designed plan-and-execute system revises the plan when needed, rather than blindly executing a now-invalid plan.
Treating plan-and-execute and interleaved reasoning-action as mutually exclusive opposites -- many practical systems combine coarse upfront planning with finer-grained interleaving within each step.
key_points: Plan-and-execute generates a full multi-step plan upfront, before executing any step, as opposed to interleaving one step of reasoning and one action at a time.
Upfront planning can produce more globally coherent plans, since the agent considers the whole task structure at once rather than one step at a time.
A risk of plan-and-execute is that an early step's actual result may invalidate assumptions baked into the rest of the plan, requiring re-planning.
A well-designed plan-and-execute agent includes a re-planning or plan-revision step when execution reveals that the original plan no longer fits reality.

Plan-and-execute and interleaved reasoning-action are not mutually exclusive -- some systems plan at a coarse level upfront, then interleave more fine-grained reasoning and action within each planned step.
TH-D2-007.rule_of_thumb: Plan-and-execute trades the interleaved pattern's step-by-step adaptability for more globally coherent upfront structure -- but needs a re-planning mechanism to handle plans invalidated by real execution results.
TH-D2-007.summary: In a plan-and-execute pattern, the agent first generates a multi-step plan in full before executing any of it, then carries out each planned step in sequence (optionally revising the remaining plan if a step's result changes what's needed). This differs from the interleaved reasoning-action pattern, which generates only one next step at a time; plan-and-execute instead commits to a broader structure upfront, which can produce more globally coherent plans but risks the plan becoming invalid partway through if an early step's actual result differs from what was assumed when the plan was made.
TH-D2-007.title: Plan-and-execute: separating upfront planning from step-by-step execution

common_confusions: Assuming tree-of-thought always finds the globally best answer -- it depends heavily on the quality of the branch-evaluation mechanism; a poor evaluator can still prune away the actually-best branch.

Using tree-of-thought on problems with no genuine branching ambiguity -- if there's really only one sensible next step at each point, exploring multiple branches wastes computation without adding value.
key_points: Tree-of-thought generates and evaluates multiple candidate next-steps (branches) at each point, rather than committing to a single linear path.
Weaker branches can be pruned, while more promising branches are explored further, similar in spirit to search algorithms.
This approach helps on problems where a single early wrong turn in a purely linear chain-of-thought would prevent ever reaching the correct answer.
Exploring multiple branches costs more computation than a single linear chain, since multiple candidate paths must be generated and evaluated.
A mechanism for evaluating or scoring branches (to decide which to pursue and which to prune) is a necessary component of this approach, not an optional add-on.
TH-D2-008.rule_of_thumb: Tree-of-thought is worth its extra computational cost specifically when early reasoning steps are genuinely ambiguous and a wrong early commitment would be hard to recover from in a linear chain.
TH-D2-008.summary: Tree-of-thought reasoning explores multiple candidate reasoning paths (branches) from a given point, rather than committing to a single linear chain of reasoning as in standard chain-of-thought. At each branching point, several different next-step options are generated and evaluated, and the most promising branches are pursued further while weaker ones are pruned, similar in spirit to a search process. This approach is valuable for problems where an early reasoning step could plausibly go several different directions, and where committing to the wrong one early (as a purely linear chain would) could prevent reaching the actual correct solution.
TH-D2-008.title: Tree-of-thought: exploring multiple reasoning branches instead of one linear chain

common_confusions: Assuming more sophisticated planning strategies (tree-of-thought) are always better -- for simple, unambiguous tasks, this adds unnecessary computational cost without improving outcomes.

Applying decomposition to tasks whose sub-steps are tightly interdependent -- decomposition works best when sub-tasks can be meaningfully separated; forcing separation onto a tightly coupled problem can produce worse results than treating it as a single unit.
key_points: Simple, linear, unambiguous tasks often need no explicit decomposition or branching strategy -- a straightforward approach suffices.
Tasks with separable, mostly independent sub-goals benefit from decomposition into sub-tasks, optionally planned upfront via plan-and-execute.
Tasks with genuine early-step ambiguity, where a wrong early commitment would be hard to recover from, benefit most from exploring multiple branches (tree-of-thought-style).
The decision also depends on acceptable cost: tree-of-thought-style exploration is more expensive, so it should be reserved for tasks where that exploration is likely to pay off.
Mismatching strategy to task structure wastes computation (e.g. branching on an unambiguous task) or risks poor outcomes (e.g. using no decomposition on a highly complex, interdependent task).
TH-D2-009.rule_of_thumb: Match planning strategy to task structure: simple and linear needs no special strategy, separable sub-goals benefit from decomposition/plan-and-execute, and genuine early-step ambiguity benefits from tree-of-thought-style exploration.
TH-D2-009.summary: The choice between no explicit decomposition, plan-and-execute, and tree-of-thought-style exploration should be driven by the task's structure: how interdependent are the sub-steps, how much does early uncertainty affect later steps, and how costly is it to explore multiple candidate paths. Simple, linear tasks with little ambiguity need no special decomposition strategy at all. Tasks with clearly separable, mostly independent sub-goals benefit from decomposition and plan-and-execute. Tasks where an early decision could plausibly branch in several directions, each requiring exploration to know which is correct, benefit most from tree-of-thought-style approaches, assuming the extra computational cost is acceptable for the task.
TH-D2-009.title: Choosing a planning strategy based on task structure

common_confusions: Equating reflection with simply asking the model 'are you sure?' and accepting whatever it says next -- genuine reflection requires checking against explicit, specific criteria, not just prompting for a vague confidence check.

Assuming reflection always catches every error -- a model's self-critique is still limited by the same underlying knowledge and reasoning limitations that produced the original error, so it is not a complete safety net.
key_points: Reflection means reviewing and critiquing a candidate output against the task's actual requirements before finalizing it.
Generation and critical evaluation are different cognitive tasks -- a model can sometimes catch its own errors on a second, critical pass even though it missed them while generating.
Reflection is not the same as blind regeneration; it specifically targets identified problems and then decides on revisions, rather than discarding and starting over with no diagnosis.
A reflection step typically checks a candidate output against explicit criteria (task requirements, factual correctness, completeness, format) rather than a vague 'does this look right' pass.
Reflection adds a review step and therefore added latency/cost per task, which is a tradeoff against its error-catching benefit.
TH-D2-010.rule_of_thumb: Genuine reflection involves checking a candidate output against explicit criteria and identifying specific issues -- not just regenerating from scratch or giving a vague approval.
TH-D2-010.summary: Reflection is the process by which an agent reviews and critiques its own intermediate or final output, checking it against the task's requirements before accepting it as final. A reflection step can catch errors that the original generation process missed, since generating an answer and critically evaluating that same answer are different cognitive tasks that can surface different issues. Reflection is distinct from simply regenerating a response from scratch -- it specifically involves examining a candidate output for identifiable problems (factual errors, missed requirements, logical gaps) and then deciding whether to revise, and how.
TH-D2-010.title: Reflection: an agent evaluating its own output before finalizing it

common_confusions: Assuming more iterations are always better -- after the first one or two rounds, additional iterations often provide only marginal improvement while still costing additional latency and computation.
Treating the critique step as automatically reliable -- if the critique itself is weak or overly lenient, the loop will converge on an output that still has unaddressed issues.
key_points: A self-critique loop alternates: generate/revise -> critique -> generate/revise -> critique, continuing until the critique finds no major remaining issues or a limit is reached.
This differs from one-shot reflection by allowing multiple rounds, each building on the issues identified in the previous round.
Diminishing returns are typical -- later iterations tend to catch progressively smaller issues than the first round, which usually catches the most significant ones.
A maximum iteration limit (or a 'no further significant issues found' stopping condition) is necessary to prevent the loop from running indefinitely without meaningful improvement.
The critique step's quality determines the loop's value -- a weak or overly lenient critique will approve a flawed output early, limiting how much benefit the loop provides.
TH-D2-011.rule_of_thumb: Expect diminishing returns from additional self-critique rounds -- the first round typically catches the most significant issues, and a stopping condition is needed to avoid unproductive extra iterations.
TH-D2-011.summary: A self-critique loop repeatedly alternates between generating (or revising) a candidate output and critiquing that output, using the critique to produce an improved next version, continuing until the critique finds no further significant issues or a maximum iteration count is reached. This differs from a single one-shot reflection pass by allowing multiple rounds of improvement, each informed by the previous round's identified issues. Diminishing returns are common: the first critique-and-revise round often fixes the most significant issues, while later rounds may surface progressively smaller or more marginal issues, meaning unlimited iteration is rarely worth its added cost.
TH-D2-011.title: Self-critique loops: iterating between generation and critique

common_confusions: Assuming self-reflection is a complete substitute for external verification -- it cannot catch errors rooted in a genuine, systematic knowledge gap shared between generation and critique.

Assuming self-reflection provides no value because it isn't a complete solution -- it remains useful for catching a real and meaningful class of errors (slips, requirement gaps, inconsistencies), just not every class of error.
key_points: If an error stems from a genuine knowledge gap, the critique step -- using the same underlying knowledge -- is likely to share that same gap and fail to catch the error.
Self-reflection is comparatively effective at catching requirement-coverage gaps, logical inconsistencies, and slips that become apparent on a more careful second pass.
Self-reflection is comparatively ineffective at catching errors rooted in the model's systematic misunderstanding or lack of knowledge about a topic.
External verification (tool-based grounding, independent review, human oversight) remains valuable specifically because it does not share the same blind spots as the model's own self-critique.
Relying on self-reflection alone for high-stakes outputs, without any external check, risks leaving systematic errors uncaught.
TH-D2-012.rule_of_thumb: Self-reflection catches slips and requirement gaps well, but shares the same blind spots as the original generation for genuine knowledge gaps -- pair it with external verification for high-stakes outputs.
TH-D2-012.summary: Self-reflection has a fundamental limitation: if a model's error stems from a genuine knowledge gap or systematic reasoning blind spot, that same gap or blind spot is likely to persist during the critique step too, since the critique uses the same underlying model and knowledge. Self-reflection is most effective at catching errors that stem from momentary slips, incomplete coverage of stated requirements, or logical inconsistencies that become visible on a second, more deliberate pass -- but it is much less effective at catching errors that stem from the model simply not knowing or systematically misunderstanding something. This is why external verification (e.g. grounding against a tool, or human review) remains important even when self-reflection is used, especially for high-stakes outputs.
TH-D2-012.title: Limitations of self-reflection: a model cannot fully evaluate its own blind spots

common_confusions: Assuming a confidently worded answer must be well-supported -- phrasing confidence and evidentiary support are independent properties of a response.

Assuming all hedged, uncertain-sounding answers are therefore more trustworthy -- genuine uncertainty should be flagged when it exists, but hedging language alone doesn't guarantee the underlying reasoning is any more or less correct.
key_points: Genuine uncertainty exists when available information is insufficient to confidently determine a single correct answer.
False confidence is a definitive-sounding answer produced despite a weak or absent underlying basis -- a serious risk because it looks the same as genuine confidence from the output's tone alone.
Tone/confidence of phrasing is not a reliable signal of actual correctness, since models can produce confidently worded answers regardless of whether the underlying basis is strong.
Mechanisms like explicit uncertainty estimation, cross-checking against external sources, or evidence-strength flags help distinguish genuinely well-supported answers from under-supported ones.
An agent that cannot distinguish genuine confidence from false confidence will tend to overstate certainty on exactly the cases where hedging or seeking more information would be more appropriate.
TH-D2-013.rule_of_thumb: Never equate confident-sounding phrasing with actual correctness -- the two are independent, and a dedicated mechanism is needed to tell them apart.
TH-D2-013.summary: An agent faces genuine uncertainty when the available information is insufficient to determine a single correct answer with confidence, as opposed to false confidence, where a model produces a definitive-sounding answer despite the underlying basis for that answer being weak or absent. The practical danger of false confidence is that it is often indistinguishable from genuine confidence just by looking at the output's tone -- a confidently worded wrong answer looks the same, on the surface, as a confidently worded correct one. Well-designed agents should have some mechanism (explicit uncertainty estimation, cross-checking against external sources, or flagging low-evidence conclusions) to distinguish cases that warrant confident answers from cases that warrant hedging, clarifying, or seeking more information.
TH-D2-013.title: Recognizing genuine uncertainty vs. false confidence

common_confusions: Assuming clarifying questions are always the best choice -- in fully autonomous, non-interactive settings, asking a question that cannot be answered just stalls the task; stating an assumption and proceeding may be more appropriate there.

Treating all ambiguity as requiring the same handling strategy -- the right choice depends on the cost of guessing wrong and how different the interpretations' consequences are, not a one-size-fits-all rule.
key_points: Proceeding with the most likely interpretation while explicitly stating that assumption keeps the choice visible, even without pausing to ask.
Asking a clarifying question is often the safest strategy, but requires an interactive setting where a question is actually answerable before the agent needs to proceed.
Presenting results for multiple plausible interpretations can be useful when the interpretations' consequences differ significantly and asking isn't feasible.
The right choice among these strategies depends on the cost of a wrong guess, interactivity constraints, and how divergent the different interpretations actually are.
Silently resolving ambiguity with no acknowledgment at all is generally the weakest option, since it hides a real decision point that the user might have wanted to weigh in on.
TH-D2-014.rule_of_thumb: When facing genuine ambiguity, make the ambiguity visible -- via a stated assumption, a clarifying question, or multiple presented interpretations -- rather than silently picking one with no acknowledgment.
TH-D2-014.summary: When a task's instructions are genuinely ambiguous -- admitting multiple reasonable interpretations -- an agent has several possible strategies: proceed with the most likely interpretation and clearly state that assumption, ask a clarifying question before proceeding, or attempt multiple interpretations and present the results of each. The right strategy depends on factors like the cost of guessing wrong, whether a clarifying question is actually feasible (e.g. an interactive setting vs. a fully autonomous batch job), and how different the possible interpretations' consequences actually are. Silently picking one interpretation with no acknowledgment of the ambiguity is generally the weakest strategy, since it hides a real decision point from the user or downstream process.
TH-D2-014.title: Strategies for handling ambiguous task instructions

common_confusions: Assuming a detected error can always be fixed by just editing the final answer -- if later reasoning steps depended on the flawed step, those steps may also need to be redone, not just the final output text.
Relying on only one type of check (e.g. only grounding checks) -- consistency checks and sanity checks can catch different classes of errors that a grounding check alone might miss, and vice versa.
key_points: Reasoning errors can occur at any point in a reasoning process -- a flawed logical step, miscalculation, or misapplied rule.
Detection mechanisms include internal consistency checks, sanity checks against known constraints or plausible ranges, and grounding checks against external verifiable sources.
The earlier a reasoning error is detected, the less subsequent reasoning has been built on top of the flawed step, reducing wasted work and compounding error risk.
Proper recovery typically requires backtracking to the point where the error was introduced and re-reasoning from there, since later conclusions may depend on the now-known-flawed step.
Simply patching the final output without addressing the underlying flawed step risks leaving related, downstream errors uncorrected.
TH-D2-015.rule_of_thumb: When a reasoning error is detected, backtrack to where it was introduced and re-reason from there -- patching only the final output risks leaving related downstream errors in place.
TH-D2-015.summary: Reasoning errors -- flawed logical steps, incorrect calculations, or misapplied rules -- can occur at any point in an agent's reasoning process, and detecting them as early as possible limits how far they propagate before being caught. Detection mechanisms include consistency checks (does this conclusion contradict an earlier established fact?), sanity checks against known constraints (does this answer fall within a plausible range?), and grounding checks (does this match an external, verifiable source?). Once a reasoning error is detected, recovery generally requires backtracking to the point where the error was introduced and re-reasoning from there, rather than simply patching the final output, since later steps built on the flawed step may also need to change.
TH-D2-015.title: Detecting and recovering from reasoning errors mid-task

common_confusions: Assuming hedging is always the 'safer' choice -- excessive hedging has its own real cost: an unhelpfully noncommittal response that fails to actually assist the user.

Treating confidence calibration as a fixed, universal setting -- the appropriate balance depends on the specific task's stakes and the actual strength of the available evidence, not a one-size-fits-all level of caution.
key_points: Overconfidence presents an uncertain or wrong conclusion as definitely correct, risking users acting on unreliable information as if it were reliable.
Excessive hedging qualifies every statement so heavily that the response fails to actually help the user make a decision, wasting the interaction's value.
The right level of expressed confidence should track the actual strength of the underlying evidence, not be fixed at either extreme regardless of the actual situation.
Higher-stakes domains generally warrant more caution against overconfidence specifically, since the cost of a wrong confident answer is higher there.
Calibration -- matching expressed confidence to actual evidentiary strength -- is the underlying goal that balances these two failure modes.
TH-D2-016.rule_of_thumb: Calibrate expressed confidence to actual evidence strength and task stakes -- avoid both overconfident wrong answers and excessively hedged, unhelpfully noncommittal ones.
TH-D2-016.summary: Both overconfidence (presenting an uncertain or wrong conclusion as definitely correct) and excessive hedging (qualifying every statement so heavily that the response becomes unhelpfully noncommittal) are failure modes, but they fail in different ways and have different costs depending on context. Overconfidence risks a user acting on a wrong answer believing it to be reliable, which can be especially costly in high-stakes domains. Excessive hedging risks the response being so qualified that it fails to actually help the user make a decision, effectively wasting the interaction. The appropriate level of expressed confidence should track the actual strength of the underlying evidence or reasoning, calibrated to the stakes of the specific task -- not a fixed, context-independent level of hedging or confidence.
TH-D2-016.title: The cost of overconfidence vs. the cost of excessive hedging

common_confusions: Assuming a detailed, step-by-step thought trace proves the agent reasoned correctly -- a coherent explanation can still rationalize an answer driven by an unmentioned factor.

Concluding that thought traces are worthless because they may be unfaithful -- they remain valuable for spotting loops, ignored observations, and visible logic errors, just not as proof of the model's true internal process.
key_points: A reasoning trace is plausible if it reads like a sensible justification, and faithful only if it reflects the factors that actually determined the model's output.
Studies of chain-of-thought show explanations can systematically omit influential features (for example a biasing hint or answer-position pattern in the prompt) while still sounding coherent.
Models can produce fluent rationalizations for an answer they were nudged toward, so a persuasive thought does not prove the action was correctly motivated.
Inspecting thoughts is still valuable for debugging, but trust in an agent's behavior should rest on grounded observations, tool results, and outcome checks, not on narration alone.
Faithfulness concerns grow with stakes: for high-impact actions, pair trace inspection with independent verification or human review.
TH-D2-017.rule_of_thumb: Read an agent's thoughts as a useful but fallible account of its behavior; verify consequential actions against external observations rather than trusting the narration to be the true reason.
TH-D2-017.summary: The 'thought' steps in an interleaved reasoning-action loop make an agent's behavior legible, but legibility is not the same as faithfulness. A written reasoning trace can be a plausible after-the-fact rationalization that omits the factors that actually drove the model's choice, such as a biasing cue in the prompt, an option ordering effect, or an injected instruction. Treating the trace as a guaranteed window into the model's real decision process can therefore create unwarranted trust, so important actions should be checked against observable evidence and outcomes rather than against the narration alone.
TH-D2-017.title: Faithfulness of reasoning traces: a legible thought is not necessarily the true cause of an action

common_confusions: Treating decoupled planning as the same thing as plain plan-and-execute -- the distinguishing feature is that the plan is written without observing any tool output and the executors do not call the model again between steps.

Assuming decoupling is strictly more accurate because the plan is global -- it saves tokens and enables parallelism, but a plan built on wrong assumptions cannot self-correct unless a re-planning step is added.
key_points: The planner writes the complete sequence of tool calls upfront, referencing earlier results through placeholder variables instead of waiting to see them.
Workers carry out the planned calls without further model reasoning, and a solver step synthesizes the final answer from the gathered evidence.
Interleaved loops re-send the accumulating thought-action-observation history on every step, so decoupling reduces redundant prompt tokens and model calls.
Independent planned calls can run in parallel, which can lower latency when steps do not depend on each other's outputs.
The trade-off is reduced adaptivity: if an early observation contradicts the plan's assumptions, the plan needs a revision or re-planning step, which a fully interleaved loop handles naturally.
TH-D2-018.rule_of_thumb: Choose decoupled planning when the needed tool calls are largely predictable and cost or latency matters; choose interleaving when each observation is likely to change what should happen next.
TH-D2-018.summary: In a decoupled, ReWOO-style design, a planner reasons about the whole task and emits a full plan of tool calls in one pass, using placeholders to refer to results that do not exist yet. Independent workers then execute the tool calls, and a solver combines the collected evidence into a final answer. Because the model is not re-invoked with the growing history after every observation, this avoids repeated prompt overhead and cuts token use compared with a step-by-step interleaved loop, at the price of less ability to adapt to surprising intermediate results.
TH-D2-018.title: Decoupled planning: planning all tool calls upfront without observations (ReWOO-style)

common_confusions: Assuming majority agreement guarantees correctness -- if the model has a systematic misconception, many samples can agree on the same wrong answer.

Confusing self-consistency with tree-of-thought -- self-consistency samples complete chains independently and votes at the end, whereas tree-of-thought evaluates and prunes partial branches during the search.
key_points: The method samples multiple diverse reasoning paths (using non-zero sampling temperature) and takes a majority vote over the final answers, not over the reasoning text.
It improves reliability on problems with a single checkable final answer, such as arithmetic or multiple-choice reasoning, by reducing the impact of one unlucky chain.
Agreement across samples can be used as a confidence signal: strong consensus suggests a more reliable answer, while a scattered vote suggests uncertainty worth flagging or escalating.
Cost scales roughly linearly with the number of sampled chains, and the samples can be generated in parallel.
It is a sampling-and-aggregation technique over independent chains, which differs from tree-of-thought search with branch evaluation and from reflection that revises a single output.
TH-D2-019.rule_of_thumb: When one reasoning chain is a gamble and the answer is easy to compare, sample several chains and trust the consensus -- and treat a split vote as a signal to escalate or verify.
TH-D2-019.summary: Self-consistency replaces a single greedy reasoning chain with several independently sampled chains of thought and selects the final answer that the largest number of chains agree on. It rests on the intuition that a hard problem usually has many valid routes to one correct answer, while flawed chains tend to scatter across different wrong answers. The degree of agreement among samples can also act as a rough confidence signal, though it multiplies cost and does not help when the model's mistakes are consistent.
TH-D2-019.title: Self-consistency: sampling several reasoning paths and voting on the answer

common_confusions: Believing Reflexion fine-tunes the model -- the model's parameters stay fixed, and improvement comes entirely from reflective text carried into later attempts.

Assuming reflection works equally well without a good feedback signal -- if the agent has no reliable evidence about why it failed, its reflection may simply restate or reinforce the original mistake.
key_points: The loop is attempt -> evaluate -> write a verbal reflection on what failed -> store it in memory -> retry with the reflection in context.
Learning happens through text in the prompt and memory, not through gradient updates or fine-tuning of the model's weights.

Feedback can be external (unit tests, environment rewards, tool errors) or model-generated, and reflections grounded in concrete external signals are generally more reliable than purely self-judged ones.
The memory buffer is typically bounded, since stuffing in every past reflection would crowd the context; keeping only recent or most useful lessons is a practical design choice.
It differs from a single-pass self-critique loop because the lessons persist across separate episodes and target the next attempt, rather than only revising the current draft.
TH-D2-020.rule_of_thumb: Use cross-attempt reflection when an agent can retry a task and receive a concrete failure signal; the written lesson, not a weight change, is what carries learning to the next trial.
TH-D2-020.summary: In Reflexion-style agents, reflection is not just a polish pass on one output: after a failed attempt, the agent converts feedback (such as test results, an environment reward, or an evaluator's judgment) into a short written lesson and stores it in an episodic memory buffer. On the next trial that lesson is added to the context, so the agent changes its behavior without any weight updates. This acts like trial-and-error learning in language, and it depends on getting a trustworthy feedback signal about what went wrong.
TH-D2-020.title: Reflexion-style learning across attempts: verbal lessons stored in episodic memory

common_confusions: Treating abstention as a failure to be minimized -- on the cases the model is likely to get wrong, abstaining is the correct behavior and improves the reliability of what is answered.

Assuming abstention and excessive hedging are the same -- abstention is a clear decision to withhold or escalate based on measured uncertainty, whereas excessive hedging buries an answer under vague qualifiers.
key_points: Abstention is driven by an uncertainty signal, such as sample disagreement, token-level probabilities, or an explicitly stated confidence, compared against a threshold.
Raising the threshold increases precision on answered cases but reduces coverage, so the threshold should be tuned to the stakes and the cost of a wrong answer versus a deferral.
Abstention is helpful for questions that cannot be answered from available information, where a fabricated answer would otherwise be a hallucination.
A good abstention outcome is actionable: the agent states what is missing or hands off to a human or a retrieval step, instead of returning a bare refusal.
Uncertainty signals are only useful if reasonably calibrated; a model that is confidently wrong will not abstain when it should.
TH-D2-021.rule_of_thumb: Set the abstention threshold by the cost of a wrong answer versus the cost of a deferral, and make every abstention hand off a next step rather than a dead end.
TH-D2-021.summary: Selective abstention means an agent deliberately declines to give a definitive answer, or escalates to a human or a verifying tool, when its uncertainty estimate indicates the answer is unreliable. A confidence threshold sets the trade-off: abstaining on the most uncertain cases raises the accuracy of the answers that are given, but lowers coverage because fewer questions are answered. Abstention is especially useful for unanswerable questions and high-stakes actions, where a wrong confident answer costs more than a deferral.
TH-D2-021.title: Selective abstention: declining to answer or escalating when uncertainty is high

common_confusions: Assuming a sufficiently advanced model could eventually act in the real world without tools -- the fundamental limitation isn't model capability, it's that text generation alone has no mechanism to cause external side effects or access live data.

Believing the model itself executes the tool's underlying code -- in practice, a separate execution layer runs the actual action and returns a result, which the model then incorporates as an observation.
key_points: A language model's only native capability is producing text conditioned on its training data and current context -- it cannot natively observe or affect the external world.
Tools provide a bridge: a tool call requests that an external system perform an action or return information, with the result fed back as an observation.
Without tools, a model cannot verify its claims against current, real-world data, nor can it cause real side effects like sending messages or updating records.
Tool use converts a model from a purely text-generating system into a system that can gather real information and take real actions mediated through defined interfaces.
The model itself does not directly execute a tool -- it requests the action, and a separate execution layer actually performs it and returns the result.
