TH-D3-001.rule_of_thumb: If a task requires information the model wasn't trained on, requires current/changing data, or requires a real-world side effect, the model needs a tool -- no amount of better prompting can substitute for actually taking that action.
TH-D3-001.summary: A language model, by itself, can only produce text based on patterns learned during training -- it has no inherent ability to observe the current state of the world, fetch live data, or cause real-world side effects like sending an email or modifying a database. Tools bridge this gap by giving the model a way to invoke external functionality: a tool call lets the model request that some external system perform an action or return information, and the result is fed back into the model's context as an observation. Without tools, a model is fundamentally limited to producing plausible-sounding text derived from its training data and the current conversation, with no way to verify that text against reality or to actually change anything outside the conversation.
TH-D3-001.title: Why language models alone cannot act in or observe the real world

common_confusions: Assuming a model trained very recently has no freshness problem -- any gap between training cutoff and actual use, however small, still exposes the model to being wrong about fast-changing facts.

Treating all information as equally freshness-sensitive -- stable facts (e.g. historical events, well-established scientific principles) are much less at risk from staleness than rapidly changing data.
key_points: A model's training data has a fixed cutoff point; anything that changed or emerged after that point is unknown to the model unaided.
Freshness-sensitive information (prices, weather, news, current events, inventory) is particularly at risk of being wrong if answered from training data alone.
Tools that query live sources fetch information at the actual moment of use, closing the gap between training cutoff and current reality.
The size of the risk from stale information scales with how fast the relevant information actually changes -- a slowly changing fact is less risky to answer from memory than a rapidly changing one.
Even if a model's training data was very recent at training time, by the time it's actually deployed and used, enough time may have passed for freshness-sensitive facts to be out of date.
TH-D3-002.rule_of_thumb: For any fact that could plausibly have changed since the model's training cutoff, prefer a tool-based live lookup over the model's internal, necessarily time-limited knowledge.
TH-D3-002.summary: A model's knowledge is fixed at the point its training data was collected, meaning anything that has changed, or any information that didn't exist, since that point is simply unavailable to the model from its training alone. Tools that query live external sources (search, databases, APIs) address this by fetching current information at the moment it's actually needed, rather than relying on the model's necessarily stale internal knowledge. This is especially important for rapidly changing information (prices, weather, news, inventory levels) where even a small gap between training cutoff and current use could make the model's unaided answer meaningfully wrong.
TH-D3-002.title: Freshness: tools provide access to information a model's training cannot have

common_confusions: Treating all tool calls as equally low-risk -- action tools with real side effects carry categorically different risk than read-only information retrieval, and should be designed and reviewed with that difference in mind.

Assuming a confirmation step is always needed for every action tool regardless of its actual reversibility or stakes -- the appropriate level of caution should scale with how consequential and reversible the specific action actually is.
key_points: Action tools cause real, persistent side effects in external systems, distinct from information-retrieval tools that only fetch and return data.
A mistaken call to an information-retrieval tool typically just produces a wrong or unhelpful answer; a mistaken call to an action tool can cause a real, potentially hard-to-reverse consequence.
This asymmetry in consequence severity is why action tools generally warrant more caution, confirmation steps, or guardrails than read-only tools.
Agents that can both retrieve information and take actions need some way to distinguish these tool categories and apply appropriate caution to each.

The real-world consequence of an action tool call persists even if the agent's subsequent reasoning realizes the action was a mistake -- unlike a bad in-context assumption, a sent email or placed order cannot simply be 'un-thought'.
TH-D3-003.rule_of_thumb: Treat action tools (with real, persistent side effects) with more caution than read-only information tools, since a mistaken call to an action tool cannot simply be undone by further reasoning.
TH-D3-003.summary: Beyond fetching information, tools also allow an agent to cause real changes in the external world: sending a message, creating a calendar event, placing an order, modifying a database record. These are fundamentally different from information-retrieval tools because they have side effects that persist and affect systems outside the conversation, meaning a mistaken or premature action-tool call can have real consequences that a mistaken information-retrieval call does not (a wrong search query just gives a wrong answer; a wrong 'send payment' call actually sends money). This distinction matters for how cautiously different categories of tools should be invoked -- side-effecting action tools generally warrant more scrutiny, confirmation, or safeguards than read-only information tools.
TH-D3-003.title: Real-world actions: tools enable agents to actually change external state

common_confusions: Assuming grounding guarantees correctness -- a retrieved source can itself be wrong, outdated, or misread; grounding provides traceability and a path to verification, not an absolute correctness guarantee.

Assuming every single claim needs explicit grounding -- stable, well-established facts can reasonably come from internal knowledge, while grounding's value is highest for current, specific, or high-stakes claims.
key_points: Grounding anchors a claim to a specific, verifiable external source, rather than relying solely on the model's internal, un-traceable knowledge.
Ungrounded claims from internal knowledge alone have no external check, creating room for hallucination -- confidently stated but incorrect claims.
A grounded claim has a traceable origin, making it possible to distinguish 'the source was wrong' from 'the model misrepresented a correct source' when an error is found.
Grounding does not guarantee correctness (the retrieved source itself could be wrong or outdated), but it does provide a path to verify and audit claims that ungrounded generation lacks.

Not every claim needs grounding -- stable, well-established facts may be safely drawn from internal knowledge, while claims about current, specific, or high-stakes information benefit most from grounding.
TH-D3-004.rule_of_thumb: Grounding doesn't guarantee a claim is correct, but it gives the claim a traceable, checkable origin -- which ungrounded generation from internal knowledge alone cannot provide.
TH-D3-004.summary: Grounding means basing a claim or answer on a specific, verifiable, external source rather than solely on the model's internal, generated knowledge. When a model answers purely from internal knowledge, there is no external check on whether that knowledge is accurate for the specific case at hand, which creates room for hallucination -- confidently stated claims that are actually incorrect. Grounding a claim in a tool-retrieved source gives that claim a traceable origin: if the claim turns out wrong, it's possible to check whether the retrieved source itself was wrong, or whether the model misrepresented a correct source, which is a meaningfully different (and more fixable) situation than an ungrounded claim with no traceable origin at all.
TH-D3-004.title: Grounding reduces hallucination by anchoring claims to verifiable sources

common_confusions: Assuming more tool calls always make an agent more capable or reliable -- unnecessary tool calls on self-contained tasks add cost and complexity without improving the outcome.

Assuming tools are only needed for exotic or rare tasks -- common tasks like checking current prices, dates, or user-specific account details routinely require tool-based grounding even though they feel mundane.
key_points: A tool is likely needed when a task references current/changing information, requires a real-world side effect, needs precise computation, or needs system-specific private data.
A tool is likely unnecessary when a task is self-contained, relies on stable/well-established knowledge, and is fully specified within the given prompt.
Reaching for a tool when none is actually needed adds unnecessary latency, complexity, and potential points of failure without a corresponding benefit.
Failing to reach for a tool when one is genuinely needed risks an ungrounded, possibly stale, or simply incorrect answer for information the model cannot reliably know.
The decision of whether to use a tool should be driven by the specific information/capability gap in the task, not by a blanket policy of always or never using tools.
TH-D3-005.rule_of_thumb: Reach for a tool specifically when the task needs current information, a real side effect, precise computation, or system-specific data the model couldn't possibly know -- not as a reflexive default either way.
TH-D3-005.summary: Not every task benefits from or requires tool use -- deciding when a tool is genuinely needed depends on whether the task requires information or capabilities the model doesn't already reliably have. Signals that a tool is needed include: the task references current or frequently changing information, the task requires a real-world side effect (sending something, modifying a record), the task requires precise computation beyond reliable mental arithmetic, or the task requires information specific to a system the model has no way to have memorized (e.g. a specific user's private account data). Conversely, tasks that are self-contained, stable, and fully specified within the prompt typically do not need a tool, and reaching for one anyway adds unnecessary latency and complexity.
TH-D3-005.title: Deciding when a task genuinely requires a tool vs. when it does not

common_confusions: Assuming tool selection errors are always a reasoning failure -- they can equally stem from unclear or overlapping tool descriptions that give the agent insufficient information to distinguish between candidates.
Assuming the most recently used or most familiar tool is always the right choice -- selection should be based on actual fit to the current need, not habit or recency.
key_points: Correct tool selection requires matching the actual task need against each candidate tool's documented purpose, not superficial name similarity or habit.

Clear, specific tool descriptions (purpose, expected inputs, return format) are essential inputs to correct selection -- an agent can only reason as well as the information it's given about each tool.
Ambiguous or significantly overlapping tool descriptions increase the risk of the agent selecting an unsuitable tool for the actual need.
When multiple tools could plausibly serve a need, the one that most precisely matches the specific requirement (not just a loosely related one) should generally be preferred.
Poor tool selection can occur even when the model's reasoning process is otherwise sound, if the available tool descriptions themselves are unclear or misleading.
TH-D3-006.rule_of_thumb: Good tool selection depends as much on clear, specific tool descriptions as on the model's reasoning -- ambiguous descriptions undermine even a well-reasoning agent's ability to choose correctly.
TH-D3-006.summary: When an agent has access to multiple tools, selecting the correct one for a given sub-task requires matching the task's actual need against each tool's documented purpose and capabilities, rather than guessing based on superficial similarity in naming or defaulting to the most frequently used tool. Clear, specific tool descriptions (what the tool does, what inputs it expects, what it returns) are essential for correct selection, since an agent reasoning about which tool to use can only reason as well as the information available to it about each candidate tool. Ambiguous or overlapping tool descriptions increase the risk of selecting the wrong tool for a given need.
TH-D3-006.title: Tool selection: choosing the right tool among several available options

common_confusions: Assuming a tool failure always means the wrong tool was selected -- correct tool selection with poorly constructed parameters is an equally common and distinct failure mode.

Assuming a 'successful' tool call result is automatically a useful or correct one -- a call can execute without error yet return a nonsensical or unhelpful result due to vague or poorly chosen parameters.
key_points: Correct parameter construction requires supplying all required arguments in the correct format and type expected by the tool.
A correctly selected tool can still fail to produce a useful result if its call parameters are vague, malformed, or incomplete.
Common parameter errors include wrong data types/formats (e.g. date formats), missing required fields, and overly vague or under-specified query content.
Validation that rejects malformed calls early with a clear, specific error is preferable to a call that fails silently or returns a misleading 'successful' but nonsensical result.
Good tool interfaces typically document expected parameter types/formats explicitly, which reduces the chance of malformed calls when that documentation is actually used.
TH-D3-007.rule_of_thumb: Even perfect tool selection can fail if the call's parameters are vague, malformed, or incomplete -- parameter construction is a distinct source of error from tool selection.
TH-D3-007.summary: Beyond selecting the right tool, an agent must also construct the call's parameters correctly: supplying required arguments, using the correct format or type for each, and avoiding missing or malformed values that would cause the call to fail or return a misleading result. Parameter construction errors can occur even when tool selection was correct -- for example, selecting the right search tool but passing an overly vague or malformed query, or passing a date in the wrong format for the tool's expected input. Robust tool interfaces often include validation that rejects malformed calls early with a clear error, which is preferable to the call either failing silently or producing a nonsensical but 'successful' result.
TH-D3-007.title: Constructing correct tool call parameters/arguments

common_confusions: Assuming parallel invocation is always faster and therefore always better -- it is only valid (and only actually faster in a meaningful sense) when the calls involved are truly independent of each other's results.
Assuming all multi-tool tasks must be sequential by default -- unnecessarily sequentializing independent calls wastes time without any correctness benefit.
key_points: Parallel tool invocation is appropriate specifically when multiple needed calls are genuinely independent of each other's results.
Parallelizing independent calls offers a real latency advantage by avoiding unnecessary sequential waiting.
Sequential invocation is required when a later call's parameters or even its necessity depend on an earlier call's actual result.
Incorrectly parallelizing dependent calls risks making a later call with missing or wrong information, since the data it needed from an earlier call isn't available yet.
Incorrectly sequentializing genuinely independent calls wastes time waiting unnecessarily, without any correctness benefit.
TH-D3-008.rule_of_thumb: Parallelize only genuinely independent tool calls; keep dependent calls sequential, since a later call needing an earlier result cannot be meaningfully issued before that result exists.
TH-D3-008.summary: When a task requires multiple tool calls, those calls can be made sequentially (one at a time, with each call potentially informed by the previous one's result) or in parallel (multiple independent calls issued at once, since they don't depend on each other's results). Parallel invocation is appropriate when the needed calls are genuinely independent -- the outcome of one does not affect what should be requested in another -- and offers a latency advantage by avoiding needless waiting between unrelated calls. Sequential invocation is required when a later call's parameters or necessity actually depend on an earlier call's result, since parallelizing in that case would mean making the later call before the information it needs is even available.
TH-D3-008.title: Sequential vs. parallel tool invocation

common_confusions: Assuming exposing every available tool at all times is always safer -- a large, overlapping tool list can itself increase the risk of incorrect selection, which is its own source of error.
Assuming tool exposure should be fixed once and never adjusted per context -- scoping the exposed tool set to the current task category is a practical, commonly used mitigation.
key_points: Too few available tools can leave genuine task needs unmet, forcing the agent to attempt tasks it has no real way to complete correctly.
Too many available tools, especially with overlapping purposes, increases the risk of incorrect tool selection and adds reasoning overhead.
Exposing only the subset of tools relevant to the current context or task category is a common mitigation that reduces both selection errors and processing overhead.
The right number of exposed tools is context-dependent -- it should reflect what's actually likely to be needed for the current task category, not a fixed universal count.
Tool exposure design is a tradeoff between coverage (not missing something needed) and selection accuracy/efficiency (not overwhelming the agent with irrelevant options).
TH-D3-009.rule_of_thumb: Expose the tools actually relevant to the current task context, not the full universe of defined tools -- this balances coverage against selection accuracy and overhead.
TH-D3-009.summary: The number and variety of tools made available to an agent at a given time is itself a design choice: too few tools can leave genuine task needs unmet, while too many tools -- especially with overlapping or poorly distinguished purposes -- increases the risk of incorrect selection and can also increase the cognitive/computational burden of reasoning about which to use. A common mitigation is to expose only the subset of tools actually relevant to the current context or task category, rather than always exposing every tool the system has ever defined, which both reduces selection errors and can reduce latency/cost from processing a large tool list on every request.
TH-D3-009.title: Deciding how many tools to expose to an agent at once

common_confusions: Assuming all tool failures look the same and can be handled with one blanket strategy (e.g. always retry) -- unavailability, explicit errors, and misleading-success results need meaningfully different responses.
Assuming a tool call that returns without an explicit error must have succeeded meaningfully -- misleading-success results specifically present this trap, requiring active result sanity-checking.
key_points: Unavailability failures (timeouts, outages, unreachable services) often warrant a retry or a fallback tool, since the issue is often transient or routable around.
Explicit error failures (invalid input, permission denied, rate limits) often warrant correcting the input and retrying, or reporting the specific failure if correction isn't possible.
Misleading-but-successful results are the most dangerous category, since the call appears to have worked while actually returning something unhelpful or wrong, with no explicit error signal.
Different failure categories call for different responses -- treating every failure the same way (e.g. always just retrying) is unlikely to be effective across all categories.

Sanity-checking a tool's result against what was actually expected or needed is an important safeguard specifically against the misleading-success category, which has no explicit error to trigger a response.
TH-D3-010.rule_of_thumb: Match the recovery strategy to the specific failure category -- unavailability often needs a retry/fallback, explicit errors often need correction, and misleading-success results need active sanity-checking since nothing else will flag them.
TH-D3-010.summary: Tool-use failures broadly fall into a few categories: the tool is unavailable (times out, is down, or cannot be reached), the tool returns an explicit error (invalid input, permission denied, rate limited), or the tool returns a result that looks successful but is actually misleading or wrong (e.g. an empty result set that gets misinterpreted as 'nothing exists' rather than 'the query was malformed'). Each category calls for a different response: unavailability often calls for a retry (possibly with backoff) or a fallback tool; explicit errors often call for correcting the input and retrying, or reporting the specific failure if it cannot be corrected; misleading-but-successful results are the most dangerous category, since nothing on the surface signals a problem, requiring the agent to sanity-check results rather than accept them uncritically.
TH-D3-010.title: Categorizing tool-use failures: unavailable, erroring, and misleading results

common_confusions: Assuming retrying is always a safe, harmless default response to any failure -- retrying a persistently failing call (e.g. due to permanently invalid input) wastes time without any realistic chance of success.
Assuming unlimited retries are more thorough and therefore better -- a sensible stopping condition is necessary to avoid wasting resources on a call that will never succeed.
key_points: Retrying is appropriate for plausibly transient failures (timeouts, temporary unavailability), where conditions might genuinely change between attempts.
Retrying a call that fails for a persistent reason (bad input, permanent unavailability) wastes resources without ever succeeding, since nothing has changed to make the retry more likely to work.
Good retry design includes a limited attempt count, backoff between attempts, and a clear stopping condition.
After exhausting retries, the appropriate next step is typically to try an alternative approach (different tool, different parameters) or to report the failure clearly, not to retry indefinitely.
Distinguishing transient from persistent failure causes is important for deciding whether retrying is actually a sensible strategy for a given failure.
TH-D3-011.rule_of_thumb: Retry only for plausibly transient failures, with a limited attempt count and backoff -- retrying a persistent failure indefinitely wastes resources without any realistic chance of success.
TH-D3-011.summary: Retrying a failed tool call is appropriate when the failure is plausibly transient (e.g. a timeout or temporary unavailability) and the retry can reasonably be expected to succeed if conditions change. Blind, unlimited retrying of a call that fails for a persistent reason (e.g. consistently invalid input, or a permanently unavailable service) wastes time and resources without ever succeeding. Good retry design typically includes a limited number of attempts, some backoff (waiting longer between successive attempts) to avoid overwhelming a struggling service, and a clear stopping point after which the agent gives up on that specific approach and either tries an alternative or reports the failure.
TH-D3-011.title: Retry strategies: when to retry, how, and when to stop

common_confusions: Assuming a fallback must be functionally identical to the primary approach -- a reasonable, even if partial, alternative that lets the task still make progress is valuable, not just a perfect substitute.
Assuming retrying is always a substitute for having a fallback -- retrying only helps with transient failures; a fallback is specifically needed for failures that retrying cannot fix.
key_points: A fallback is an alternative tool, source, or approach used when the primary one fails or is unavailable.
Fallbacks are especially valuable for failures unlikely to resolve via retrying, where an alternative path offers a genuinely different chance of success.
Good fallback design anticipates plausible failure modes in advance and prepares a reasonable alternative, rather than improvising ad hoc in the moment of failure.
A fallback does not need to be perfectly equivalent to the primary approach -- it needs to provide a reasonable, if sometimes partial, way to still make progress on the task.
Having no fallback at all means a single point of failure: if the primary tool/approach fails, the task simply cannot proceed.
TH-D3-012.rule_of_thumb: Design fallback paths in advance for plausible failure modes of a primary tool -- relying on improvised, in-the-moment alternatives is less reliable than a deliberately prepared fallback.
TH-D3-012.summary: A fallback strategy involves having an alternative tool, data source, or approach ready to use if the primary one fails or is unavailable, rather than the agent having only a single path with no alternative when that path doesn't work. Fallbacks are valuable specifically for failures that are unlikely to resolve through retrying (e.g. a tool being fully deprecated or a particular data source genuinely lacking the needed information), where an alternative path offers a real chance of still completing the task. Designing good fallbacks requires anticipating, in advance, which failures are plausible for a given primary approach and what a reasonable alternative would be -- fallback behavior invented ad hoc in the moment of failure, with no advance thought, is less reliable than a deliberately designed fallback path.
TH-D3-012.title: Fallback strategies: alternative tools or approaches when the primary one fails

common_confusions: Assuming an empty search result always means 'nothing exists' -- it may just as easily mean the query itself was too narrow, malformed, or pointed at the wrong source.

Assuming the absence of an explicit error is sufficient confirmation that a tool call fully and correctly answered the actual question -- this is exactly the gap that misleading-success failures exploit.
key_points: A tool call without an explicit error does not guarantee the result is actually correct, complete, or useful for the agent's actual purpose.

Empty or unexpected results are a common trigger for this failure mode -- they can reflect either a genuine true negative or a flawed, overly narrow query, and these two cases need to be distinguished rather than conflated.
Sanity-checking means actively questioning whether a result makes sense given what was expected, rather than treating any error-free call as having fully answered the actual question.
For high-stakes conclusions, cross-checking a surprising or pivotal result against another independent source adds a further safeguard against this failure mode.
This failure mode is dangerous precisely because nothing on the surface (no exception, no error code) signals that something went wrong -- active scrutiny is required to catch it.
TH-D3-013.rule_of_thumb: Treat an empty or surprising 'successful' tool result as a prompt to sanity-check the query and result, not as automatic proof of a true negative.
TH-D3-013.summary: The most insidious tool-use failure is a call that returns without an explicit error but produces a result that is actually wrong, empty, or misleading for the agent's actual purpose -- for example, a search tool returning zero results that gets misinterpreted as definitive proof something doesn't exist, when the real cause was an overly narrow or malformed query. Guarding against this requires the agent to sanity-check a tool's result against what was actually expected, rather than treating 'no explicit error' as equivalent to 'this result answers my question correctly.' Useful sanity checks include considering whether an empty or surprising result might indicate a flawed query rather than a true negative, and cross-checking surprising results against another source when the stakes are high enough to warrant it.
TH-D3-013.title: Detecting misleading 'successful' tool results through sanity-checking

common_confusions: Assuming protocol discovery makes every tool safe.
Confusing a tool schema with authorization.
Treating a successful invocation as proof that the result is correct.
key_points: Tool schemas make capability discovery and argument construction more explicit.
A protocol is an interoperability layer, not an authorization policy.
Descriptions should state inputs, outputs, errors, and side effects.
Discovered tools still require validation, least privilege, and result checking.
TH-D3-014.rule_of_thumb: A protocol can make tools discoverable and interoperable; it cannot replace permission checks or evaluation.
TH-D3-014.summary: Protocol-mediated tool discovery gives an agent structured descriptions of available capabilities, inputs, outputs, and operational boundaries. The research literature on tool-using language models shows why models need explicit interfaces and schemas rather than guessing how external functions work. An MCP-style protocol applies that interface principle at the host-to-tool boundary; it improves discoverability and interoperability but does not itself grant authorization or guarantee safe results.
TH-D3-014.title: Protocol-mediated tool discovery and context exchange

common_confusions: Assuming that attaching a source link to an answer proves the answer is supported -- the link may point to a passage that does not contain or even contradicts the claim.
Treating citation quality as the same thing as answer correctness -- a correct answer can be uncited, and a well-cited answer can still be wrong if the source itself is wrong.
Assuming citations must be generated after the fact -- recording provenance at retrieval time is more reliable than asking the model to recall sources later.
key_points: Attribution links individual claims in an answer to the specific retrieved passages that support them, making the answer auditable.

Citation quality is a separate dimension from answer fluency and answer correctness: an answer can read well and be right yet still lack supporting citations, or carry citations that do not support it.
A citation can be wrong in two ways: pointing to a source that does not contain the claim (unsupported), or pointing to a source that contradicts it.
Requiring the agent to record references as it gathers evidence (rather than reconstructing them afterward) makes attribution far more reliable.
Even strong systems often leave a meaningful share of statements without complete citation support, so attribution should be checked, not assumed.
TH-D3-015.rule_of_thumb: A claim is grounded only if the cited passage actually supports it -- verify that each citation entails its claim, not merely that a citation exists.
TH-D3-015.summary: Retrieving a source is only half of grounding; the answer must also make clear which claim rests on which piece of evidence. Systems such as WebGPT required the model to collect references while browsing so that humans could check factual accuracy, and the ALCE benchmark evaluates citations separately from fluency and correctness. Attribution turns 'trust me' into 'check this passage', but a citation is only useful if the cited source really supports the specific claim attached to it.
TH-D3-015.title: Citation and attribution: grounded answers should point to the evidence behind each claim

common_confusions: Assuming a code tool makes the answer automatically correct -- the interpreter computes exactly what the program says, so a mis-specified program yields a precisely wrong result.
Assuming a longer written chain of thought is just as reliable as executing code for exact arithmetic -- text-based calculation remains error-prone even when the decomposition is right.
Treating model-generated code as safe to run directly with full privileges -- it must be executed in a restricted sandbox.
key_points: Separating problem formulation (the model's strength) from calculation (the interpreter's strength) improves accuracy on numerical and symbolic tasks.
The model's output becomes a program whose execution result is the observation, rather than a chain of text calculations the model must get right token by token.
A correct-looking program can still encode a wrong formulation of the problem, so the result should be sanity-checked against expectations.
Generated code is untrusted input: execution should be sandboxed with limited permissions, resources, and network access.
Code execution is unnecessary for simple tasks the model handles reliably; it adds latency and a new failure surface.
TH-D3-016.rule_of_thumb: When a task needs exact multi-step computation, have the model write the code and let a sandboxed interpreter run it, then sanity-check the formulation rather than trusting the number blindly.
TH-D3-016.summary: Language models decompose problems well but often make arithmetic and logic slips when they carry out the calculation step themselves. Program-aided approaches such as PAL and Program of Thoughts have the model write a program as its reasoning and delegate the actual execution to an interpreter, so the model handles understanding and the runtime handles exact computation. This makes a code-execution tool the right choice for precise numeric, date, or data-transformation work, with the caveat that generated code is itself untrusted and must run in a restricted environment.
TH-D3-016.title: Delegating exact computation to a code-execution tool instead of reasoning it out in text

common_confusions: Assuming a schema-valid call is a correct call -- it can be well-formed yet reference the wrong entity or an unsafe value.
Equating 'the model was told to answer in JSON' with 'the output is guaranteed to match the schema' -- only constrained generation or validation provides that guarantee.
Assuming strict schemas remove the need for error handling -- incomplete, refused, or semantically invalid calls still need a defined response path.
key_points: Schema-constrained output guarantees syntactic validity (parseable, required fields present, types and enums respected) but not semantic correctness.
Constraining the output format is different from merely asking for JSON in the prompt, which gives no guarantee that a particular schema is followed.
Tight schemas -- enums for closed sets, explicit formats, required versus optional fields -- shrink the space of possible mistakes at the interface.
Business-rule validation (does this record exist, is this amount within limits, is the caller permitted) belongs in the execution layer, after schema validation.
A refusal or truncated output can still occur, so the caller must handle responses that do not contain a complete, valid call.
TH-D3-017.rule_of_thumb: Use schema constraints to eliminate malformed calls, then validate meaning and permission separately -- a valid shape says nothing about whether the values are right.
TH-D3-017.summary: Structured function calling asks the model to emit tool arguments as data that must match a declared schema, and constrained decoding can enforce that every output parses and respects field names, types, and enumerations. This removes a whole class of malformed-call failures such as invalid JSON, missing required fields, or wrong types. It does not make the values correct: a call can be perfectly schema-valid while naming the wrong customer, an out-of-range quantity, or a nonexistent record, so semantic validation and authorization checks must still happen in the execution layer.
TH-D3-017.title: Structured function calling: schema-conformant arguments are not the same as correct arguments

common_confusions: Assuming returning everything the API provides is safest -- oversized or noisy responses consume context and can bury the signal the agent needs.
Assuming an error response only needs a status code -- actionable error text is what lets the agent self-correct its next call.
Treating tool design like designing an API for deterministic developers -- the consumer is a non-deterministic reader whose behavior depends on how the output is phrased.
key_points: Return high-signal fields that inform the next step (names, statuses) rather than cryptic internal identifiers; resolving opaque IDs to meaningful values reduces retrieval errors.
Bound response size with pagination, filtering, range selection, or truncation, and tell the agent how to narrow its request when output is cut off.
Error messages should say what was wrong and how to fix the call, rather than returning bare codes or stack traces.
Offering a concise-versus-detailed option lets the agent fetch identifiers only when it needs them for a follow-up call.
Good tool design is validated empirically by running agents against evaluation tasks, since the best response format varies by task and model.
TH-D3-018.rule_of_thumb: Write each tool's output for the agent that must act on it next: small, meaningful, and with errors that explain the fix.
TH-D3-018.summary: A tool's return value is the observation the agent reasons over, so its design directly shapes later decisions. Responses that dump low-level identifiers, huge payloads, or opaque error codes waste context and invite mistakes, while responses that return high-signal, human-meaningful fields, limit size through pagination or filtering with sensible defaults, and explain errors in actionable terms help the agent choose its next call correctly. Tool design is therefore partly interface design for a non-deterministic reader, and it benefits from being evaluated with real agent runs.
TH-D3-018.title: Designing tool responses for the agent: concise, meaningful, and actionable output

common_confusions: Assuming a failed or timed-out response means the action did not happen -- the effect may have occurred and only the response was lost.
Assuming backoff and attempt limits alone make retrying an action tool safe -- they bound load but do nothing to prevent duplicate side effects.
Assuming idempotency means the call can only be made once -- it means repeated calls converge to the same end state, not that repeats are rejected with an error.
key_points: A timeout or dropped connection on an action tool is ambiguous: the action may have been completed even though no confirmation arrived.
An idempotent operation produces the same end state whether it is executed once or several times, which makes retries safe.
A client-generated unique request key lets the receiving system detect and ignore duplicate submissions of the same intended action.
When an action is not idempotent, verify the actual state by a read-only query before retrying, rather than blindly repeating the call.
Retry policy should differ by tool risk tier: automatic retries for reads, guarded retries for idempotent writes, human confirmation for non-idempotent irreversible actions.
TH-D3-019.rule_of_thumb: Before retrying a side-effecting call, ask whether the first attempt may already have succeeded -- if so, use an idempotency key or check state first.
TH-D3-019.summary: Retrying a read-only call is harmless, but retrying an action tool after an ambiguous failure can repeat the side effect: a timeout on a payment or ticket-creation call does not reveal whether the action actually happened. Making such operations idempotent, for example by attaching a unique request key so a repeated call is recognized as the same request, lets the system retry safely. Where idempotency is unavailable, the agent should first check the current state of the external system, or escalate to a human, before repeating a non-reversible action.
TH-D3-019.title: Idempotency and side-effect safety when retrying action tools

common_confusions: Assuming self-reflection without new evidence is as good as tool-based verification -- without external feedback the model often just reaffirms its draft.
Assuming any tool can verify any claim -- the verifier must be capable of testing the specific property in question.
Treating the verifier's verdict as infallible -- an empty search result or a missing test case does not prove the draft is wrong or right.
key_points: A verify-then-revise loop uses tools as independent checks on a draft, for example search for facts or execution for code.
External feedback is more reliable than asking the model to re-read its own answer, which tends to reinforce its original mistakes.
The choice of verification tool should match the property being checked: factual claims need evidence sources, code needs execution or tests, format needs a validator.
The loop needs a stopping rule, such as a verification pass or a revision limit, to avoid endless revision.
The verification tool can itself be wrong or incomplete, so a failed check is a signal to investigate rather than automatic proof of an error.
TH-D3-020.rule_of_thumb: Verify with a tool that is independent of the model and suited to the property being checked, and cap the number of revision rounds.
TH-D3-020.summary: Models are unreliable at judging their own outputs from introspection alone, but they can improve when they check claims against external tools and revise based on the evidence. The CRITIC framework has the model draft an answer, use appropriate tools (a search engine for factual claims, a code interpreter for program correctness) to evaluate it, and then revise using that feedback. The key lesson is that independent external feedback, not self-assessment, is what makes the correction loop trustworthy.
TH-D3-020.title: Verifying outputs with external tools: tool-interactive critique and revision

common_confusions: Assuming working memory is unlimited just because a context window is large -- a large window raises the limit but does not remove it; something can still eventually be pushed out as a long task continues.

Confusing information falling out of working memory due to displacement with deliberate, intentional forgetting -- these are different mechanisms with different implications for whether the information can be easily recovered.
key_points: Working memory is the information immediately available within the current context -- no separate retrieval step is needed to use it.
Working memory is naturally bounded in size (limited by context window constraints), unlike long-term memory, which can in principle store much more.
Information can fall out of working memory simply by being displaced by newer information, which is a different mechanism from a deliberate decision to discard something from long-term memory.
Working memory is well suited to the current task's immediate context: the ongoing conversation, recent tool outputs, and the current reasoning chain.
Because working memory is limited, agents handling long or complex tasks need some strategy for managing what stays in working memory versus what gets moved to or retrieved from long-term storage.
TH-D4-001.rule_of_thumb: If information is directly present in the current context with no retrieval step needed, it's in working memory; if it requires an explicit retrieval step to bring back, it's in long-term memory.
TH-D4-001.summary: Working memory (or short-term memory) in an agent context refers to the information immediately available within the current reasoning context -- the current conversation, recent observations, and intermediate reasoning steps that the agent can directly reference without any separate retrieval step. This is distinct from long-term memory, which persists across sessions or beyond what fits in the immediate context, and must be deliberately retrieved before it becomes usable. Working memory is naturally limited in size (bounded by the context window), meaning older information can be pushed out or 'forgotten' simply by virtue of new information displacing it, not because it was deliberately discarded.
TH-D4-001.title: Working memory: what's immediately available within the current context

common_confusions: Assuming simply storing information in long-term memory is sufficient -- without an effective retrieval mechanism to surface it at the right time, stored information provides no practical benefit.

Assuming long-term memory retrieval happens automatically with no design effort -- a deliberate retrieval mechanism (e.g. a relevance-based search) must be built and tuned for retrieval to actually work well.
key_points: Long-term memory persists beyond the current context window and across sessions, unlike working memory which is tied to the current immediate context.
Using long-term memory requires an explicit retrieval step -- information doesn't become usable just by existing in storage; it must be actively brought into working memory.
A retrieval mechanism (e.g. relevance-based search over stored memories) is necessary to decide what to actually pull from long-term storage for the current situation.
Long-term memory enables continuity across sessions (e.g. remembering past user preferences or facts) that working memory alone, being limited to the current context, cannot provide.
The quality of an agent's long-term memory use depends heavily on how well its retrieval mechanism identifies genuinely relevant stored information for the current situation.
TH-D4-002.rule_of_thumb: Long-term memory's value depends entirely on having a good retrieval mechanism -- information that's stored but never retrieved when relevant provides no actual benefit to the agent's behavior.
TH-D4-002.summary: Long-term memory refers to information stored outside the immediate working context, persisting across sessions or far beyond what any single context window could hold, and requiring a deliberate retrieval step before it can actually be used in reasoning. This retrieval step is itself a design point: an agent needs some mechanism (e.g. a search over stored memory, keyed by relevance to the current situation) to decide what to pull from long-term storage into working memory when it's actually needed. Long-term memory enables an agent to maintain continuity across sessions (e.g. remembering a user's past preferences) and to accumulate knowledge beyond what any single context window could hold at once.
TH-D4-002.title: Long-term memory: persistent storage retrieved on demand

common_confusions: Assuming a bigger context window eliminates the need for long-term memory entirely -- even a large window is still finite, and long-term memory additionally provides persistence ACROSS sessions, which no context window size can provide on its own.

Assuming long-term memory alone, with no working memory concept, is sufficient -- the agent still needs an immediately available context to reason over moment to moment, which is what working memory provides.
key_points: Working-memory-only designs don't scale: as context grows, older (possibly still relevant) information eventually gets pushed out or truncated.
Long-term-memory-only designs don't make practical sense either, since the agent always needs some immediately available working context to actually reason over.
Effective designs typically combine both: working memory for the current task context, long-term memory as a supplementary store retrieved into working memory when relevant.
The two memory types are complementary, not substitutes for each other -- each addresses a limitation the other has.

A key design question is WHEN to move information between the two -- what to proactively or selectively save to long-term memory, and what to retrieve back into working memory given the current situation.
TH-D4-003.rule_of_thumb: Working memory and long-term memory are complementary, not substitutes -- effective agent memory design uses both together, each addressing a limitation the other has.
TH-D4-003.summary: Relying solely on working memory (keeping everything in the immediate context) is simple but doesn't scale: as a task or conversation grows, eventually the context window fills up, forcing older information to be dropped or truncated, potentially losing something still relevant. Relying solely on long-term memory with no working memory concept doesn't make sense either, since the agent still needs some immediately available context to reason over at any given moment -- long-term memory supplements, rather than replaces, the need for a working context. Effective agent memory design typically uses working memory for the immediate task context and long-term memory as a supplementary store that's retrieved into working memory when relevant, rather than treating either as a complete solution on its own.
TH-D4-003.title: The tradeoff between working memory and long-term memory for agent design

common_confusions: Assuming it's always safer to save everything to long-term memory just in case -- this risks cluttering the store and making genuinely useful information harder to find and retrieve later.
Assuming long-term memory should only ever store explicit user preferences -- useful persisted information can include a range of recurring facts and context, not just stated preferences.
key_points: Not all working-memory content is worth persisting; deciding what to save requires judgment about likely future relevance, not blanket saving or blanket discarding.
Over-saving nearly everything risks a cluttered long-term store where genuinely useful information becomes harder to retrieve amid low-value noise.
Under-saving risks losing information that would have been valuable in a future session, if it's discarded without ever being persisted.
A useful signal for what to save is whether the information is likely to recur in relevance (e.g. a stated long-term preference) versus purely transient, one-off task details.

The specific policy for what to persist is a design choice that should reflect the actual use case -- a customer-preference-tracking agent has different save criteria than a one-off calculation assistant.
TH-D4-004.rule_of_thumb: Save to long-term memory based on likely future relevance, not blanket save-everything or save-nothing policies -- both extremes have real costs.
TH-D4-004.summary: Not everything that passes through an agent's working memory is worth persisting into long-term storage -- deciding what to save requires judgment about what's likely to be useful again later versus what was only relevant to the immediate moment. Over-saving (persisting nearly everything) risks a cluttered long-term store where genuinely useful information becomes harder to find amid low-value noise, and can waste storage/retrieval resources. Under-saving risks losing information that would have been valuable to retrieve in a future session. A reasonable approach weighs signals like whether the information is likely to recur in relevance (e.g. a stated user preference likely to matter again) versus information that was only relevant to resolving the current, one-off request.
TH-D4-004.title: Deciding what information should be moved from working memory into long-term storage

common_confusions: Confusing episodic memory with general factual knowledge -- 'the user mentioned they prefer email on Tuesday the 3rd' is episodic (a specific event), while 'the user generally prefers email over phone calls' is more like a general fact drawn from or informed by episodic observations.
Assuming episodic memory retrieval is just exact keyword matching -- useful episodic retrieval often requires matching based on situational similarity, not just literal text overlap.
key_points: Episodic memory stores specific past events or experiences, tied to a particular time, context, and situation.
Examples include a record of a specific past conversation, a specific action and its outcome, or a specific interaction with a particular user.
Episodic memory is valuable for recalling precedent -- what happened in a similar past situation -- and for maintaining continuity in an ongoing relationship or process.
Episodic memory is distinct from general factual knowledge, since it's about a specific occurrence, not a general truth that holds regardless of any particular event.
Retrieving relevant episodic memories typically requires matching the current situation against stored past situations for similarity, not just exact keyword matching.
TH-D4-005.rule_of_thumb: Episodic memory answers 'what specifically happened, when, in what situation' -- if the content is tied to a specific past occurrence rather than a general truth, it's episodic.
TH-D4-005.summary: Episodic memory refers to records of specific past events or experiences -- what happened, when, and in what context -- as opposed to general facts or skills. For an agent, episodic memory might include a record of a specific past conversation, a specific action taken and its outcome, or a specific interaction with a particular user at a particular time. Episodic memory is valuable for tasks that benefit from recalling precedent (what happened in a similar situation before) or for maintaining continuity about a specific ongoing relationship or process, as opposed to general world knowledge that applies regardless of any specific past event.
TH-D4-005.title: Episodic memory: records of specific past events and experiences

common_confusions: Assuming semantic memory must come only from explicit statements of general facts -- it can also be generalized or inferred from a pattern across multiple specific episodic observations.

Treating episodic and semantic memory as needing identical retrieval approaches -- episodic retrieval often benefits from situational similarity matching, while semantic retrieval often benefits more from topical/conceptual relevance matching.
key_points: Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge that hold true independent of any specific past event or occasion.
Unlike episodic memory, semantic memory content is useful on its own as a standing fact, without needing to reference a specific originating event.
Semantic memory can be built up by generalizing from multiple episodic observations over time, though the two remain distinct in how they're used.
Examples of semantic memory include general domain facts, generalized user preferences, and stable rules or definitions relevant to the agent's tasks.
Retrieval of semantic memory is typically based on topical/conceptual relevance to the current need, rather than situational similarity to a specific past event.
TH-D4-006.rule_of_thumb: Semantic memory answers 'what's generally true' -- if the content is useful as a standing fact without needing to reference a specific past occasion, it's semantic.
TH-D4-006.summary: Semantic memory refers to general facts and knowledge that hold true independent of any specific event or occasion -- for example, a general fact about how a particular process works, a stable preference a user has expressed as a general rule, or domain knowledge not tied to any one specific interaction. Unlike episodic memory, semantic memory content doesn't need to reference when or in what specific context it was learned to be useful; it's useful simply as a standing fact. Semantic memory can be built up FROM episodic memories over time (e.g. observing the same preference stated in several different episodes might generalize into a standing semantic fact), but the two serve different purposes and are retrieved differently.
TH-D4-006.title: Semantic memory: general facts and knowledge independent of specific events

common_confusions: Confusing a procedural memory (a general reusable method) with an episodic memory of one specific instance where that method happened to be used -- the general method itself is procedural, while a specific past application of it is episodic.
Assuming procedural memory, once stored, should never be revised -- a procedure that consistently underperforms should be updated, not treated as an unchangeable fixed recipe.
key_points: Procedural memory stores knowledge of HOW to accomplish a type of task -- a sequence of steps, strategy, or reusable procedure.
This is distinct from episodic memory (specific past events) and semantic memory (general facts) -- procedural memory is specifically about method or process.
A reusable multi-step plan template for a recurring task type is a clear example of procedural memory.
Procedural memory's value is avoiding re-deriving the same successful approach from scratch every time a similar task recurs.
Procedural memory can be refined over time -- if a stored procedure consistently underperforms, that's a signal it may need to be updated or replaced, not treated as a fixed, permanent recipe.
TH-D4-007.rule_of_thumb: Procedural memory answers 'how to do this type of task' -- if the content is a reusable method, strategy, or sequence of steps, it's procedural, not episodic or semantic.
TH-D4-007.summary: Procedural memory refers to knowledge of HOW to do something -- a sequence of steps, a learned strategy, or a reusable procedure for accomplishing a type of task -- as opposed to episodic memory (what happened) or semantic memory (general facts). For an agent, procedural memory might include a reusable multi-step plan template for a recurring task type, a learned strategy for handling a certain category of problem, or a refined approach that worked well in the past and is worth reusing rather than re-deriving from scratch each time. Procedural memory is valuable specifically because it lets an agent avoid re-deriving the same successful approach repeatedly, instead reusing (and potentially refining) a known-good procedure.
TH-D4-007.title: Procedural memory: knowledge of how to perform tasks or sequences of actions

common_confusions: Assuming all memory types should always be stored and searched together as one pool -- this risks retrieving the wrong TYPE of memory for the current need, even if something superficially relevant is found.

Assuming this three-way distinction means the types are entirely unrelated -- semantic memory can be generalized FROM episodic memory, showing they can be connected even while serving different functional roles.
key_points: Each memory type (episodic, semantic, procedural) is typically retrieved differently and serves a different purpose in reasoning.
Conflating all memory into one undifferentiated store risks retrieval mismatches -- surfacing the wrong type of memory for the actual current need.
Separately organized (or at least separately taggable) storage for each type allows more targeted, relevant retrieval than one large undifferentiated pool.
A reasoning process that needs 'how to do this' benefits from procedural memory retrieval specifically, not a mix of episodic anecdotes and general facts.
This distinction is a design and organization tool, not a claim that the three types are entirely unrelated -- semantic memory can be generalized from episodic observations, for instance.
TH-D4-008.rule_of_thumb: Organize and retrieve episodic, semantic, and procedural memory separately when possible -- matching retrieval to the actual type of need reduces mismatches versus one undifferentiated memory pool.
TH-D4-008.summary: Distinguishing episodic, semantic, and procedural memory matters because each type is retrieved differently, used differently in reasoning, and benefits from a different storage/organization approach. Conflating them into one undifferentiated memory store risks retrieval that mismatches the actual need -- for example, retrieving a specific past event when what's actually needed is a general fact, or retrieving a general fact when what's actually needed is a proven step-by-step procedure. Designing separate (or at least separately taggable) storage and retrieval paths for each memory type allows an agent to request the kind of memory that's actually relevant to its current need, rather than searching one large undifferentiated pool and hoping something useful surfaces.
TH-D4-008.title: Why distinguishing episodic, semantic, and procedural memory matters for agent design

common_confusions: Assuming retrieving more memories is always safer or better -- surfacing too many memories, including marginally relevant ones, can dilute focus and bury the genuinely useful content.

Assuming relevance is purely about literal word overlap -- genuinely relevant memories can be phrased very differently from the current context, requiring similarity measures that go beyond exact text matching.
key_points: Relevance-based retrieval selects memories based on actual pertinence to the current situation, not blanket retrieval of everything stored.
Similarity-based ranking (e.g. semantic similarity between current context and stored content) is a common mechanism for assessing relevance.
Retrieving only the most relevant few memories, rather than everything that loosely matches, keeps the retrieved content focused and useful.
Poor relevance assessment risks two failure directions: surfacing superficially similar but unhelpful memories, or missing genuinely relevant memories phrased differently.
The quality of relevance assessment directly determines whether long-term memory's stored content actually translates into better agent behavior.
TH-D4-009.rule_of_thumb: Good retrieval surfaces the few memories most pertinent to the current situation -- not everything stored, and not merely whatever is superficially similar in wording.
TH-D4-009.summary: Relevance-based retrieval means selecting which stored memories to surface for the current situation based on how pertinent they actually are to what's needed right now, rather than retrieving everything stored or retrieving based on an arbitrary or purely chronological criterion. A common approach uses similarity between the current context and stored memory content (e.g. via semantic similarity) to rank candidates, surfacing the most relevant few rather than everything that technically matches some loose criterion. Poor relevance assessment can surface memories that are superficially similar but not actually useful for the current need, or miss genuinely relevant memories that happen to be phrased very differently from the current context.
TH-D4-009.title: Relevance-based retrieval: surfacing the right memories for the current situation

common_confusions: Assuming the most relevant memory is always the right one to use, regardless of how old it is -- a highly relevant but very outdated memory can be actively misleading if the underlying fact has since changed.

Assuming frequency alone (how often something was observed) is sufficient without considering relevance -- a frequently observed but currently irrelevant pattern isn't useful just because it recurred often in the past.
key_points: Recency (how recently formed or used) is a signal that more recent information may better reflect current reality, especially for facts that can change over time.
Frequency (how often something has recurred) is a signal that a repeatedly observed pattern is more likely stable and generalizable than a one-off anomaly.
Relying on relevance alone, with no recency consideration, risks surfacing an outdated memory that was once relevant but no longer reflects current reality.
Relying on relevance alone, with no frequency consideration, risks treating a one-off anomaly with the same weight as a well-established, repeatedly confirmed pattern.
Combining relevance, recency, and frequency generally produces more robust retrieval than relying on any single signal in isolation.
TH-D4-010.rule_of_thumb: Combine relevance with recency and frequency signals -- relevance alone can surface outdated information or treat a one-off anomaly as if it were an established pattern.
TH-D4-010.summary: Beyond pure topical/situational relevance, two other signals commonly inform what memory to retrieve or prioritize: recency (how recently a memory was formed or last used) and frequency (how often a similar memory or fact has recurred). Recency matters because more recent information is often more likely to reflect the current state of affairs, especially for information that can change over time; frequency matters because something observed repeatedly is more likely to be a stable, generalizable pattern rather than a one-off anomaly. Good retrieval systems typically combine relevance with recency and frequency rather than relying on any single signal alone, since each addresses a different kind of blind spot the others have.
TH-D4-010.title: Recency and frequency as additional signals alongside pure relevance

common_confusions: Assuming forgetting is always bad and should be minimized at all costs -- deliberately removing clearly outdated or superseded information actually improves the quality and usefulness of what remains.

Assuming any forgetting mechanism is equally good -- indiscriminate forgetting (with no judgment about what's actually safe to remove) risks losing genuinely useful information, which is a different problem from targeted, judgment-based forgetting.
key_points: Deliberate forgetting -- removing or deprioritizing outdated or superseded memories -- is a useful mechanism, not purely a limitation to be avoided.
Without some forgetting mechanism, a memory store accumulates outdated content indefinitely, risking clutter and stale information surfacing in retrieval.
Effective forgetting policies typically target explicitly superseded information (e.g. an old address replaced by a new one) or reliably irrelevant content.
Indiscriminate forgetting (discarding content with no judgment about what's actually safe to remove) risks losing genuinely useful information, just as indiscriminate saving risks clutter.
A well-designed memory system treats forgetting as an active maintenance process, not simply the passive result of running out of storage space.
TH-D4-011.rule_of_thumb: Deliberate forgetting of outdated or superseded information is a useful maintenance mechanism, not just an unfortunate limitation -- the goal is targeted removal, not indiscriminate discarding.
TH-D4-011.summary: While forgetting is sometimes framed purely as a limitation (losing information that might have been useful), deliberate forgetting -- actively removing or deprioritizing stored memories that are outdated, superseded, or no longer relevant -- is also a useful mechanism for keeping a memory store effective. Without some form of deliberate forgetting, a long-term memory store accumulates outdated or superseded information indefinitely, which can clutter retrieval and risk surfacing stale content alongside or instead of current, accurate information. Effective forgetting policies typically target information that has been explicitly superseded (e.g. an old address replaced by a new one) or that has become reliably irrelevant, rather than discarding content indiscriminately.
TH-D4-011.title: Forgetting as a deliberate, useful mechanism rather than only a limitation

common_confusions: Assuming every contradiction should automatically be resolved by trusting whichever information is newer -- some contradictions reflect noise or a special-case exception rather than a genuine, permanent update.

Assuming contradictions should always be flagged to a human rather than resolved automatically -- for low-stakes, clearly-an-update situations, automatically treating the newer information as current is often perfectly reasonable.
key_points: Contradictions between stored memory and newly observed information require some resolution policy, rather than silently retaining both with no reconciliation.
Treating newer information as superseding older information is a reasonable common default, since it often better reflects current reality.
This default isn't universally correct -- some apparent contradictions reflect noise, a misunderstanding, or a context-specific exception, not a true, permanent update.
For high-stakes contradictions, a clarifying check may be more appropriate than silently assuming the newer information is simply correct and overriding the old.

Good memory design distinguishes between information that should be replaced, information that should coexist as still relevant in some contexts, and information needing explicit clarification before being resolved either way.
TH-D4-012.rule_of_thumb: Default to treating newer information as superseding older information, but add a clarifying check for high-stakes contradictions rather than always resolving silently.
TH-D4-012.summary: When a newly observed piece of information contradicts something already stored in memory (e.g. a user states a new address that differs from a previously stored one), an agent needs a policy for resolving the contradiction rather than simply holding both pieces of information with no resolution. A common, reasonable default is to treat the newer information as superseding the older one, since it more likely reflects current reality -- but this isn't universally correct, since some contradictions reflect a genuine correction while others might reflect noise, a misunderstanding, or a context-specific exception rather than a true update. Good design distinguishes between information that should be fully replaced, information that should be retained alongside the new information as still contextually relevant, and information that warrants a clarifying check given the stakes of acting on the wrong version.
TH-D4-012.title: Handling contradictions between stored memories and current information

common_confusions: Assuming a summary is a lossless substitute for the original turns -- it keeps the gist but can drop or alter exact details that later turns turn out to need.
Assuming truncation and summarization are equivalent ways to 'make room' -- truncation removes information entirely, while summarization retains a compressed (and possibly distorted) version.
key_points: Truncation drops the oldest content outright; it is simple and cheap but can discard facts the task still depends on.
Rolling summarization compresses older turns into a running summary that is updated as new turns arrive, keeping the recent turns verbatim.
Summaries are lossy: exact values, identifiers, and precise constraints are the details most likely to be distorted or omitted.
Information that must survive exactly (user constraints, IDs, commitments) is better pinned or written to a separate store than left to the summarizer.
Summarization has its own cost and error profile: every summarization pass can introduce drift, and errors compound when summaries are summarized repeatedly.
TH-D4-013.rule_of_thumb: Summarize old turns to keep the gist, keep recent turns verbatim, and pin must-keep exact facts outside the summary rather than trusting the summarizer to retain them.
TH-D4-013.summary: When a long conversation or task outgrows the context window, an agent must decide what to do with older content. The simplest option is truncation (dropping the oldest turns), which is cheap but silently loses facts, decisions, and commitments. A common alternative is rolling (recursive) summarization: older turns are periodically compressed into a running summary that is carried forward alongside the most recent turns verbatim. Summarization preserves gist at a lower token cost but is lossy, so exact details such as IDs, numbers, or quoted constraints can be blurred or dropped.
TH-D4-013.title: Managing context overflow: truncation versus rolling summarization of working memory

common_confusions: Assuming tiered memory makes the context window effectively infinite at no cost -- every page-in or page-out is an extra operation, and facts the agent fails to retrieve are as good as forgotten.

Confusing a tiered, agent-managed design with plain RAG -- RAG usually retrieves into context automatically on each query, while a tiered design also lets the agent write, evict, and reorganize its own memory.
key_points: A small in-context tier (working memory) is backed by larger external tiers, analogous to RAM backed by disk in an operating system.
The agent manages data movement through explicit memory operations (search, read, write, evict) rather than the system silently deciding what is in context.
Eviction is typically triggered by context pressure, with evicted content summarized and/or written to external storage so it remains retrievable.
The illusion of unbounded memory is only as good as the agent's decisions about what to page in and out; poor paging decisions mean needed facts are not in context when required.
Paging adds extra model calls and latency, a real cost that must be weighed against simply using a larger window or a summary.
TH-D4-014.rule_of_thumb: Treat the context window like fast, scarce memory: keep only what is needed now in it, and page everything else to external tiers the agent can explicitly search.
TH-D4-014.summary: MemGPT-style designs borrow the operating-system idea of hierarchical memory: a small, fast 'main context' (working memory inside the prompt) is backed by larger, slower external tiers such as a recall store of past messages and an archival store of long-term knowledge. The agent itself issues explicit memory operations, such as searching external storage or writing a fact out, to move data between tiers, which creates the appearance of an unbounded context. Pressure signals, such as the main context nearing its limit, trigger eviction and summarization so that the working context stays within budget.
TH-D4-014.title: Tiered memory with agent-managed paging: MemGPT-style virtual context

common_confusions: Treating scratchpad content as long-term memory -- it lives in the working context and disappears or gets displaced unless explicitly saved elsewhere.
Assuming a longer scratchpad is always better -- it consumes context budget and can bury the information the next step actually needs.
key_points: A scratchpad holds intermediate computations, partial results, and notes for the current task, written into the context so later steps can read them.
Writing out intermediate steps improves accuracy on multi-step problems that cannot be reliably solved in a single pass.
Scratchpad content consumes context budget, so long scratchpads compete with other working-memory content and may need condensing.
It is transient by default: only conclusions worth reusing should be promoted from the scratchpad into long-term memory.
A scratchpad differs from a final answer or a stored memory: it records the work in progress, not the outcome to be persisted or shown.
TH-D4-015.rule_of_thumb: Use a scratchpad to hold work in progress; promote only durable conclusions to long-term memory and drop or condense the rest.
TH-D4-015.summary: A scratchpad is a region of the working context where an agent writes out intermediate results, partial plans, and notes while working through a multi-step task, rather than trying to produce the final answer in one pass. Externalizing intermediate steps lets later steps condition on earlier results and substantially improves performance on tasks that need unbounded multi-step computation. A scratchpad is working memory by nature: it is scoped to the current task, consumes context tokens, and is normally discarded or condensed when the task ends unless something is deliberately promoted to long-term storage.
TH-D4-015.title: Scratchpads: working memory for intermediate reasoning steps

common_confusions: Assuming reflection updates the model's weights -- it writes text into memory that is later retrieved into context; the model itself is unchanged.
Assuming reflections are always accurate because the agent produced them -- they are inferences from limited evidence and can encode a mistaken lesson that then gets reinforced.
key_points: Reflection reads recent episodic memories and writes new higher-level memories (lessons, patterns, conclusions) back into the store.
Reflections can be triggered periodically or when the accumulated importance of recent events passes a threshold.
Reflexion-style agents store verbal lessons from failed attempts and condition later attempts on them, improving without any weight updates.
Consolidation is how semantic and procedural knowledge is derived from episodes: many specific events become one general insight or reusable lesson.
Reflections are model-generated and can be wrong; an incorrect lesson that is stored and retrieved repeatedly can bias behavior, so provenance back to source episodes is valuable.
TH-D4-016.rule_of_thumb: Periodically distill raw episodes into compact lessons and store them as new memories -- but keep a link back to the evidence, because a wrong reflection is retrieved as confidently as a right one.
TH-D4-016.summary: Reflection is a process in which an agent periodically reviews its recent episodic memories (or the outcomes of failed attempts) and writes new, higher-level memories that summarize patterns, lessons, or conclusions. In generative-agent designs, reflections are triggered when accumulated importance of recent events passes a threshold, and the resulting insights are stored back into the memory stream so they can be retrieved like any other memory. In Reflexion-style loops, verbal self-critique after a failed trial is stored in an episodic buffer and consulted on the next attempt. Consolidation converts many specific episodes into compact semantic or procedural knowledge that is cheaper and more useful to retrieve.
TH-D4-016.title: Reflection-based memory consolidation: turning raw episodes into higher-level insights

common_confusions: Confusing a skill library with an episodic log of past runs -- the library stores generalized, verified methods, while an episodic log records what happened in specific past attempts.
Assuming any procedure the agent produced should be saved -- unverified or failed procedures pollute the library and get reused later.
key_points: A skill library stores reusable procedures (for example executable code or step templates) that can be retrieved and reused for new tasks.
Admission to the library should be gated on verification: only procedures shown to work through execution feedback or checks are stored.
Skills are typically indexed by a description of what they do, so retrieval is by task similarity rather than by exact name.
Stored skills can call or build on one another, letting simple learned behaviors compose into more complex ones.
Stale or failing skills must be updated or removed; an unmaintained library can confidently reuse procedures that no longer work.
TH-D4-017.rule_of_thumb: Save a procedure to the skill library only after it is verified to work, retrieve it by task description, and revise or retire it when it starts failing.
TH-D4-017.summary: A skill library is a store of reusable, executable procedures that an agent has learned and verified, indexed so that a relevant skill can be retrieved for a new task. In Voyager-style designs a skill is added only after execution feedback or self-verification shows it works, and later skills can call earlier ones, so capabilities compose and accumulate over time. Because skills are retrieved by task description and reused rather than re-derived, they cut planning cost and avoid repeating past mistakes.
